lawyer:
Abdul Quayum with Mokbul Hossain and Swapan Kumar Dutta, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 
Syed Mokaddas Ali with Rowshan Ara Begum, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Shamsul Hoque and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Moze Ali Mollah and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
4. The plaintiff-opposite parties examined 4 PWs and the defendant-petitioners, on the other hand, examined 2 DWs in support of their respective case. During the trial the plaintiff-opposite parties proved and exhibited SA and RS Khatians and the defendant-petitioner filed and proved relevant documents showing that there was a mortgage suit and the suit land was subsequently purchased in auction-sale by them in execution of a mortgage decree by filing an execution case and got possession thereof. 

 6. On an appeal by the plaintiff-opposite parties the appellate Court below decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court only on point of law namely, that the order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in favour of the defendant-petitioners setting aside the entries in the SA Khatian was without jurisdiction and was thus liable to be set aside. 

 7. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners, submits that since the instant suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the trial Court rightly dismissed the same and the appellate Court below committed an error of law by decreeing the same when it was liable to be dismissed in limini. The learned Advocate elaborating his augment submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties had no locus standi to file the present suit inasmuch as they could not be said to have any legal character or right to property in respect of the suit land inasmuch as SA Khatian standing in their names had no presumptive value as regards proprietary right to the suit land. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff-opposite parties failed to seek any declaration as to their own status and also failed to pray for a further or consequential relief by way of possession. In support of his aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate referred to and relied on the cases reported in 18 DLR 706, to show that the plaintiff must have legal character or right to property, 6 BCR (AD) 57 showing that mere declaration in the absence of consequential relief is fatal, 42 DLR 24 and 13 DLR 676 showing that symbolical possession by defendant requires plaintiff to seek relief for recovery of possession. The learned Advocate also relied on the case reported in 19 DLR 9 in support of his contention that the SA Khatian does not give rise to any presumption of title to the suit land. 

 9. Admittedly, both the SA Khatians as well as RS Khatians in respect of the suit land stand in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names. It is true that the SA records, in view of section 19(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, do not provide conclusive evidence as regards title but it provides conclusive evidence as regards their preparation and revision. But entries in the SA records; in my opinion, provide a prima facie evidence as regards title. In order to maintain a suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff is required to have prima facie evidence showing that he has a legal character or right to a property in respect of the subject matter of the suit and granting or refusal to grant a decree in such suit shall always depend on final adjudication thereof on evidence. Since the SA records vide Exts 3 and 3(Ka) stand in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names it should be taken to be a prima facie evidence of title of the plaintiff-opposite parties in respect of the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite parties were competent to file the present suit. I do not dispute the legal principles deduced in the aforesaid cases cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. Since the present suit was not for a declaration of title but for a declaration of the act of the revenue authority namely, the order of mutation outside the purview of law as illegal the same is certainly maintainable. Reference may be made in this connection to the case reported in 16 DLR 298.

lawyer:
M. A. Aziz ------ For the Appellant

Syed  Shamsur Rahman ------ For Respondent
parties:
Shahabuddin & ors ------Appellant
Vs.
Saijuddin & ors ------Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the plot No. 1292 of khatian No. 66 and prayed for for injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with plaintiff's possession in the suit land on the allegation that the suit jote belonged to the father of plaintiff No. 1 and plaintiff No.2 in equal 8 annas share by inheritance which was sold to defendant No. 1 by two kabalas dated 29-1-37 and 3-5-38 respectively. But their sale deed did not include plot Nos. 1290 and which they got by exchange from one Jalaluddin and others prior to C.S. operation. They have been living there by erecting house and the defendant had not title and possession of the same that being so the defendant No. 1 had no right to lease out of the land. It was their further case the defendant No.1 on their asking leased out to them plot No. 1292 of khatian No. 66 and executed a patta on 28-2-45 as to plot No. 1292 and delivered possession to them and in the said patta defendant fraudulently inserted the plot No. 1290 and 1291 of Khatian 65 covering the area of 2'46 acres instead of plot No. 1292 which was agreed to be leased out by the registered patta. 

 3. The defendant's case is that plot No. 1292 which is the disputed plot including. plot of 1291 and 1304 of Khatian 65 belonged to Jalauddin and others in korfa under the jote recorded in khatian No. 63 in the name of Kalimuddin Shaikh. The Babus purchased the jote of khatian No. 65 but the said was subsequently purchased in auction by one Baru Bibi. It was the further case of the defendants that Baru Bibi after having gone into khas possession of the same sold it to one Saila Bala by registered kabala dated 11-8-38 and the said Saila Bala thereafter leased out to defendant no. 1 by a registered kabuliyat (Ext. C) dated 19-3-40 1'52 acres of plot no. 1290,1291 and 1261 and they had been in possession of the same by erecting Basa Bari on plot no. 1292. The further case of the defendant that the aforesaid lease was taken in the banami of his minor son and that he never leased out to the plaintiff at any point of time the plot bing no. 1292 and there was no talk of leasing out the same at the time of the patta dated 28-2-1945 and there was no fraudulent insertion also in the said Kabuliyat as alleged. The defendant's further case is that the plaintiff forcibly entered into his homestead in plot no. 1292 and erected huts there and are in possession thereof. The land has been rightly recorded in his name and the plaintiff has no case. 

 6. Mr. Syed Shamsur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents of the other hand has argued that the judgment and decree as passed by the learned Additional District Judge need not be interfered by this Court in appeal because the court in arriving at the finding that there was nothing to prove any fraud on record or mistaken description of the property inadvertently by the parties concerned it can not be said to be finding falling under proviso (1) to Section 92 of the Evidence Act and that being so plots described in a registered document being the terms of the contract cannot be varied by oral evidence between the parties and the document need be read as it is found written, expressing the intention of the  parties in executing the document. He further submits that there was no question of fraud or mistake in the case as the document clearly recited the plots to be plot nos. 1290, 1291 total area being 2'46, under khatian no 65. (and that being so plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 each is more than the area of 2'46 as in the disputed kabuliyat cannot be read into because in that case it will change not only the plot numbers but also the area of the land leased out and there cannot be mistake on both the counts and thus he submits that the court of the learned Additional District Judge was correct in holding that the plaintiff is not entitled to the relief sought for. Mr. Rahman, the Advocate argued also on the point of limitation. 

 7. In the instant case, the point for consideration is whether the terms of the document as to disposition of property, evidenced by the registered patta dated 28-2-45 executed by defendant no.2 purporting to lease out plot no. 1290 under khatian no. 65 of an area of 1'14 (Bastu) and an area of 1'32 of plot no. 1291 (Bilan) in total an area of 2'46 of land could be read as only plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 acres of land instead of 2'46 acres under khation no. 66 as urged by the plaintiff in the instant suit. There is no dispute that a patta of this nature dated 28-2-45 existed and there is also no dispute that plaintiff 1 and 2 did ask the defendant no.1 to lease out to them certain property on an agreed salami. What was disputed was that according to the plaintiff the said plot, agreed to be leased out by the defendant no. 1, was plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 decimals of land under khatian no 66 when according to the defendant it was plot no. 1290 and 1291 covering an area of 2'46 under khatian no.65 as it is in fact written so in the patta in black and white. 

 10. In the instant case however the question is whether there was any fraud in executing the document as alleged by the plaintiff or just a bonafide mistake without fraud calling for rectification. There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction and therefore he who alleges fraud or bad faith need to prove the same by leading evidence to the satisfaction of the Court as to the existence of a fraud which would invalidate the document itself to the extent of the fraud committed. It is again the settled principle of law that a finding of a court as to the existence of fraud or the non-existence of the same would be a question of fact and not a question of law. It would be a question of law if however it could be shown that in arriving at that conclusion, as to the existence of fraud or mistake of fact, a wrong inference was drawn by a non consideration of the evidence on record or by a misreading of the same, thereby, causing the wrong inference to be drown in coming to a wrong conclusion, as to fact. This could only also be shown by showing that there was a misreading of a document which is a title document, causing a wrong inference. In the instant case the dispute is related to Ext, 4, being the patta, dated 28-2-45 and it is the title document. On a reference to the said patta it is seen that the said document written in Bengali referred to plots no. 1290 of khatian no. 65 and not a plot under khatian no. 66 and the said plot is described to be 1'14 decimals and the nature of the land is described as Bastu. It also includes plot no. 1291 under khatian no.65 covering an area of 1'32 decimals and the nature of the land is described to be Bilan and the total area of the land leased out of those plots, is described to be 2'46 acres of land. Plaintiff claims this plot to be only plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 under khatian no. 66. So appears that the mistake as alleged by the plaintiff would refer not.only to the plot numbers but also to the area involved to a considerable extent. It 4 also change the khatian because plot no. 1290 a 1291 stands in khatian no. 65 and the area of the 2 plots in total is recorded in that khatian to he 2.55 decimals where according to the plaintiff plot 1292 would cover 2.86 acres. This is not a mistake of minor description but this is a mistake which in total in nature specially in view of the allegation I made by the plaintiff that plot no. 1290 and 1291 could not be taken from the defendant because those were their own properties from before the lease of their own property. This was not, thus. a mistake of fact as to description but a deliberate fraud committed by the defendant while inserting the plots already belonging to the plaintiff.. 

 12. In matters like this circumstantial evidence as to the subsequent dealing with the property would be also relevant in proving the conduct of the parties to the transaction, operating as an estoppel. It appears that the relevant khatian had long been recorded in the name of the defendant as to disputed-plot no. 1292. Is not in the name of the plaintiff and to his knowledge. There is noting on record also to show that the plaintiff had ever paid any rent to the defendant as their lessee as it would have been done if he was in fact a tenant, a lessee as to plot No. 1292. It is true that nonpayment rent alone will not extinguish or disprove a tenancy but when it is a question of the very existence of the status of a tenant payment of rent would be relevant as conduct subsequent of the parties concerned. It was the plaintiffs case that he came to know for the first time about the insertion of the wrong plot in the to at the time the lands were recorded in S.A. an in the name of the defendant, about 12 years after the document was duly executed and duly registered on 28-2-1945. What prompted the plaintiff to sleep all these years only to file the instant suit in the year 1969 to correct a mistake crept in a document registered in 1945. It is plaintiffs allegation that after the erroneous recording he has come to the court for a declaration of title by filing a suit in the year 1969 A.D. Of course, it is true, that the plaintiff will not be compelled to come to a court of law and file a suit for declaration that there was a wrong recording in the S.A. Khatian, immediately, after it was so recorded because he would be entitled to wait till his possession if any would be invaded and time would run from that date. in the instant case the court of appeal below found that as to that attempt of dispossession also there was no evidence on record to the effect that the plaintiff was threatened to be evicted from plot No.1292 by the defendant in Jaishta 1376 B.S. corresponding to 1969 A.D. So, the learned Court of appeal below found that there was neither a mistake of fact nor there was anything on record to show that any fraud was committed by defendant No. 1 upon the plaintiff in executing the kabuliat dated 28-2-45 which he was in fact seeking to rectify by this suit for declaration of title in the year 1969 which is more than 20 years after the alleged fraud. In that view of the matter the finding that there was no fraud or mistake in executing the document could not be said to have been arrived at by the learned Court of appeal below illegally. The said finding.of fact need not be disturbed by this Court in Second Appeal as there was no misreading of the patta or evidence by the courts below. 

 13. It is not a case of adverse possession and none fought out the suit on such an issue. Further, though an entry in khatian is not an evidence of title, it would be a prima facie evidence of possession. Possession is so recorded in the Government record in the name of defendant No. 1. and not in the name of the plaintiff. This the court of the first instance filed to take into consideration, as to the presumption of possession that would arises in favour of the defendant in view of the entry in the S.A. Khatian and the pleader Commissioner report has not rebutted the said presumption in proving, that the plaintiff was in possession of the instant homestead plot to the exclusion of the defendant. Further, a Pleader Commissioner's report is not binding upon the court. It is like any other evidence and need be considered in the light of the circumstances of each case.

lawyer:
Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, Mozammel Huq, Senior Advocates, Supreme Court, A Y Masihuzzaman, Advocate, Supreme Court, with him, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain. Advocate on Record -----For the Appellant.
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman and Mustafa Neaz Mohammed, Advocates, Supreme Court, with him instructed by B. C. Panday, Advocate on Record ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, being dead his heirs: -Amena Khatun and -----Respondents
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.- This appeal by special leave which arises out of a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The respondents filed application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the auction sale on 24-10-1973 in Certificate Case No 408 of 1967-1968 held by the Certificate Officer, Chittagong, for arrear rent dues from H E Percival, the recorded tenant, transferring land of P.S. Plot No. 108 of P.S. Khatian No. 14. The respondents claimed to be co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor by purchase of 1 kani 10 gondas of land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 appertaining to said Khatian No. 14, from H.E. Percival by registered kabala dated 29-12-1965 and their names were duly mutated in Khatian No. 14, which has been described in Schedule No. 2, which is part of Schedule 1 containing P.S. Khatians Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 owned by H.E. Percival in Mouza Kashim Bazar, P.S. Kotwali Chittagong, Their further case is that in the Oerti6cate Sale it was wrongly shown that P.S. Plot No. 108 appertained to P.S. Khatian No. 18 created after amalgamation and consolidation of the holdings held by H.E. Percival, because, such ambulation was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. The pre-emption case was contested by the pre-emptee contending inter alia that the pre-emptors though were co sharers of the P.S. Khatian No. 14, but they ceased to be co-sharers after the lands in different plots in Kbatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 in Mouza Kashim Bazar still owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one Khatian, namely Khatian No. 18 and the auction sale was held on the basis of the new Khatian No. 18, wherein they were not co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor. 

 2. The pre-emption case was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge and on appeal the learned District Judge. Chittagong allowed the pre-emption case in part and remanded the case to the trial Court for assessment of the cost of improvement in the case land. The appellant unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division in revision and thereafter obtained leave from this Court. Leave was granted to examine the question whether after creation of a new tenancy by amalgamation and consolidation of holdings the respondent pre-emptors could rightly claim to be co-sharers of the recorded tenant H.E. Percival. Leave was also granted to consider the question whether a person claiming to be co-sharer in the holding, and not in the land transferred, could validly, maintain an application for pre- emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings having been made by the Revenue Officer in due course of his official duties, it should be presumed that it was validly done and in accordance with law, besides it is not correct to say that a new tenancy in P.S Khatian No. 18 in the name of H.E. Percival as the sole owner was made in the absence of any written application by the recorded tenant H.E. Percival in this regard; and the order was made without giving any notice to the co-sharers of H.E, Percival. With reference to different documents on record the learned Counsel submitted that the record would show that the amalgamation proceeding was initiated at the instance of H. E. Percival. When Certificate Case No. 408/67-68 and six other Certificate Cases were started against H.E. Percival by the Certificate Officer Chittagong for realization or arrear rents, on 12-3-69, the certificate debtor filed an application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. in the aforesaid 7 Certificate Cases denying his liability for the huge arrear revenue dues on the grounds, inter alia that the lands of some of the khatians had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands bad been transferred by him to different persons; and praying for permission to pay the proportionate amount of the rent dues for him existing land in different khatians. On this application an order was passed by the Certificate Officer on 21-6-1973 directing the Tahsilder concerned for filing revised certificate on fresh assessment of correct rental dues, after amalgamation and consolidation of the lands in deferent khatians still in the possessions of H.E. Percival. The learned Counsel submitted that a regular case under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was started by the Revenue Officer concerned and as a result new khatian No. 18 solely in the name of H.E. Percival was created, and on the basis of this khatian revised certificate was filed. The learned Counsel further submitted that auction was held on the basis of this amalgamated newly created khatian No. 18 wherein the respondents not being co- sharer are not entitled to pre-empt the certificate sale 

 5. On perusal of the material on record it appears that admittedly the land of khatian No. 18 was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the pre-emptors were not co- sharers in the said khatian. H.E. Percival was a recorded tenant in respect of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, and for recovery of a huge arrear of rent in respect of those khatians Certificate Case Nos. 408, 109, 411, 412, 413 and 414 of 1967-68 were started. H.E. Percival filed an application under section 9 of Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 on 12-3-69 stating inter alia that he was not liable for the entire arrear rent dues, because some of the lands had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands had been transferred by him to different persons. He stated therein that he was prepared to pay the proportionate rent for the lands still in his possession. This application was duly signed by H.E. Percival. On this application, it appears from the order sheet that the relevant Revenue authority took certain actions on the direction of the Circle Officer (Revenue) and a proposal for consolidation and amalgamation of several holdings of H.E. Percival was submitted, and on the basis of this recommendation for amalgamation and consolidation the relevant Revenue Officer passed the order. From the Circular of the Board of Revenue dated 26-6-69 it appears that the district authorities were instructed to the effect that the work of amalgamation of holdings should be started in all the circles in the month of July and complete by the end of October, 1969. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, rightly pointed out with reference to the Circular that the amalgamation of the lands belonging to H E. Percival was not a solitary case, because, the process of amalgamation and consolidation had already been started in the district There is no doubt the action was taken at the instance of H.E. Percival, and it was taken up in this background Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for amalgamation, sub-division and consolidation of holdings. Section 116 provides that where various parcels of land are held by One tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue- officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. Section 117 provides the at notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue-officer may.- 

 (c)for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co- sharer tenants..................’' 

 Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for maintenance and revision of the record- of fights. Section 143 of the Act provides that the Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of rights prepared or revised under Part IV or under this Chapter by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 6. With reference to section 117 of the Act Khondkarm Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the entire proceedings and the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings as claimed by the appellant being not in accordance with Jaw, was illegal, and as such the new khatian 18 having no legal basis, it should be presumed that the khatians 14, 18, 20 and 24 continued to be the existing khatians and khatian 14 to which Plot No. 108 appertained, the respondents continued to be co-sharers of H.E. Percival in the said, holding, and it is not correct to say that H.E. Percival was the sole owner of Plot No. 108 without any co-sharer, He also argued that the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under section 116 of the Act was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. In the absence of any notice upon the co-sharers the alleged amalgamation and consolidation of holding is not tenable in law. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, however submitted by pointing out from the record that the noting in the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73 (under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act) sufficiently showed that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings of HE. Percival was made after the service of notice on all the parties concerned as per provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. In view of the circumstances as noted above, it would not be correct to say that the proceeding for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was initiated suo motu without having any basis. In the auction sale P.S. Plot No. 108 as appearing appertained to new P.S. Khatian No. 18 was sold. It is admitted that plot No. 108 previously appertained to khatian No. 14, and in its 16 annas belonged to H.E. Percival. So separation of plot No.108 from khatian No. 14 and its amalgamation in khatian No. 18, could not prejudice the pre-emptors who claimed to be a co- sharer in khatian No. 14 on the basis of their purchase from H.E. Percival. Apart from that there is a presumption under the law that all official acts are presumed to have been rightly and regularly done. 

 9. Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act deals with "Amalgamation Sub-division and Consolidation of holdings." Section 116 provides for amalgamation of holding of a tenant in the same village. This section requires that where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue-officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. This section however provides that if the tenant concerned has any objection thereto which appears to such officer to be reasonable and sufficient no such amalgamation shall be ordered by the Revenue-officer. Section 116 read with section 117(1) (a) provides that amalgamation and consolidation can be taken by the Revenue-officer, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf Section 17(1)(c) contains the provision for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof subject to the conditions indicated therein. On examining sections 116 and 117 Hind that the learned Judge of the High Court Division is completely in error in taking the view that it is a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy as provided under section 117(1)(c) for which an application was required to be filed; and in the absence of an application by the parties the Revenue officer had no authority of his own motion to sub-divide a joint tenancy. He was however conscious that "Amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of collection of revenue and for that purpose the Revenue-officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction." The relevant finding of the learned' Judge is quoted below: 

 "So I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate case before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be suo motu brought in the Miscellaneous case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer" 

 10. Khondkar	Mahbubuddin	Ahmed only faintly argued that as a matter of fact this was a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy. He however failed to give sufficient reasons in support of this view. Prior to amalgamation Khatian No. 14 contained plot Nos. 108, 107, 87 and 124; Khatian No. 20 contained Plot No. 116; and Kbatian No. 24 contained plots 117 and 121. By the process of amalgamation and consolidation Plot 108 of Khatian 14, plot 119 of khatian 18, plot 16 of khatian 20 and plots 117 and 121 of khatian 24 were amalgamated and consolidated into one khatian, that is khatian 18. This sufficiently shows that it was a case of amalgamation and consolidation as contemplated under section 116 read with section 117(1)(a) and not a case of sub-division of a tenancy recorded in kbatian 14, as provided in section 1l7(1)(c). The order of the Certificate officer who was also the Revenue Officer, shows that the action for amalgamation and consolidation was taken at the instance of the tenant when it was considered necessary for the purpose of collection of revenue. Plot 108 solely owned and possessed by H. E. Percival was amalgamated with Plot No. 119 of khatian 18 plot No. 116 of Khatian No. 20 and plot Nos. 117 and 121 of khatian 24 and thereby new khatian 18 was brought into being and a new jama was fixed for the amalgamated and consolidated khatian. Endorsement on khatian 14 filed by the respondents itself shows that separation of plot No. 108 from that khatian and its amalgamation to khatian 18 was noted on it. Payment of rent at the old rate even after the amalgamation and consolidation as claimed by the respondents cannot set at naught the process and the order of amalgamation and consolidation which was duly made and acted upon. The learned Subordinate Judge took the correct view on this question saying:- 

 “As there was no short payment it was accepted when the petitioners paid rent at the old rate. This payment of rent at the previous rate itself does not show that the amalgamation and separation of tenancy was not given effect to." 

 11. There is another point to be discussed which is that the learned District Judge as wen as the learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the so called amalgamation and consolidation of holdings suo motu and that too after death of H.E. Percival cannot be said to have any legal sanction and must be treated as a void one and need not be avoided. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury In support of his submissions that the order of amalgamation and consolidation was made in accordance with law, further submitted that when such an order has been passed by the competent authority and in accordance with law, its validity cannot be challenged in the pre-emption proceeding. In support of this proposition he relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Pakhal Chandra Mondal, 33 DLR (AD) 309. This is a case of separation of jam a under section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and not a case of amalgamation and consolidation, but the principle laid down therein provides the necessary guidance. In that case it has been held as follows:- 

 14. The land under pre-emption is plot No. 108 of Khatian No. 14 which belonged to one Percival. Khatian No. 14 consisted of three plots, Nos. 87, 107 and 108 and this Khatian, it is needless to say, constituted a non-agricultural holding under Percival. Respondent, pre-emptor purchased Plots Nos. 87 and 107 by a registered kabala dated 29 December 1965 and thereby became a co-sharer in the holding and in due course his name was mutated as Percival's co-sharer under a joint Jarna of Rs.4 and annas 7. Percival also held many other parcels of land such as in Khatians Nos. 18, 20 and 24, but the Respondent is not interested in those lands as he is not a co-sharer there. A Certificate Case being C.C. No. 408 of 1967-68 along with other such cases was filed against Percival for recovery of money due asarrear of rent under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 and this case was pending when he die in August, 1971. Two years five months after his death that is, on 24 December 1973, the appellant-pre-emptee, a stranger, auction purchased Plot No 108 along with other lands of Percival in connection with that Certificate Case. Respondent filed the pre-emption case on 15 April 1976, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act alleging that he had come to know of the sale for the first time on 3 January 1976. He further alleged in his application that by an inquiry be had ascertained that, for the purpose of avoiding pre-emption, the pre-emptee had, by collusion with the Revenue Officer, got a Mutation case, being Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73, started and thereby made a show of separation of Plot No. 108 from the joint tenancy under Khatian No. 14 and amalgamation of the separted hare with the other lands of late Percival, which were shown constipated as a new tenancy under Khatian N.18. Separation of this plot from the original holding having been made in total disregard of mandatory provisions of section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor alleged, the separation is void and not binding upon him and that he continued to be a co-sharer of the holding in Khatian No. 14. 

 15. The application for pre-emption was resisted on grounds of limitation and maintainability, particularly the latter. It was contended that "the separation and amalgamation" was effected by the Revenue Officer in accordance with law and that the Revenue Officer's order could not be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the pre-emption case. The trial Court accepted both the grounds and refused pre-emption holding the pre-emptor ceased to be a co. sharer in the holding since 24 April 1973 when plot No. 108 of Percival was validly separated from the original holding. But on appeal the learned District Judge reversed the findings on both the points and allowed the pre-eruption subject to payment of compensation for improvement of the land the amount of which was to be determined on remand after arriving at the findings that the Revenue Officer's order for separation of Percival's share was void in that the said order was passed by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion's and not upon any application from a co-sharer and that no notice of the 'Separation' was served upon the other co-sharer and further that the order was also acted upon as rent of the joint tenancy continued to be paid at the old rate. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not find anything to interfere with the District Judge's order in revision. 

 16. Leave was granted on both the grounds, limitation and maintainability, but the ground as to the limitation was not pressed. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants directed his arguments on the question of maintainability of the application for pre-emption contending that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in the holding since the separation of Percival's share and creation of a new tenancy comprising the separated portion and other lands of Percival. Mr. Chowdhury next contends that when the Record of the Revenue Officer prima facie shows the separation and amalgamation according to law, his order cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the instant one. Yes, if the original holding under Khatian No.14 were subdivided and plot No. 108 were separated therefrom according to law, then the pre-emptor got no case, as on sub-division of an original holding the former co-sharers cease to remain co-sharers with right to pre-emption. This is a settled law; reference. if at all necessary, may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Begum Asia Rahman, 26 D.L.R, (S.C ) 58, and the decision of this Court in the case of Mofizuddin Patwary; 33 D.L.R. (AD) 305. But the question is whether the alleged separation of Plot No. 108 from Khatian No. 14 was made in conformity with law and to determine this question to what extent a civil court can go into the matter in a collateral proceeding such as the one at hand. 

 17. It appears that some confusion has crept in during the bearing of this appeal because of using, in a loose sense, the terms "separation" and "amalgamation" of holdings. These are quite distinct things each having specific meaning and implication; and as such, these terms should be understood in their proper perspective. For this purpose section 116 and 117(a), 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which are relevant in this case, are quoted below: 

 "116. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subjects to separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy." 

 (c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable: 

 18. It appears clearly that 'amalgamation' means joining of various parcels of lands held by only one tenant so as to constitute one tenancy; and as such it is that tenant's problem alone. No other person, such as his co-sharer, is interested in it and that is why it may be ordered by the Revenue Officer either on his own motion or on an application made to him by the tenant; no notice of the amalgamation is required to be served upon anybody. Sub-division on the other hand, means physical division of a joint-tenancy as well as distribution of the rent thereof among the co-sharer tenants. Sub-division can be made by the Revenue Officer only on an "application made to him by one or" more co-sharer tenants". It shall not be ordered by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion". Secondly, notice of the sub-division shall be served upon all other co-sharers. Non-fulfillment either of these two requirements shall render the order of sub-division void. The term 'separation' is not a legal term like "amalgamation" or "sub-division"; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless it denotes in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy and as such 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117 Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding. A co-sharer after getting his share separated may get his portion constituted into a new tenancy or he may tag this share with his other land, if any, and if he does so, his case may be referred to as a case of 'separation and ‘amalgamation' for the sake of convenience though the two terms are quite different. His former co-sharers are not interested in such amalgamation. But whether amalgamation or not, for separation of a share from a joint tenancy the two mandatory provisions of clause (c) of section 117 must be first complied with. These provisions cannot be avoided or bypassed by saying that it is not a case of subdivision but it is 'separation and amalgamation'. An undivided share in a joint tenancy cannot be amalgamated with other independent holdings of a co-sharer without first getting his undivided share separated from the joint tenancy. This procedure shall apply even if he has applied for both in the same application. 'Amalgamation' cannot precede 'separation' as cart cannot be put before horse. It is the very case of the appellant that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in Khatian 14 from 24 April 1973 when plot 108 was" taken out and constituted into a new tenancy along with his other lands. If the original tenancy was not subdivided how the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer as the appellant claims? Revenue Officer's order shows that the original jama was also divided, out of Tk. 4.45 respondents jama was re-fixed at Tk. 2 55 and that of Percival at Tk. 1.90, which thereafter was added to the jama of the other holdings making his total jam a at Tk. 18.60 for the newly created separate tenancy under Khatian No. 18. This is subdivision pure and simple of the original holding under Khatian No.14. Again, whether a case attracts clause (c) depends upon its nature and implication and not upon how it has been described or designated by the Revenue Officer, The Revenue Officer took this case as 'separation and amalgamation'; but separation as shown above resulted necessarily in subdivision of the old tenancy. 'Separation' is synonymous with 'subdivision' under clause (c) of section 117 The argument that the original holding was not subdivided but was separated and amalgamated is self-defeating and self-contradictory. 

 20. 00 24 April 1973 the Circle Officer (Revenue) passed the final order on receipt of the Tahshilder's report allowing 'separation and amalgamation on the basis of his (Percival's' petition' The trial Court treated the carbon copy of the Certificate Debtor's objection petition as an application for separation of his share in the joint tenancy; but the lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division held that the unsigned carbon copy of an objection petition denying liability in a certificate proceeding under the Public Demands Recovery Act can, under no circumstances. be treated as an application for subdivision or separation of a joint tenancy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that objection petition, the Certificate debtor did not pray for 'separation or amalgamation' but expressed his readiness to pay the proportionate rent; the objection was filed in 1969 by Percival but he died in August 1971. This objection petition could not have been treated as an application for separation of his share in the joint holding two years after his death. Even if it is taken that Percival while filing the objection petition also intended the petition to be an application for separation of his share in his joint tenancies it abated on his death in 1971 whereupon his legal, representatives were not substituted. In the Certificate proceedings however his legal representatives were brought on record. From the proposal submitted by the Dealing Assistant and the order of the Revenue Officer starting the proceeding for separation and amalgamation, it is crystal clear that the Revenue Officer, whatever might have prompted him, had initiated the matter on his own motion. Had it been the case of mere amalgamation under clause (a) it would have been perfectly lawful. But this being a case of separation first, it comes well within the mischief of clause (c), and the 'separation' not having been made on an application it is void. 

 21. As to the contention about non service of notice-another mandatory provision for separation of the share-it is only the order-sheet of the Mutation case, which shows "notice duly served" Khandker Mahbubuddio Ahmed con- tends that the Record does not contain the. Service Return nor the name and address of Percival's co-sharer were stated in the carbon copy petition nor in any other document or paper of the Record and the Firisti of documents forming the record does not show any paper missing either. In these circumstances, the learned Counsel contends that prima facie this mandatory provision was not complied with by serving notice upon the respondent, The learned Counsel has in this connection relied upon a decision of this Court in the case Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatun, 33 D.L. R. (A D) 323, wherein if was held that the splitting,up of a joint tenancy effected behind the bat of a co-sharer was void. Mr. Harnidul Huq Chowdhury however, contends that the entry in the order-sheet of the Mutation Case made in usual course of official business is sufficient proof of prima facie service of notice and that in the proceeding for pre-emption the Court is not competent to go further into the matter to ascertain whether the notice the actually served in support of this contention the learned Counsel has referred to another decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. The purport of that decision is that when an order is passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act and the order is inconformity with the statutory requirements and the order has been given effect to by the co-sharer tenants of the holding the holding stands separated under law and.................the civil court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a court of appeal while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption", I do not find any conflict between these two decisions. The questions raised there related to prima facie compliance of mandatory provisions as to splitting up of a joint tenancy by a competent Revenue Officer and the scope of enquiry in a collateral proceeding. In one case the order for splitting up was found prima facie valid and in the other the order was not so found. These cases were decided on their respective facts and circumstances. In the instant case apart from the question of compliance with the two statutory requirements, there is the question of giving effect to the order for splitting up of joint jam a of Khatian No.14. Though Plot No. 108 was separated and constituted into a new tenancy with effect from 24 April 1973 as alleged by the appellant, the record or right was not amended accordingly until two years after the filing of this pre-emption case. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury relies upon Ext. R which is purportedly the amended Khatian No. 14 showing the splitting up of the joint tenancy between Percival and the respondent by an order of the Revenue Officer dated "28-1-67". But it also shows that this splitting up of the original jama was made on the basis of the Mutation Case. No. 89 of 1972-73. How the amendment was made six years before the filing of the Mutation Case its basis? Obviously, Ext. R bas been created for the purpose of this instant case and as such is not reliable. As to its rent it continued to be paid at the old rate of Tk. 4.45 till 1978. Tile trial Court is of course right in its observation that mere non-payment of rent at the new rate will not affect the splitting up; but this omission is a factor which must be considered when the question is whether the splitting up order was given effect to as against the consistent claim of the respondent that everything was done behind his knowledge in the Dame of a dead co-sharer. Facts of this case attract Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatunand not "Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal:" The order of Revenue Officer splitting up a joint-tenancy whichever way it may be designated if it serves the old relationship of its co-sharers and thereby destroys a co-sharer's statutory right of pre-emption, must be examined by the Court in a pre- emption proceeding in order to be satisfied that prima facie the order was passed in accordance with law, that is to say the mandatory provisions of section 117(c) were complied with on the face of the record. The scope of this examination cannot be so limited as to ask the Court to keep its eyes closed and to accept without hesitation whatever order is placed before it simply because the order was passed by a competent Revenue Officer. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the scope of enquiry in a case for pre-emption is wide enough to include the question of benami transaction in certain cases placing his reliance upon the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Nibaran Chandra Das 51 C.W.N. 644. In that case two long lines of cases, one line reo presenting the view that question of benami was outside the scope of s. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the other line representing the contrary view were elaborately discussed and considered and it was held that the question of benami transaction fell within the scope of s. 26F only in two classes of cases. In one class, the transfer is made to a co-sharer tenant in the benami of a stranger, and in the other class no transfer at all takes place but a show of transfer is made as in the case of plaintiff Nibaran. The suit was decreed and the order of pre-emption was declared void. 

 22. In the instant case it has been argued, the aggrieved co-sharer got proper remedy against the Revenue Officer's order by appeal. But his case is that the whole matter was manipulated after Percival's death and behind his knowledge and as such he got no opportunity to seek remedy by appeal. Be that as it may, on perusal of the records of the Miscellaneous case I find no difficulty to bold that the proceeding for separation of Plot No. 108 from Kbatian No. 14 was void ab initio as it was taken suo motu by the Revenue Officer and behind the co-sharer's knowledge and consequently the joint tenancy was Dot divided but it still continues and this being the position the pre-emption is a co-sharer in the holding having right to pre-emption. I find nothing to interfere with the order of the High Court Division which rightly confirmed that of the lower appellate Court. I would therefore dismiss the appeal' with costs.
justice_names: Mr. Justice F. K. M. Abdul Munim
Mr. Justice Chowdhury A.T. M. Masud

lawyer:
Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mahbubey Alam and Fida M. Kamal ----- For the petitioner. 
M. A. Muttalib ----- For the O. P. No. 1-7.
parties:
Jainuddin Howlader & others ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Nabab Ali Mollah & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the appellate decree in a suit for declaration of the plaintiff's title to 2.39 acres of land representing 8 annas share in the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 27 corresponding to R. S. Khatian No. 65 and S. A. Khatian No. 178 of Mouza Uttar Shubidkhali, under P.S Mrijagonj. The learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Patuakhali decreed the suit. On appeal the learned District Judge, Patuakhali reversed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif and dismissed the suit. 

 2. It is undisputed that 4.94 acres of land in 18 different plots recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 27 belonged to Dhalai and Arabdi in equal shares. The plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Arabdi. Defendant Nos. 1.6 are the successive heirs of Dhalai and defendant No. 7 is the heirs of one Mokim Mridha. The lands of the disputed holding with a diminished area of 4.78 acres have been recorded in both the R S. and S.A. Khatians in the names of defendants 1-6 who are heirs and successors of Montazuddin, son of Dhalai, as well as in the name of Mokim Mridha, predecessor-in-interest of defendant No. 7. The plaintiffs were unaware of the wrong recording until 1.12.76 when the defendants denied their interest on the basis of the wrong record. The plaintiffs claimed that they were in continuous possession of their 8 annas share in the suit properties by cultivating paddy and living on the homestead plot. 

 Only the defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement and denying the plaintiffs title and possession in the suit lands; He contends that Arabdi's son and only ultimate heir Tomiruddin mortgaged his 8 annas interest in the lands of the disputed khatian to one Nimchand Roy who in Mortgage Execution Case No. 117/18 auction purchased Tomiruddin's interest on 6.9 18 and took khas possession thereof on 13.4.1919. Thereafter he sold the interest under a registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 in favour of Dhalai who possessed the same. After the death of Dhalai his heirs and successive heirs including the defendants possessed the same. Ainuddin, a deceased grandson of Arabdi took settlement of .42 acres of land of the disputed holding for 12 years on payment of Tk. 50 as salami and at an annual rental of 9/- executing a registered kol karsha kabuliyat on 18.9.29 in favour of Montaruddin, son of Dhalai. The Kabuliyat was executed by Ainuddin on his own behalf and on behalf of plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2, then minors. This under-tenancy fell into arrears of rent and in Rent Execution Case No. 273/44 Montazuddin auction purchased the land and took delivery of possession thereof on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiffs and since then the defendants are in possession of the lands of the entire holding. 

 3. The plaintiffs examined 4 P.Ws. and the contesting defendant examined 3 D.Ws and exhibited several documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif on consideration of the oral evidence on record found that the plaintiffs were in possession of suit land. The learned District Judge, on the other hand, considered the exhibits filed by the contesting defendant showing that Nimchand Roy, the decree-holder auction purchased the 8 annas share of Tomiruddin, heir of Arabdi and also showing that he took delivery of possession through Court on 13.4.1919. He noticed the certified copy of the sale certificate. He also noticed the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 executed by Nimchand Roy in favour of Dhalai in respect of his auction purchased 8 annas share. The karsha kabuliyat executed by Ainuddin was also noticed by the learned District Judge. He also noticed the certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession of .42 acres of land on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2 and Ainuddin. The learned District Judge found that the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 and the registered kol karsha kabuliyat came from proper custody and the other documents were certified copies of Court documents. He then discussed the evidence of P.Ws. and found that they were not competent to say anything about the transactions of mortgage and auction sale taking place as far back as in 1918 and 1919. The learned District Judge also found that except for homestead plot No. 1388 the plaintiff's evidence on possession was not convincing On the other hand, the contesting defendant's evidence on possession was satisfactorily proved by the D.Ws., except with regard to homestead plot No. 1388 which, even according to D.W. 2, was in possession of the plaintiffs. The learned District Judge held that since the defendants' possession in at least 8 annas share of the disputed khatian is undisputed, the plaintiffs have the burden to prove that they possess the remaining 8 annas share in suit They have failed to prove the same, except that they are in possession of homestead plot No. 1388. The learned District Judge was also of the view that the plaintiffs have failed to rebut the presumption that the R.S. and S.A. records were correct. He, however, held that the suit was not barred by limitation. The learned District Justice set aside lodgment and decree of the learned munsif with the modification that the plaintiffs right, title and interest in plot no. 1388 in suit was declared and the suit was decreed to that extent only. Thereafter the plaintiffs obtained the present Rule. 

 4. Mr. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the court of appeal below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by approaching the suit from a wrong view of onus which has completely vitiated his findings. Mr. Ahmed submits that admittedly the C.S. Khatian record Arabdi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs as 8 annas co-sharer of the disputed khatian. If it is the case of the defendants that a mortgage, a mortgage execution case, an auction sale, a sale of the auction purchased land, a kol karsha kabuliyat of a part of the purchased land and finally a rent execution case in respect of the kabuliyat lands took place subsequent to the C.S. operation, the onus was on the contesting defendant not only to prove these subsequent developments but also conclusively to prove that after each alleged event the defendants predecessor had obtained actual physical possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. Instead, the learned District Judge has proceeded from the wrong standpoint that since till defendants are in possession of their 8 annas share, which is undisputed, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that they possessed the remaining 8 annas share in suit. It is this wrong view of onus which has prompted the court of appeal below to merely weigh on balance the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. on possession of the suit land except the homestead plot No. 1388. Had the learned District Judge approached the question from the right standpoint, namely, that it is for the contesting defendant to prove the transactions subsequent to C.S. operation as well as possession be would have looked into the evidence of actual physical possession of the predecessors of the defendants after each alleged event. He having not done so, Mr. Ahmed submits, the appeal should be re-heard by the appellate Court below keeping the question of onus uppermost in view. 

 5. It is true that the plaintiffs have based their claim on the simple proposition that they are the heirs and successors of the 8 annas recorded tenant in the C.S khatian The C.S. khatian supports their case. It is however the contesting defendant's case that several developments have taken place after the C.S. operation resulting in the transfer of ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi in the hands of the defendants predecessor. To prove that point, the defendants have filed a number of documents, as already stated, which have been believed by the Court of appeal below. The presumption of correctness of entry in the C.S. Khatian was never in doubt. The defendants also admit the correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian. The defendant’s documents have convinced the Court of appeal below that subsequent to the C.S. operation the defendants' predecessor acquired ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. What the Court of appeal below held in substance is that the latter developments after the C.S. operation have been proved by the contesting defendant. Under the circumstances, it is difficult to hold that the defendant has not discharged his onus to prove the subsequent developments.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 595 of 1963
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmed with A. Halim—For the appellant.
B. N. Chowdhury—For the respondent.
parties:
Meherjan Bibi ------- Appellant
Vs.
Naimuddin Dhali being dead, one of his heirs: Raisuddin Dhali and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
4. At the trial of the suit the plaintiff produced C S. Khatian Est. 1 showing that the suit land wan recorded in the name of Adam Munshi alone. It also shows that one Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord of the suit land. The concealing defendant No. 32 produced two Chittas Exts. B and B(I) prepared in 1883 in a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and one Amal Prasanna Bal and other by an Amin of the Collectorate in connection with partition of Touzi No 115 under the Estate Partition Act. The trial Court held that only parts of the suit land are covered by Chitta Dags in some of which Sada Dhali were found to be in possession with Abbas Dhali and in some with others. Only in some of the Chitta Dags, Sada Dhali was found to be in exclusive possession. The Trial Court held that under no circumstance could it be said that the suit land in their entirely belonged to Sada Dhali at any time; There were other interested persons also. Apparently, the trial Court held, three were great changes in possession. 

 5. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contended that the appellate Court below erred in coming to finding that Sada Dhali was the owner at the time of  reparation of CS record without there being any evidence on record to that effect. It erred in law in relying upon the Ext. B and B(I) which have got no relevance at all to the facts and circumstances of the case. Ext. 1 the CS khatian which was prepared some time in 1910 or 1911 shows that Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord and Adam Munshi alone was in possession of the suit land. Exts. B and B(I) were prepared in 1883 ie. about 30 years before the C. S. operation. In a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and Kamal Prosonna Bal and others. The defendant adduced no evidence to show that Jogesh Chakraborty was in any way connected with either Uma Sundar Debya or Kamal Prosonna Bal, Sada Dhali might have been in possession of some suit plots in 1893 under a different landlord but in the meanwhile with in the course of 30 years the superior landlord of the suit land changed and with the change of the landlord tenants also changed. There is no evidence at all that Sada Dhali continued to be in possession of the entire suit land for the next 30 years. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed submits that no evidence having been adduced by the defendant as to what happened in the meanwhile the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights stand unrebutted. 

 6.. Mr. B. N. Choudhury, the learned advocate for the respondent, has contended that the question whether the presumption as to correctness of entry in the record of rights has been rebutted or not is a question of fact and however erroneously the appellate Court below might have come to that finding of fact, it cannot be interfered with In a second appeal. He had cited several decisions to that effect. 

 "Merely because there Is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption is not rebutted to view of the provision of section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the other concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may go to show that the presumption has been rebutted”. 

 8. Yet, the appellate Court below merely because the plaintiff failed to produce any basis of the C.S Khatian held that Sada Dhali was in possession of at least 2 C.S. plots in respect of which the defendant did not file any Chitta papers. This finding cannot be sustained. For it is well settled, as has been held in the case of Aminuddin Biswas Vs, Miajan Biswas, reported in 12 D L R. 103. 'The presumption of correctness, as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it.". There was no evidence at all in respect of the said 2 plots that Sada Dhali was in possession even in 1883. In respect of the 10 remaining suit plots the appellate Court below in common with the trial Court held that in some plots Sada Dhali is found to be in exclusive possession and in some other plots he is found to be in Joint possession with Abbas Dhali and others. While the trial Court held that apparently there were great change in possession after the Chitta Dags were prepared, the appellate Court below without any further evidence on record came to hold that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land. It is no doubt well settled, contended by Mr B.N. Chowdhury that where evidence was led in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights and the appellate Court below comes to a finding that the preemption stands rebutted, that finding is final and cannot be interfered with in the second appellate jurisdiction. In all the decisions cited before me, namely, the case of Wali Mohammad and others Vs. Mohammad Bakhsh, reported in 51 C.L J. 518 Ghulam Mohammad Vs. Secretary of State reported in A.I.R 1938 (L) 445-and Charu Bala Rudra Vs. Narayan Prasad Sen reported in 14 DLR 159 the presumption was rebutted on the basis of relevant evidence on record. In the present case, however, the defendant had not adduced any evidence at all as to what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of C S. records or approximately earlier to that Mr. B N. Chowdhury submits that by producing Exts. B and B (I) the defendant has discharged the onus of proving that CS khatian has no basis. Thereafter, he argue, it is for the plaintiff to show that her predecessor in interest was in possession of the suit land at the relevant lime. It is difficult to agree with Mr. B.N Chowdhury. By adducing evidence of certain state of affairs 30 years back, how can it be said that the basis of C.S. khatian has been shaken? All that the attendant has produced in this case in the state of affairs relating to 10 out of 82 suit plots as far back as in 1883 which shows superior ownership and possession in the names of a different set of persons. How that evidence is evidence at all in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights is difficult to appreciate. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has failed to cite a tingle decision to show that evidence of such remote chamber has any bearing upon the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has cited the case of Maurabgi Tewari Vs. Kanhaiya Tewari reported In 123 IC 390 in support of his contention that when Chitta Dags and C.S. record show plan of two different persons it must be presumption that at some time between the two periods the person recorded In in the Chitta Dags lost their possession and that the person whose name appears in the C.S. khatian obtained possession, although there Is no presumption regarding the exact time at which the change of affairs took place. I entirely agree with the ratio decidendi of that decision.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 380 of 1965.
lawyer:
A.T. M. Kamrul Islam ------- For Appellant.
B.N. Chowdhury ------- For Respondent.
parties:
Osman Ali Talukder ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Sukumar Majumder  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants. The plaintiffs' case, in short is that the suit land was recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 160 of mouza Borai and the plaintiffs, by an amicable partition amongst themselves and pro-defendants, were possessing the same; that during the last c.s. operation Jasmat Sardar  was possessing the suit land as a barga darunder Girish Chandra and others, the plaintiffs predecessors, on delivering half of the produce of the land from year to year; and that during Jasmat Sardar's life time the land was taken and given borga bandabosta to others. As Jasmat was possessing the land as borgadar his name was wrongly recorded in the C.S. record as tenant paying borga rent though he was never recognized as a tenant by the plaintiffs' predecessors. Acting on rumors, that lands recorded in the names of bargadars paying half the produce as rent, had vested in the bargadar's ; defendants, 1, 2, and 3, got fraudulent kabala from Jasmat's daughters, defendants 4 and 5 and forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff's from the suit land in Baishak, 1364 B.S. and hence the suit. 

 6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725. 

 7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent has submitted that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right has been lost by passage of time, and that where it is on record that Jasmat Sardar  gave kabuliyat to the landlords as a borgadar before the preparation of the C.S. record and there is no other evidence that there had been any other agreement creating a tenancy in favor of Jasmat Sardar  the C.S. record must be held to have been wrongly prepared. 

 "that this proviso does not debar a person against whom a suit is now filed for recovery of a share of the crop as a bargadar, to set up the defense that he is not a bargadar but a tenant. In such a suit the presumption of correctness of the record of rights may also be invoked in aid as a circumstances supporting the defense but this will certainly not be a conclusive presumption. The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 -B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct stale of affairs on the elate that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section; but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof". 

 9. The C.S. Khatian recorded Jasmat Sardar  as a borgadar as well as a rayotisthitiban under Girish Chandra Majumdar and others at a rental of half of the produces inclusive of cess. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that Jasmat took borga settlement by a kabuliyat (Ext. 1) for a term of 7 years from 1321 B.S. and the preparatory works of C.S. operation started in the locality after 1327 B.S. and the record of rights was finally published in 1925 corresponding to 1332 B.S. He has observed that "it is quite likely that the settlement operation actually began at a stage when the term of the barga lease did not expire. It is, therefore, clear borga has been mentioned in the khatian. In the absence of any other stipulation between the parties Jasmat would be deemed to have continued in possession as a borgadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in section 116 of the T.P. Act and as enunciated in principle in section 51 B.T. Act". 

 10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has empathetically urged that a finding as to the rebuttal of a statutory presumption is a finding of a fact and cannot be challenged in second appeal. In support of his contention he has referred 10 Aminuddin Biswas Vs. Miajan Biswas, (1960) 12 DLR 103, CharuBalaRudra Vs. Narayan Prosad Sen(1962) 14 DLR 159 and Dabiruddin Molla Vs. Prem Dasi(1967) 19 DLR 371. 

 11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence. 

 13, In 1929 by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change with regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding the following provision to the definition of 'tenant' to section 3(17) of B,T. Act. 

 "It seems to us that the only change that the Legislature has labored to bring about is 10 lay down that; only in the first instance there will be a presumption 'that" a person holding under a system of adhi, barga or bhogis not a tenant, but this presumption will be rebutted only if it is established that he has been admitted by the landlord to be a tenant or is declared in a previous suit to be a tenant or if he can in a suit where this question is put in issue establish status as such tenant, In effect it seems that the Legislature has labored in in vain or worse avoided its responsibility and really thrown the burden upon the Court to resolve this question, for the net result appears, in substance, to leave the question where it was, apart from shifting the burden of proof on the tenant. To this extent possibly there has been a departure from the old principle." 

 “Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the 'record-or-rights, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of section l03(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records-of-rights. There mutbe further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may be to show that the presumption has been rebutted. " 

 The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this case, though relied on by the learned Munsif. For want of proper approach to the material question in the matter and non-appreciation of the evidence on the records particularly the evidence of the D.Ws. he has arrived at an erroneous decision. In the present case, apart from merely asserting that the C.S. Khatian was 'Wrongly recorded, the plaintiff did not adduce any other evidence in support of his contention. There was no averment that Jasmat continued to possess the land on the expiry of the terms of the kabuliyat on the same terms and conditions. In fact there is no mention of a borga kabuliyat in the plaint. On the other hand, defendant No.1, apart from relying on the C.S. record, produced Defendant 2, the Tahsildar of the landlords, who stated that at the time of C.S. operation he himself and another amin looked after the preparation of the C.S. record and the suit land belonged to Jasmat on payment of paddy lent to the landlords. This witness admitted the kabuliyat to be written in his hand. He further stated in cross-examination that he held some lands of the landlords as bargadar but his name was recorded as mere borgadar possessor with an entry in the rent column. 

 16. I, therefore, hold that the presumption of correctness of the C.S. record has not been rebutted in this case. The next question is whether the presumptive value of the C.S. record, under section 114 of the Evidence Act, has been destroyed in this case or whether its presumptive value is still available to defendant 1. 

 19. From the evidence on record it is clear that the predecessors of Defendant 1 never possessed the land as a bargadar of the plaintiffs and the defendant’s assertion that Jasmat and his heirs possessed the land in their own rights has been amply substantiated by the evidence on record. From Ext. 1it cannot be said, though contended by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, that the subsequent possession of Jasmat was one of a bargadar . I do not find any mention of the kabuliyat in the C.S. Khatian. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed, on a total misrepresentation of evidence on the record, that since Jasmat died 6/7 years back the sui t is within twelve years of possession through a recorded bargadar. From the evidence on record it is clear that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the institution of suit. The learned Munsif rightly dismissed the suit.

lawyer:
Rafiqur Rahman and Serajur Rahman------------For Petitioners. 
Nurul Haque Bhuiya-----------For opposite party No. 1.
parties:
Nayeb Ali and others ----------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Akhtar Rahman & others --------- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
2. The case was contested by the pre-emptee contending that the pre-emptors are strangers to the holding to which the land transferred appertains. The original jote recorded under C.S. khatian No. 21 was partitioned amongst the co-sharers and separate new jamas were created and the same were recorded in separate record of right. Opposite parties 17 and 18 claiming to be co-sharers to the holding by inheritance, prayed for pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record rejected the pre-emptor's claim for pre-emption holding inter alia, that the tenants ledger, the Register No. 11 and the new record-of-rights 37-40 indicate that 4 separate jamas were created by splitting up the jote recorded in C.S. khatian No. 21. The learned Munsif in that view of the matter, held that "the original jote under c.s. khatian No. 21 do no longer exist after conversion of it into 4 new jamas, the petitioners have no co-sharership to the case jote which falls within the ambit of record-of-right No. 40. The O. P. 1 has purchased from Khatejan in whose name stands the R.O.R. jote No. 40 and the case land also falls within that R.O.R." 

 4. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the learned Munsif and granted pre-emption in the following terms: "That the Misc. Appeal be allowed on contest with costs against the contesting respondents and exparte against the rest. The judgment of the learned Munsif is set aside. The petitioners are entitled to pre-emption along with O. P. 17 and 18". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the jote recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 21 continued to exist and that there was no splitting up of the jama ass contended by the pre-emptee. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the creation of the 4 R.O. R. No. 37-40" cannot be treated as a regular partition by metes and bounds". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the "presumption of jointness as recorded in C. S.
