Julfiquir Bulbul Chowdhury with Md. Shariful Islam, Advocates— For the Petitioners. 
Md. Ekramul Islam, Advocate—For Opposite party Nos. 1-13.
parties:
Younus Sonar alias Younus Ali Sonar and others ------- Petitioners
vs
Abdul Samad and others ------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, are that Ismail Sonar, the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-13, as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 155 of 1922 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Rajshahi against Gulzar Ali Sonar and others in which the present petitioner was defendant No. 34 praying for a decree of partition of 0.89 acre land claiming eight anna four gonda share upon deducting 0.07 acre land there from. The suit was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Charghat, Rajshahi and renumbered as Other Suit No. 46 of 1990. The case of the plaintiff is that 0.89 acre land as described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Emran Sonar in eight anna share, Jarimon Bibi in three anna four gonda share, Sabjan Bewa in sixteen gonda share and Kamani Bewa in four anna share and accordingly, CS Khatian No. 220 was prepared and finally published in their name. Sabjan Bewa died leaving behind one daughter Jamiron Bibi and husband Emran Sonar. Jamiron Bibi died leaving behind three sons Koshimuddin Sonar. Abdul Hamid, Abdul Kader and four daughters Sokina, Hamidon, Samina and Maleka (defendant No. 30). Abdul Kader died leaving behind five sons (defendant Nos. 12-16). one daughter (defendant No. 17) and one wife (defendant No. 18) as his heirs. Abdul Hamid died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 8-10) and one daughter (defendant No. 11). Kashimuddin Sonar died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 1-3), three daughters (defendant Nos. 4-6) and one wife (defendant No. 7). Hamidon died leaving behind two sons (defendant Nos. 22-23), one daughter (defendant No. 24) and husband (defendant No. 23). Sokina died leaving behind one son (defendant No. 19) and two daughters (defendant Nos. 20-21). Samina died leaving behind husband (defendant No. 25), one son (defendant No. 26) and two daughters (defendant No. 27-28). Kamani Bewa died leaving behind one son Abdus Shukur, who died leaving behind two daughters (defendant Nos. 31-32) and one wife (defendant No. 33). Thereafter, Emran Sonar died leaving behind one son, the plaintiff. In the aforesaid way the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share out of 0.89 acre suit land. The plaintiff has got his ancestral homestead in Plot No. 1912 and out of his share he sold 0.07 acre land of Plot No. 1873 to Sairuddin long ago who got his joma separated from the original jote by mutation and, as such, he was not impleaded in this suit. Said 0.07 acre land would be deducted from the share of the plaintiff. 

 6. Out of the defendants, only defendant No. 34 contested the suit by filing written statements contending that the suit was not maintainable, barred by limitation and there was no community of interest between the parties for partition of the suit property. The positive case of the defendant was that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their rayoti right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took pattan and paid rent to the landlords. The plaintiff took settlement of 0.23 acre land from the suit jote from Bashanto Kumar and erected dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 and RS Khatian No. 134 were prepared and finally published in his name. Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land out of the suit property along with other land measuring total 2.305 acre by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-5-1952 to Younus Sonar (defendant No. 34). While Younus Sonar was owning and possessing said 0.59 acre land from the suit jote separate SA Khatian No. 155 and RS Khatian No. 117 were prepared and finally published in his name. The plaintiff has no right, title to or interest in 0.59 acre land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 2. Though CS record was prepared and finally published in one Khatian but during SA and RS operation the land of CS Khatian was separated and three separate SA Khatians and three separate RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published out of which one SA Khatian and its corresponding RS khatian have been prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and two other separate SA Khatians and its two separate RS Khatinas have been prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff and, as such, the plaintiff is not a co-sharer of defendant No. 34. Moreover, in the plaint the plaintiff himself stated that defendant No. 34 was not a co-sharer in the suit holding. 

 6. Defendant No. 34 purchased 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land from Bashanto Kumar by registered sale deed dated 9-10-1952 following which separate SA and RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been paying rents to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government and has been possessing 0.59 acre land continually and uninterestedly from 1952 and, as such, defendant No. 34 acquired title therein by adverse possession and the right, title or interest, if any, of the CS recorded tenants have been extinguished and the plaintiff could not acquire title through CS recorded tenants. 

 4. Since 0.54 acre land of CS and SA Plot No. 1912 corresponding to RS Plot No. 4003 has not partitioned by metes and bounds, publication of said land in separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of plaintiff and defendant No. 34 did not cease their co-sharership and, as such, the par ties have community of interest in the suit property and the suit is maintainable. 

 12. Apart from adducing three oral witnesses the plaintiff produced CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1), the application of Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 (Exhibit-2), the judgment and order passed in the pre-emption case (Exhibit-3), certified copy of RS Khatian Nos. 117, 133 and 134 (Exhibits-4 series) and SA Khatian Nos. 156 and 157 (Exhibits-5 series). On the other hand, defendant No. 34 adduced three oral witnesses and also produced Jamindary rent receipt (Exhibit-Ka), the rent receipt showing payment of rent by Emran Sonar to Bashanto Kumar (Exhibit-Kha series), rent receipts showing payment of rent by Ismail Sonar (Exhibit-Ga series), one pattani receipt (Exhibit-Gha), twelve rent receipts showing payment of rent to the Government (Exhibit-Uma series), the original sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha), certified copy of SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha), certified copy of RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja), order passed in a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and application filed therein (Exhibits-Jha and Neo). 

 13. Admittedly, 0.89 acre land appertaining to 0.07 acre of CS Plot No. 1873, 0.28 acre of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre of CS Plot No. 1912 belonged to the father of the plaintiff in eight anna share and three others in eight anna share as CS Khatian was duly published in their name which has been proved by certified copy of CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1). The plaintiff claimed eight anna four gonda share after deducting 0.07 acre land out of total 0.89 acre land of CS Khatian No. 220. His case is that his father Emran Sonar had eight anna share in the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) and he also inherited four gonda share from his wife Sobjan Bewa and after his death the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share from the suit jote. The plaintiff also claimed title to 0.26 acre land on the basis of judgment dated 27-6-1979 passed in Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 and to prove the judgment, he produced its certified copy (Exhibit-3). On the contrary, defendant No. 34 contended that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their raiyoti right to the superior landlords and after surrender, Bashanto Kumar took settlement and paid rent to the landlords and thereafter, Ismail Sonar (the plaintiff) took settlement of 0.23 acre land from Bashanto Kumar and constructed dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 [Exhibit-5 (Ka)] and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4(Kha)] were prepared and finally published in his name. His further contention is that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land along with other land to him by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) and thereafter, separate SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Cha) and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 [Exhibit-Ja (4)] have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been owning and possessing the same uninterruptedly, on payment of rent for more than 12 years. 

 15. PW2 Abdus Sattar, deposed in support of the case of the plaintiff, stated in his cross-examination that the plaintiff possesses 14/15 decimal land. Upon Evaluation of the evidence of the PWs, the trial Court held that the PWs could not prove the case of the plaintiff rather, they deposed adversely to the plaintiff and admitted that defendant No. 34 had possession in the suit land and that the plaintiff could not adduce any evidence to show that defendant No. 34 was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff or his predecessor. The trial Court finally came to conclusion that the plaintiff could not prove his claim. However, the trial Court found title to and possession in 0.23 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of the plaintiff as per admission of the defendant No. 34. The Court of appeal, it appears that, did not discuss oral or documentary evidence of the parties independently but concurred with the findings of the trial Court. The plaintiff did not challenge the adverse findings of the Courts below by preferring any appeal before higher forum. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that he accepted the findings and decision of the courts below that he acquired title to 0.23 acre land as per admission of defendant No. 34 and that the CS recorded tenants including the father of the plaintiff surrendered tenancy right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took settlement afresh and then settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and on the basis of such settlement SA Khatian No. 157 and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 were rightly prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff in respect of 0.23 acre land and that the plaintiff could not prove permissive possession of defendant No. 34. 

 19. In this case, it appears that the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government. But without giving any finding in regards acquisition of title to 0.59 acre land by defendant No. 34, the trial Court erroneously held that the plaintiff would get saham of 0.26 acre land from CS Plot No. 1911 as per judgment of Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1970. The Court of appeal committed the same error and illegally allotted 0.26 acre land. 

 21. As mentioned earlier, the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) produced by defendant No. 34 observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government which has been upheld by the Court of appeal. Defendant No. 34 produced original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) from which it appears that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34. This sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is more or less admitted by the plaintiff in the way that Bashanto Kumar had no saleable interest to transfer said 0.59 acre land to defendant No. 34 because he was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff. But both the Courts below as well as the Court who passed judgment in the pre-emption case found that the plaintiff or the petitioner in the pre-emption case could not prove the fact of permissive possession. Moreover, sale deed dated 9-10-1952 was attained 30 years of age at the date when it was tendered to evidence on 23-9-1997, original "of which was produced from proper custody and, as such, as per section 90 of the Evidence Act it is to be presumed as genuine document and that the signature and every other part of the document is genuine. As per section 92 of the Evidence Act oral or extraneous evidence to contradict the terms of contents of a document is inadmissible. However, the plaintiff did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence to prove that Exhibit-Cha was a product of forgery. As per recital of sale deed dated 9-10-1952, Bashanto Kumar was a tenant of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 under Putia Jaminder of Rajshahi. The plaintiff was under-tenant from Bashanto Kumar in respect of 0.23 acre land out of 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 and Bashanto Kumar transferred entire land of his khas possession and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 and handed over possession of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.31 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of defendant No. 34. Since sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is an old document of avove 30 years, as per section 90 read with section 91 of the Evidence Act, the recital of the deed dated 9-10-1952 are presumed to be correct. Moreover, during SA operation said 0.59 acre land was recorded in the name of defendant No. 34 in SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit Cha) and 0.23 acre land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff in separate SA Khatian No. 157 (Exhibit-5 Ka) and thereafter, their corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 ( Exhibit-Ja) in respect of 0.59 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4 (Kha)] in respect of 0.23 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff. Moreover, the courts below found that defendant No. 34 paid rent to the Jaminder and Government. The above facts lead to irresistible presumption that the sale deed dated 9-10-1952 has been acted upon. The plaintiff could not produce any evidence to discard the such presumption. 

 22. Considering the evidences of the parties, it is evident that though total 0.89 acre land was recorded in CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) in the name of Emran Sonar, the father of the plaintiff and others, as tenant under superior landlords but subsequently, Bashanto Kumar became tenant of 0.89 acre land under the superior landlords out of which he settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and thus the plaintiff became under-tenant under Basanto Kumar and then Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land under his khas possession along with rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 following which separate SA and RS khatians were prepared and finally published in their respective names and defendant No. 34 acquired title to 0.59 acre land and the plaintiff acquired title to 0.23 acre land. 

 24. The suit property is an agricultural land and that the defendant No. 34 is a stranger purchaser to the suit holdings and the tenancy of CS Khatian in respect of the suit holdings has been separated by preparation and publication of three sets of separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of the plaintiff and defendant No. 34. Accordingly, the plaintiff and defendant No. 34 are not co-sharers of the suit holdings. Moreover, in one part of the plaint, the plaintiff asserted that he has no community of interest with defendant No. 34 and in other part, he stated that cause of action of the suit arose in the event of pronouncement of judgment in the pre-emption case. Accordingly, the plea of the plaintiff is self contradictory leading to no cause of action for filing this suit. In view of the above, question of community of interest between the parties does not arise at all and the present suit for recovery of khas possession in the guise of suit for partition is not maintainable.

full_judgment:
9. The learned Senior Advocate Mr S.M. Shahjahan appearing along with learned Advocate Mr Md. Jahangir Hossain on behalf of respondent No. 2 submits that there is a presumption under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 that drawer of the cheque issued the cheque in favour of the complainant for consideration and admittedly the appellant signed the cheque which proved that the appellant issued the cheque in favour of the complainant for payment of the debt. Therefore, he committed an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He also cited a decision made in the case of Syed Anowar Towhid vs Tayobbi vs Syed Zahid Ali and another reported in 13 BLC(2008) 428. 

 10. The issue involves in the instant appeal whether the complainant proved ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and whether the appellant rebutted the presumption under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 13. The presumption of innocence was subsequently expressed by the French cardinal and canonical jurist Jean Lemoine, the first canon lawyer, to formulate the legal principle of the presumption of innocence in the phrase "item quilbet presumitur innocens nisi probetur nocens (a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty)", based on the legal inference that most people are not criminals. It requires that the trier of fact, be it a juror or judge, begin with the presumption that the state is unable to support its assertion.[Words and phrases, 1914, P.1168]. “To ensure this legal protection is maintained, a set of three related rules govern the procedure of criminal trials. The presumption means: 

 15. Although the Constitution of the United States of America does not cite it explicitly, the presumption of innocence is widely held to be followed from the Fifth, Sixth, and Fourteenth Amendments. Coffin v. United States, 156 U.S. 432 (1895) was an appeal case before the Supreme Court of the United States in 1895 which added the principle that the accused is presumed to be innocent until his guilt is proved beyond a reasonable doubt. In the referred case, The Supreme Court of America has held that- 

 “Now the presumption of innocence is a conclusion drawn by the law in favor of the citizen, by virtue whereof, when brought to trial upon a criminal charge, he must be acquitted unless he is proven to be guilty. In other words, this presumption is an instrument of proof created by the law in favour of one accused, whereby his innocence is established until sufficient evidence is introduced to overcome the proof which the law has created. This presumption on the one hand, supplemented by any other evidence he may adduce, and the evidence against him on the other, constitute the elements from which the legal conclusion of his guilt or innocence is to be drawn. The fact that the presumption of innocence is recognized as a presumption of law and is characterized by civilians as a presumptio juris, demonstrates that it is evidence in favor of the accused. For in all systems of law legal presumptions are treated as evidence giving rise to resulting proof to the full extent of their legal efficacy.” 

 17. Negotiable Instruments Act.1881 is a special law. An offence under Section 138 is not compoundable and before filing a case the drawer and the drawee of the cheque are at liberty to make a compromise between them. Since an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not compoundable, after filing the complaint petition, there is no scope to settle the dispute out of Court. An offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 is a pure and simple criminal offence. Therefore, the age-old principle that the accused is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty beyond all reasonable doubt is required to be proved by the complainant based on clear, cogent, credible or unimpeachable evidence. The presumption of innocence is a fundamental right of the accused. An accused has a constitutional right to remain silent. The presumption of innocence itself is evidence in favour of an accused. 

 18. In P. Ramanatha Aiyar's Advanced Law Lexicon, 3rd edition, at page 3697, the term 'presumption' has been defined as under: 

 "A presumption is an inference as to the existence of a fact not actually known arising from its connection with another which is known. 

 A presumption is a conclusion drawn from the proof of facts or circumstances and stands as establishing facts until overcome by contrary proof. 

 A presumption is a probable consequence drawn from facts (either certain, or proved by direct testimony) as to the truth of a fact alleged but of which there is no direct proof. It follows, therefore that a presumption of any fact is an inference of that fact from others that are known". (per ABBOTT, C.J., R. v. Burdett, 4 B. & Ald, 161). The word 'Presumption' inherently imports an act of reasoning- a conclusion of the judgment; and it is applied to denote such facts or moral phenomena, as from experience we know to be invariably, or commonly, connected with some other related facts. (Wills on Circumstantial Evidence). 

 A presumption is a probable inference which common sense draws from circumstances usually occurring in such cases. The slightest presumption is of the nature of probability, and there are almost infinite shades from slight probability to the highest moral certainty. A presumption, strictly speaking. results from a previously known and ascertained connection between the presumed fact and the fact from which the inference is made." 

 19. By Act No. XVII of 2000 the legislature repealed section 139 and amended Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 by repealing the words and commas i.e. “for the discharge in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability” without making any amendment in Section 43 of the said Act wherein it has been stated that a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails, creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction. Therefore, because of the provision of Section 43 of the said Act a person who issued a cheque without consideration has no obligation to pay the cheque amount. The presumption under section 118 (a) of the said Act is not conclusive proof of the fact that the drawer issued a cheque in favour of the drawee for payment of the consideration. When the accused cross-examined P.Ws. and examined himself as D.W. denying the issuance of the cheque in favour of the complainant and make out a probable deference case, heavy-duty lies on the complainant to prove the consideration for which the cheque was issued in favour of the drawee. In the complaint petition, it has been stated that the complainant paid Tk. 500000 to the appellant in cash as a loan but no date of payment of loan has been mentioned in the complaint petition. It is further stated that after due date, the complainant went to t he house of appellant to get back the money without mentioning any date, but no evidence has been adduced to that effect. The burden of proof that a cheque had not been issued for consideration is on the accused. If the accused failed to discharge the onus lies on him it is to be presumed that he issued the cheque for consideration. However, the Court will not insist upon the accused to disprove the existence of consideration by adducing direct evidence. 

 25. In Section 4 of the Evidence Act, 1872 three classes of presumption have been mentioned namely (i) may presume (refutable), (ii) shall presume (also refutable) and conclusive presumption (irrefutable). To refute the statutory presumption under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 an accused is not required to prove his defence case beyond all reasonable doubt as required by the complainant in a criminal case. An accused may either adduce direct evidence to show that the cheque is not supported by consideration as required under Section 43 of the said Act or by cross-examining the witness/witnesses he is entitled to show that the cheque was issued without consideration. The accused may also rely on circumstantial evidence or Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872. 

 26. In Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the legislature used the words “until the contrary is proved”. A bare reading of Section 118(a) of the said Act makes it clear that presumptions to be raised under the said section is discretionary and refutable. The accused has to make out a probable case that the cheque has been issued without consideration or for a consideration which fails. The complainant is bound to prove all relevant facts stated in the complainant petition. In the complainant petition, it has been stated that he paid Tk. 500000 to the accused as a loan. No evidence has been adduced to prove said loan or consideration as required under Section 43 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881. 

 28. In determining whether a reverse burden is compatible with the presumption of innocence regard should also be had to the pragmatics of proof. How difficult would it be for the prosecution to prove guilt without the reverse burden? How easily could an innocent defendant discharge the reverse burden? But courts will not allow these pragmatic considerations to override the legitimate rights of the defendant. Pragmatism will have greater sway where the reverse burden would not pose the risk of great injustice Where the offence is not too serious or the reverse burden only concerns a matter incidental to guilt. And greater weight will be given to prosecutorial efficiency in the regulatory environment. Presumption of Innocence and Reverse Burdens: A Balancing Duty, by David Khamer published in [2007] C.L.J. (March Part) 142 

 29. The presumption is a rule of evidence and does not conflict with the innocence of the accused. The presumption of innocence of accused is a legal presumption. The duty of the prosecution may be discharged with the help of the presumption of law or fact or with both unless the accused adduces evidence to show the reasonable possibility of the non-existence of the presumption. A fact is said to be proved, when, after considering the matters before it, the Court either believes it to exist or considers its existence so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that it exists. 

 Upon consideration of various judgments as noted hereinabove, the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted, the presumption under Section 118(a) would arise that it is supported by consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttable. The defendant can prove the non-existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the defendant is proved to have discharged the initial onus of proof showing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the plaintiff who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the defendant of proving the non-existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In such an event, the plaintiff is entitled under law to rely upon all the evidence led in the case including that of the plaintiff as well. In case, where the defendant fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non-existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) in his favour. The court may not insist upon the defendant to disprove the existence of consideration by leading direct evidence as the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated and even if led, is to be seen with a doubt. 

 32. The nature and extent of presumption came up for consideration before the Supreme of India Court in M.S. Narayana Menon v. State of Kerala' Judgment dated 4.7.2006, Criminal Appeal No. 1012 of 1999 para 30 wherein it has been held that; 

 “Applying the said definitions of 'proved' or 'disproved' to the principle behind Section 118(a) of the Act, the court shall presume a negotiable instrument to be for consideration unless and until after considering the matter before it, it either believes that the consideration does not exist or considers the non-existence of the consideration so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that the consideration does not exist. For rebutting such presumption, what is needed is to raise a probable defence. Even for the said purpose, the evidence adduced on behalf of the complainant could be relied upon." 

 “A statutory presumption has an evidentiary value. The question as to whether the presumption whether stood rebutted or not, must, therefore, be determined keeping in view the other evidences on record. For the said purpose, stepping into the witness box by the appellant is not imperative. In a case of this nature, where the chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration. Presumptions are rules of evidence and do not conflict with the presumption of innocence, because by the latter, all that is meant is that the prosecution is obliged to prove the case against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt The obligation on the prosecution may be discharged with the help of presumptions of law or fact unless the accused adduces evidence showing the reasonable possibility of the non-existence of the presumed fact.” 

 “The Act contains provisions raising presumption as regards the negotiable instruments under Section 118(a) of the Act as also under Section 139 thereof. The said presumptions are rebuttable ones. Whether the presumption stood rebutted or not would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.” 

 “When a presumption is rebuttable, it only points out that the party on whom lies the duty of going forward with evidence, on the fact presumed and when that party has produced evidence fairly and reasonably tending to show that the real fact is not as presumed, the purpose of the presumption is over. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the cheque in question was not supported by consideration. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of consideration apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something, which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. The burden of proof of the accused to disprove the presumption under sections 118 and 138 of the Act is not so heavy. The preponderance of probability through direct or substantial evidence is sufficient enough to shift the onus to the complainant. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn from the materials on record and also by reference to the circumstances upon which the party relies.” 

 36. The presumption under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is always rebutable and the standard of proof of doing so is that of the preponderance of probabilities. The accused either adducing evidence or by cross-examining the PWs are entitled to rebut the said presumption. The accused is not bound to prove his innocence by adducing evidence. A negative fact cannot be proved by adducing positive evidence. The issue as to whether the presumption stood rebutted or not must be determined based on the evidence adduced by the parties. In a case under Section 138, the false implication cannot be ruled out. Therefore, the Court shall not put on a blind eye to the ground realities. In that case, the background of the case and the conduct of the parties are required to be taken into consideration. No explanation has been given by the complainant as to why no instrument was executed between the parties although handsome money was claimed to have been paid to the appellant. 

 37. Although there is a presumption under section 118(a) of the said Act as regards the payment of consideration in favour of the payee but section 118(a) of the said Act does not absolve the complainant to prove other requirements of the law. D.W. 1 in the examination of chief stated that “নালিশকারী বা তার প্রতিষ্ঠানকে আমি কোন চেক দেয়নি। চেকের স্বাক্ষর ব্যতীত অন্যান্য লেখা আমার হাতের নয়।” The above statement of D.W. 1 has not been denied by the complainant during cross-examination. When a cheque is issued by any person in favour of any other private individual without mentioning the name of the payee and date of issuance of the cheque, a doubt creates as regards the actual payee of the cheque, if there is no debt or any liability to be discharged by the accused. Admittedly the appellant did not mention the name of the payee and the date in the cheque. During cross-examination no suggestion was given to D.W. 1 that he has written the name of the complainant as a payee in the cheque. Therefore, it is to be presumed that the complainant himself or somebody on his behalf has written the name of the complainant as a payee in the cheque. 

 38. It is found that the complainant is neither friend nor he had any business transaction with the appellant. The complainant has failed to prove that the appellant has taken a loan from him. On consideration of the evidence of both parties in a juxtaposition, I am of the view that the appellant has rebutted the presumption under sections 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 188. Therefore, there was no reason for the issuance of cheque by the appellant in favour of the complainant.

Surojit Bhattacharjee with Farhana Siraj Ronnie, Advocate—For the Petitioners in both Civil Revisions.

parties:
Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigraha, Hasanpara (Bazarhat), Dhaperhat and another ------ Petitioner
vs
Shree Pravat Chandra Adhikary and anothers ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
5. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that before immemorial time, Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Deity was installed on the land of CS Khatian Nos. 175 and 176 and after the promulgation of permanent settlement the said property came under the Zamindari of Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury and the said Zamindar was appointed Sebait. The homestead of Mahendra Ranjan was far from the Deity for which Puma Chandra Adhikary was appointed Pujari. Accordingly, CS Khatian was prepared and published in the name of Pujari Puma Chandra Adhikary under Sebait Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury. A total of 1.19 acres of land is Debutter property but not private property and there is no personal right, interest or possession over the suit property. The temple is situated on plot No.70, which was used and enjoyed by the Hindu people at large and the usufructs of the other lands are used for the Puja of the Deity. Pujari Puma Chandra Adhikary was permitted to live in 05 decimals of the land of plot No.69, Pujari Puma Chandra Adhikary subsequently left the temple premises for the village Kadimnagar and was appointed Sebait of Shree Shree Gopal Giridhary Jew Deity in the said village Kadimnagar and defendant Nos.1-3 were born therein. In the meantime, the local people carried out the Puja of the Deity in suit through various pujaris. But subsequently, defendant No.1 came back, and the Puja Committee again appointed him Pujari and he used to live in the said 05 decimals of the land of plot No.69, The Government acquired 08 decimals of land from plot No.69 while the plaintiff erected 10 shops on the rest 09 decimals of land of the said plot No.69 and rented it to various persons by which the expenditure of the puja is met up. The SA record was wrongly prepared and published in the name of Pujari Puma Chandra Adhikari and because of that wrong record, the defendants illegally created Deed of Gift Nos. 6704 and 1657 dated 16-11-1996 and 25-2-1998 respectively in favour of the Deity and defendant No.4. By the said wrong records-of-rights and illegal Deeds of Gift, the title of the plaintiff has been clouded and hence the suit. 

 6. Defendant Nos.1-4 contested the said suit by filing a written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and contending inter alia, that the suit property belonged to Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury. He appointed Puma Chandra Adhikary as the 'Purohit' in his house. As the consideration for his religious service Raja Mahendra Ranjan gave him nishkar pattan of 1.19 acres of land of CS Khatian No.176 for permanently residing therein as well as for maintenance of his livelihood. Accordingly, the said land described in Schedule 'Kha' was recorded in his name in CS Khatian No.176. He possessed 22 decimals of the land of Plot No.69 by making a homestead thereon, by performing religious rites towards the Deity established in the land of Plot No.70 and by cultivating 91 decimals of the land of Plot No.67. RS Khatian No.188 was duly published in his name. At the request of the people in general belonging to the Hindu Religion, Puma Chandra dedicated, by registered Deed of Gift No.6704 dated 6-11-1996, 32 decimals of land from Plot No.67 and 52 decimals from Plot No.91 to the Radha-Gobinda Deity. He died leaving behind his three sons namely, Prabhat, Ashutosh and Shachin. Shachin and Ashutosh gifted their share to defendant No.4 by registered Deed of Gift No.1657 dated 25-2-1998. The defendants have title and possession over the 'Ka' schedule land. The defendants have been possessing the shops established in the suit land and also filed Other Suit No.110 of 2002 for a decree of permanent injunction as the plaintiff threatened to forcibly dispossess them from the suit property. The plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit land and hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 13. Having placed the Civil Revision, Mr. Surojit Bhattacharjee along with Ms. Farhana Siraj Ronnie, learned Advocate for the petitioner in both the Civil Revisions submits that both the Courts below concurrently erred in law and facts as to that as per CS Khatian No.176, admittedly the suit property along with the entire property appertaining to that CS Khatian No.176 belonged to the Deity, Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigraha and the predecessor of the defendants in Other Suit No.49 of 2003 and the plaintiffs of Other Class Suit No.110 of 2002 was the Purohit of the Deity and, as such„ they cannot claim the property as the personal property of their predecessor. Both the Courts below again concurrently committed errors of law resulting in errors in the decision occasioning failure of justice by failing to consider that once the Debutter property, it cannot be claimed as personal property and, as such„ the subsequent records-of-rights such as SA and BRS Khatian prepared in their names have no legal basis and similarly, the subsequent transfer based on such wrong recording has also no legal effect. 

 14. On the other hand, Mr. Subrata Chowdhury along with Mr. Rabin Chandra Paul, learned Advocate for the opposite parties in both the Civil Revisions submits that as per the CS Khatian No.176, the property was under the control and management of the Courts of Wards and the predecessor of the opposite parties were tenant as Chakran Purohit. Accordingly, both the Courts below rightly found title in favour of the predecessor of the opposite parties as well as in favour of the opposite parties themselves and thus, there being no legal infirmity in the concurrent findings and observations of the Courts below, both the Rules are liable to be discharged. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further submits that since the predecessor of the opposite parties acquired title based on the CS Khatian, the property was rightly recorded in the SA and BRS Khatian in their names and accordingly, they had also the transferable interest by executing the said Deed of No.1657 dated 25-2-1998 and thus, again there being no legal infirmity and illegality in the concurrent findings and observations of both the Courts below, both the Rules are liable to be discharged. 

 16. It appears that both the parties claimed their respective titles based on CS Khatian No.176, which has been marked as exhibit 1(Ka) on behalf of the plaintiff of Other Suit No.49 of 2003 and as exhibit 'Ka' on behalf of the plaintiff of Other Suit No.110 of 2002. The plaintiff of Other Suit No.49 of 2003 also submitted CS Khatian No.175, which has been marked as exhibit 1. As per the case of the plaintiff of Other Suit No.49 of 2003 and defendants of Other Class Suit No.110 of 2002, the entire properties appertaining to CS Khatian Nos. 175 and 176 belonged to the Deity namely, Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigrah, which was within the zamindari of Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury, and he appointed himself as the Sebait of the Deity. As per CS Khatian No.176, the Sebait of the Deity was the superior landlord and the name of the predecessor of the defendants of Other Suit No.49 of 2003 and plaintiff of Other Class Suit No.110 of 2002 was recorded as the Purohit of the Deity and, as such, no personal title was created in favour of the predecessor of the opposite parties. On the other hand, it is the case of the opposite parties that their predecessor was the Chakran Purohit of 1.19 acres of land appertaining to CS Khatian No.176 and, as such, he acquired personal title therein. Both the Courts below found that the property personally belonged to the predecessor of the opposite parties. 

 17. I have meticulously perused and analysed the said CS Khatian Nos. 175 and 176. It appears from CS Khatian No.175 that the superior landlord of the land measuring 1.19 acres appertained thereto was the Court of Wards for Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury MBE, and it was debutter property and the tenant in possession was also the Court of Wards for Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury, Sebait of Radha Gobinda Jew Bigrah. It further appears from the 2nd page of CS Khatian No.175 that CS Khatian No.176 was prepared under CS Khatian No.175. Similarly, it appears from CS Khatian No.176 that the superior landlord was the Court of Wards for Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury MBE, '175 Sebait' and the name of Puma Chandra Adhikary, the predecessor of opposite parties was recorded as the 'Chakran Purohit in possession. The words '175 Sebait' that appeared in CS Khatian No.176 contemplate that the Sebait mentioned in CS Khatian No.175 was also the Sebait or continued to be the same Sebait of the property of CS Khatian No.176 i.e., CS Khatian No.176 was prepared under CS Khatian No.175. Thus, there are only 1.19 acres of land under CS Khatian No. 175 and its Sub-CS Khatian No.176 and the entire property is debutter property. Had the properties of both CS Khatian No.175 and its sub-Khaitan No.176 belonged to Raja Mahendra and had he installed the Deity therein, the said properties might have not been recorded in the name of the Court of Wards in the said two CS Khatians. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties also submits that as per the CS Khatians, the said properties were under the control and management of the Court of Wards and Zamindar Raja Mahendra was Sebait thereof. So, I find substance in the pleadings and submissions made in this regard by the petitioner that before immemorial time, Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigraha was installed on the land of CS Khatian Nos. 175 and 176 and after the promulgation of permanent settlement the said property came under the Zamindari of Raja Mahendra Ranjan Roy Chowdhury and the said Zamindar was appointed Sebait. 

 18. But it is the case of the defendant-opposite parties that Puma Chandra Adhikary, their predecessor was the 'Purohit' of Zamindar Raja Mahendra and as the consideration of his religious service, the Zamindar gave him 'niskar pattan' of 1.90 acres of land of CS Khatian No.176 for permanently residing therein and maintenance of his livelihood. It is their further case that at the request of the local people, in general, belonging to the Hindu Religion, he dedicated by registered Deed of Gift No.6704 dated 6-11-1996 in total 84 decimals of land to the Radha-Gobinda Jew Bigraha. Thus, from the case of the defendant-opposite parties, it appears that the suit property was beyond the debutter property. But it has already been found that the entire property of CS Khatian No.175 and its Sub-Khatian No.176 is debutter property. At this stage, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that as per the CS Khatians, the property was under the control and management of Courts of Wards and not under the control and management of the Sebait and the predecessor of the opposite parties was a Chakran Purohit under the Courts of Wards. However, they could not produce any evidence to prove that they were ever tenant under the Court of Wards. Moreover, as per sections 6 and 7 of the Courts of Wards Act, 1879, no Debutter property can be claimed by any Court of Wards. However, the Court of Wards also claimed on behalf of the Deity. 

 19. Therefore, it appears that the entire property of CS Khatian No.175 and its Sub-Khatian No.176 belonged to the Deity represented by its Sebait. Moreover, it is admitted by both parties that in the suit premises, the Deity namely Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigraha is situated. Therefore, the Sebaitwas the Sebait of the Deity of Shree Shree Radha Gobinda Jew Bigraha. Accordingly, as per the CS Khatians, the predecessor of the opposite parties was a tenant under the Deity without any rent. Moreover, from the remarking column of the CS Khatian, it appears that Puma Chandra Adhikary, the predecessor of the opposite parties was in the possession of the property as Chakran Purohit i.e. in his official capacity and not personal capacity. Accordingly, so long he was in the office of the Purohit, he was entitled to possess and enjoy the said property. Moreover, it appears from the pleadings of both parties that by Deed of Gift No.6704 dated 6-11-1996, the opposite parties gifted the property to the Deity. However, the plaintiff did not accept the deed rather, claimed that the opposite parties had no legal right to make such a gift.It appears from both Sub-CS Khatian No.176 and SA Khatian No.188 that 32 decimals of land of Plot No.67 were jungle, 22 decimals of Plot No.69 were homesteads consisting of five houses, 13 decimals of Plot No.70 were Mandir (Debosthan)consisting of 04 houses and 52 decimals of Plot No.91 were for public usage. Thus, the entire property was debutter property. Therefore, gifting the debutter property to the same 'Debata' i.e., the Deity was nothing but an attempt to establish their title in the remaining properties. But except for the property gifted by the opposite parties, there remain only 22 decimals of land in their names. 

 21. Since the entire property of Sub-CS Khatian No.175 belonged to the Deity, the Purohit thereof cannot claim the property as his personal property. Accordingly, the transfer deed bearing No.1657 dated 25-2-1998 transferring some portion of the debutter property had also no legal basis and implication and thereby, no title has been transferred to the transferee thereof. 

 23. It transpires from the discussions, findings and observations made above that both the Courts below committed gross errors of law resulting in errors in the decision occasioning failure of justice having not considered that the entire property appertaining to CS Khatian No.175 and its Sub-Khatian No.176 is Debutter property and no one whatever might his status can claim the same as his personal property. Hence, I find merit in both the Rules.

Khatian No.955 to the predecessor of the plaintiff Mohabbat Ali Kha, Atahar Ali Kha, Amina Khatun and Samertaban Bibi on 27.03.1954; Haji macnonuaain Talukder died leaving two sons Defendant No.53 Hatem Ali, Yousuf Ali and 5 daughters Poribanu, Kodbanu, Iful Bibi, Rupshon Bibi and Rizia Khatun and wife Defendant No.50 Joynab Bibi; Rupshon Bibi died leaving one son Mohammad Ali and one daughter Dholai Bibi; Mohammad Ali and Dholai Bibi jointly inherited 12 decimals of land from their father and 24 decimals of land of S.A. Khatian No.955 from mother and jointly sold the same i.e. 36 decimals of land to Plaintiff Nos.2/5/6 on 24.03.1985; Atahar Ali Kha died leaving Plaintiff Nos.8-10 as heirs; Plaintiff Nos.9 and 10 sold 31 decimals of land to the Plaintiff Nos.2 and 12; Samertoban Bibi sold her entire share to Plaintiff Nos.3 and 4; Son of Haji Hachonuddin Talukder i.e. Yousuf Ali sold 1.19 acres of land to Defendant No.36 Yousuf Ali Munshi, Nurali and Abdur Razzak on 02.10.1963; Against the said transfer Mohabbat Ali Kha, Amina Khatun, Arabia Khatun and Atahar Ali Kha filed Preemption Case No.136/1964 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and obtained order of preemption on 19.11.1965 from the 1st Munsif Court of Patuakhali; Yousuf Ali died leaving mother Defendant No.50 Joynab Bibi, two wives Defendant Nos.] and 51 Maleka Begum and Kulsum Bibi respectively, one son Defendant No.49 Abdus Sobhan and one daughter Defendant No.52 Farida Begum; Hatem Ali son of Haji Hachonuddin Talukder sold 65 decimals of land to Danesh Ali and Moslem Ali Kha on 08.11.1955; Against the said transfer father of Plaintiff No.6 Mohabbat Ali Kha, Atahar Ali Kha, Amina Khatun, Art bia Khatun and Samertoban Bibi filed Pre-emption Case No.164/1959 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and obtained order of pre-emption on 23.01.1960 in which Plaintiff Nos.6-8 jointly got 45 decimals of land; Said Adorn Ali, Sorbanu, Ayesha Bibi, Hajera Bibi, Anowara Khatun and Minara Khatun sold 38 decimals of land to Plaintiff No.2 Moslem Ali Kha on 19.03.1973; Plaintiff No.2 Moslem Ali Kha transferred 10¾ of land to Defendant No.13 Shajahan; Plaintiff No.1 purchased 49½ decimals of land on 19.02.1982 and Plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 jointly purchased 80+22+42-144 decimals of land on 03.02.1985, 01.08.1987 and 02.03.1987 respectively; In this way plaintiffs' became owner and possessor of 4.41¼ of land of S.A. Khatian No.955 and 1.39 acres of land of S.A. Khatian No.954, in total 5.80¼ acres of land; Inspite of repeated requests of the plain-tiffs', the defendants refused to make amicable partition of the suit land which con-strained to file the suit for partition since there is no earlier partition by metes and bounds. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 3/5/14 and 19 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending interalia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, barred by the law of limitation and also for defect of parties; Their further case is that the suit land originally belonged to Someruddin and Sher Ali in equal share; Sher Ali died leaving two sons Osman Ali and Abdul Ali; Kashem Ali obtained 1.29 acres of land of Plot No.960 from Osman Ali and Abdul Ali on 05.05.1942 through pattan and Osman Ali received rent from Kashem Ali for the years 1349-1352 B.S. admitting Kashem Ali as an under rayat of Osman Ali who executed and registered dakhila on 16.04.1946; Sahed Ali pur-chased Marsha right from Osman Ali and Abdul Ali on 27.02.1946; Sahed Ali gave pattan through unregistered dakhila to Kashem Ali on 11.11.1946 and the said pattan was made during revisional survey and for that reason R.S. and S.A. Khatians were not published in the name of Kashem Ali; Though the land.was not recorded in S.A. Khatian in the name of Kashem Ali but he had been owning and possessing said land through pattan; Sahed Ali and Abdul Ali transferred 1.42 acres of land of Khatian No.955 on 05.11.1955 to Hatem Ali, Yousuf Ali, Hochen Ali and Kashem Ali; By virtue of the said deed Kashem Ali acquired 35½ of land; Kashem Ali being the owner of 1.64½ of land by way of pattan and kabala executed registered will infavour of his two sons and others i.e. Defendant Nos.3/14 Dholu Kha and Asmot Ali; Said Dholu Kha died leaving wife Nurjahan Begum, son Delowar Hossain and 3 daughters namely Rahima, Halima and Reba; Kashem Ali took pattan of 65 decimals of land trom Haji Hachonuddin Talukder on 22.12.1952 from C.S. Khatian No.410 and subsequently transferred the said land to Kobbat. Ali; Sobder, Sadar, Hachon Uddin and Hochon Uddin were owners and possessor of the land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.545 in equal share; Sobder Ali died leaving two sons and 3 daughters namely Arshed Ali, Kodom Ali, Borujan, Mayajan and Dwitiya Bibi where each son got 1.01 acres of land and each daughter got 50½ of land; Sadar Ali died leaving his mother Meherjan and two cousin Arshed Ali and Kodom Ali as heirs and they sold their 4 annas share to Haji Hachonuddin Talukder, Ketab Ali, Ahad Ali and Arena Bibi on 25.04.1941; Arshed Ali died leaving two sons Ketab Ali and Akkel Ali; Akkel Ali died leaving his full brother Ketab Ali as heirs; Ketab Ali (son of Arshed Ali) transferred his land to Ketab Ali (son of Haji Hachonuddin Talukder) on 12.03.1940 through pattan and gave dakhila admitting him as under tenant and in the said pattan the share of Borujan and Mayajan was not included; Dwitiya Bibi transferred 50½ decimals of land to Haji Hachonuddin Talukder; Again Borujan Bibi transferred 50½ decimals of land to Haji Hachonuddin Talukder on 21.10.1953; In this way Haji Hachonuddin Talukder obtained 5.54 acres of land amongst which 4.58½ acres of land was his recorded land and he transferred 1.89½ acres of land to Azahar Ali and Paribanu; Said Paribanu sold her portion of land to the defendants on 19.07.1979; Rest land of Haji Hachonuddin Talukder was put in auction and Sirajuddin and others purchased 4.86 acres of land in that auction; Against the said auction Yousuf Ali filed Case No.38/1967 in the 1st Munsif Court of Patuakhali to set-aside the auction. In the said case the auction purchaser amicably released 90 decimals of land infavour of Yousuf Ali; On the death of Yousuf Ali this defendants inherited said 90 decimals of land; Ketab Ali son of Haji Hachonuddin Talukder acquired 1.90 acres of land by way of pattan and kabala and thereafter died leaving wife Borujan, one son Hochen and father Haji Hachonuddin Talukder as heirs; Said Hochen Ali died leaving wife Rejia and two consanguine paternal uncle Hatem Ali and Yousuf Ali; Rejia sold 23 decimals of land on 09.04.1979 to Defendant Nos.3/19 and Plaintiff No.1 jointly; Haji Hachonuddin Talukder being owner of four annas of land of C.S. Khatian No.545 died leaving wife Amina Bibi and one son Ahad Ali; Said Amina Bibi died leaving one son Ahad Ali; Said Ahad Ali being the owner of 5.32 acres of land died leaving two sons Sekander Ali and Tajem Ali; Said Tajem Ali sold 22 decimals of land of S.A. Khatian No.954 to Abdul Khobir on 31.03.1964; In this way the defendants acquired 7.01½ of land of S.A. Khatian No.954 by way of inheritance and purchase and have been using and possessing their portion of land peacefully; Plaintiffs' filed this suit with false and baseless claim which is liable to be dismissed. 

 19. Admittedly, the suit land appertaining to C. Khatian No.559 belonged to Someruddin and Sher Ali in equal share. Plaintiffs/respondents claimed that their predecessor got the suit land by auction purchase and subsequently plaintiffs/ respondents got the same through some registered sale deeds. On the other hand, the contested defendants/appellants denied the alleged auction purchase of the plaintiffs and also claimed that the suit is barred b defect of parties and bad for hutch-pot. Again, they claimed that their predecessor got the suit land through settlement and later on they got the same by way of deed of will as well as some registered sale deeds. 

 23. On perusal of the evidence on record it appears that P.W.-0 1 admitted in his cross-examination that the wife of Defendant No.14 i.e. Moiful Bibi and 3 sons namely Malek, Sultan and Altaf Hossain are in possession of the suit land. Thus, from such admission it is crystal clear that the fact of possessing a portion of suit land by the Moiful Babi, Malek, Sultan and Altaf Hossain is in the knowledge of the plaintiffs, as such it was the duty of the plaintiffs/ respondents to implead them as parties to avoid multiplicity of proceedings. But on perusal of plaint it appears that the above mentioned four persons are not made parties to the suit, Again, according to the plaint, the land of C.S. Khatian No.559 is subsequently recorded in R.S. Khatian Nos.54,55,607 and S.A. Khatian Nos.418,954,955,951/1, 911 respectively. But on scrutiny of the plaint it appears that the plaintiffs/ respondents did not give any description about the names of individuals in whose names R.S. and S.A. Khatians were recorded. So, in the absence of such description it is not possible to ascertain whether all the R.S. and S.A. tenants are made parties to the suit. 

 27. On perusal of record it appears that P. -01 admitted in his cross-examination that he doesn't know how much land there is in the former (sabek) plots and how much lands of the former (sabek) plots has been recorded in current (hal) plots. Again, the appellate court below on perusal of exhibit-2 and 2 (lea) arrived at a finding that the former (sabek) plot numbers of the current (hal) Plot Nos.2282 and 2285 are 96 and 909 respectively. The appellate court below also arrived at a finding that in the said exhibited docu-ment no former (sabek) plot number of current Plot No. 2284/2935 is mentioned. On perusal of plaint 2935 and exhibit-01 i.e. C.S. Khatian No.559 it appears that former Plot Nos.96 and 909 are not included in the schedule of the plaint as well as in the C.S. Khatian No.559. In this context appellate court below upon evidences on record arrived at a conclusive finding that the suit is barred by hutch-pot for non-inclusion of the land of former (sabek) Plot Nos.96 and 909 in the schedule of the plaint. Inspite of such finding of the appellate court below, the High Court Division did not utter a single word to controvert such finding of the appellate court below. 

 The contesting defendants raised a dispute regarding auction sale of the suit property in Rent Suit No.229 of 1948 and Rent Decree Execution Case No.226 of 1949 and stated that the land of C.S. Khatian No.559 was not sold in auction. It has been clearly stated that the land in Sabek Khabot No.410 has been subsequently recorded in C.S. Khatian No.559 and the land of said Khabot No.410 corresponding to C.S. Khatian No.559 was sold in auction." 

 34. Plaintiffs/respondents claimed that their predecessor purchased the suit land through auction. The plaintiffs filed the suit for partition of C.S. Khatian No.559 and claimed that the land mentioned in C.S. Khatian No,559 and Khabot Khatian No.410 are same and on perusal on exhib-it-06 i.e. sale certificate of land in Rent Suit no. 229 of 1948 it appears that the same do not contain any C.S. Khatian number, rather contain only Khabot Khatian No.410, so it was the duty of the plaintiffs/respondents to establish such claim through relay of the land of C.S. Khatian No.559 with that of Khabot Khatian No.410 by appointing a survey knowing advocate commissioner. But on perusal of record it appears that the plaintiffs/ respondents did not take any such initiatives to establish their claim. Moreover, on perusal of exhibit-06 it appears that Arshed Ali purchased 7 acres of land in that auction. Again, exhibit-06 stated that Arshed Ali purchased the land corresponding to Khabot Khatian No.410 which is under annual rent of 51 taka 9 annas. On perusal of exhibit-1 i.e. C.S. Khatian No it appears that the entire 7 acres of land of that khatian is under annual rent of 64 taka. It is to be mentioned here that if the land of Khabot Khatian No.410 and C.S. Khatian No.559 are same then the annual rent of two khatians should be the same, but in reality the annual rent of both the khatians are not same. Thus, from the above discussions it appears to us that the plaintiff failed to prove that their predecessor purchased the land of C.S. Khatian No.559 through auction, as such the claim of auction purchase of the land of C.S. Khatian No. 559 by the plaintiffs is not proved.

Jannatul Maowa Runa and others ------------ Petitioners 
Vs.
AHM Roushan Ali Miah and others ----------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
6. Per contra, the present-petitioner as pre-emptee-purchaser contested the said Miscellaneous Case by filing a joint written statement denying all the material allegations so made in the petition for pre-emption contending, inter alia, that, one Akbar Ali had been in possession over 30 decimals of land on mutating his name in the khatian and while he had been enjoying title and possession over that 30 decimals of land he at first proposed the pre-emptor to sell the case land even the father of the pre-emptees named, Nazrul Islam also proposed the pre-emptor and his son to purchase the land but as they refused to purchase the same, the pre-emptees then purchased the case land by registered kabala dated 11-9-2001. Soon after purchasing the case land, the pre-emptees then started enjoying title and possession over the suit properties by planting various trees that cost Taka 65,000. It has further been stated that, there has been a Madrasha located in the case land though it was not made party in the case. It has then stated that, the vendor, Korban Ali who transferred 5 decimals of land upon purchasing 10 decimals of land had separated his jama before selling 5 decimals of land to the pre-emptor. It has stated in the written objection that, inspite of having no preferential right the pre-emptor filed the case having absolute knowledge about the disputed transfer. It has further been stated that, if the pre-emption case is allowed in that event, the pre-emptee Nos. 1-3 will suffer irreparable loss and injury and therefore the pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed. 

 15. By filing two supplementary-affidavits, the petitioners also produced the registered kabala dated 26-11-1997 and registered kabala dated 11- 9-2001, a filed porcha bearing khatian No. 721 appertaining to plot No. 629 standing in the name of the pre-emptees-petitioners in respect of 17 decimals of land. By filing another supplementary-affidavit dated 22-11-2017, the petitioners also annexed some documents which were marked as exhibits `E1 -E2.' In another supplementary-affidavit the pre-emptees-petitioners also produced a registered kabala dated 15-7-2001 through which 20 decimals of land was transferred by the son of the pre-emptor in favour of the opposite party No. 1 Akbar Ali. 

 19. The learned Counsel further submits that, since under the provision of clause (C) of section 117(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there has been gulf of difference between separation of holding and separation of jama so mere mutating the name in the khatian by the predecessor of the present-pre-emptors will not deprive the pre-emptor to exercise his statutory right of pre-emption to pre-empt the case land. 

 20. The learned Counsel further submits that. though the pre-emptees in its written objection allegedly stated that, before selling 5 decimals of land in favour of the pre-emptor by Korban Ali, he had mutated his name in the khatian vide mutation case but nothing of that sort of document has ever been produced by the said pre-emptees during the process of taking evidence so it clearly shows that, the mutation proceedings so have been alleged by the pre-emptees-petitioners has got no existence in the eye of law. 

 27. Now, only point remains, whether the pre-emptor ceased to have any right as a co-sharer by purchase to have the case land by way of purchase. It is alleged by the pre-emptees that, the vendor that is, Korban Ali before transferring 5 decimals of land infavour of the pre-emptees mutated his name in the khatian vide mutation case No. 2762 (9-1) 86/87 dated 11-11-1987 so before transferring the said case land, the khatian since has been spitted up so the pre-emptor cannot claim to be a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding. It has further been claimed by the pre-emptees that, after purchasing the case land even they also mutated their respective name in the khatian vide Mutation Case Nos. 1250, 1251 and 1252 in the year 2001 and 2002. Though there has been no mutation case number ever stated in the written objection but OPW 1 who is the father of pre-emptee purchaser No. 1 and 3 and the father in-law of the pre-emptee No. 2 has deposed that, in the month of March 2002 they got their names mutated in the khatian. 

 29. Now, for argument sake, had the vendor of the pre-emptee ever mutated his name, in that event whether the pre-emptor would have barred in exercising his right to pre-empt the case land or not. It is the contention of learned Counsel for the opposite party that, mere mutating the name in the khatian will never deprive the pre-emptor to exercise his right of pre-emption. In countenance of his submission, the learned Counsel has placed his reliance in the decision so have been reported in 3 ALR 58, which is propounded here: 

 31. To substantiate that very submission, the learned Counsel has also placed his reliance in the decision reported in 18 BLT (HC) 83 where it has clearly been held that, as regards to point of law, the later decisions will always prevail over. Though in the decision reported in 3 ALR 58. the decision so have been given by the Hon'ble Appellate Division on that particular point made under section 117(C) has not been referred even though I find substance in it because in all along the subsequent decision always prevails over. And in the decision reported in 3 ALR it has vividly been discussed how a separation of jama and a separation of holding can be distinguished. Because, under the provision of clause (C) of section 117(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, if any-person wants to separate a holding, in that event several procedure has to be performed but in the process of separating a jama which is generally called mutation in the khatian an application is simply filed before the respective Tohsil Office who then refers the same to the Assistant Commissioner (land) and the Assistant Commissioner land upon performing some procedure just mutates the khatian enabling the applicant to pay the rent in respect of his portion of land by which it cannot be said that separation of holding is held. Moreover, in separating a holding there must have some procedure to be carried out by issuing notice to all the co-sharer of the case holding but nothing of this sort has ever been complied with in the instant case. 

 35. Now let me asses the contention made in two supplementary-affidavits so submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner one, at the time of issuance of the Rule and another, on 22-11-2017. By way of first supplementary-affidavit dated 7-2-2013 the petitioners have produced two deeds dated 26-11-1997, 11-9-2001, the khatian No. 437 when the survey reached at the stage of DP and that of the field porcha (মাঠ পর্চা) with regard to khatian No. 721 appertaining to plot No. 629 stands in the name of the present pre-emptees-petitioners. By filing those documents, the learned Counsel for the petitioners tried to give emphasis on the point that, since the present khatian number is different from that of the purchased deed of the pre-emptor dated 26-11-1997 and 11-9-2001 where the recent plot number has been mentioned as 435 and 437 so the khatian has already been changed so the pre-emptor has ceased to have any right to pre-empt the case land for having enjoyed the land that fails in separate khatian. In order to give emphasis to that, the learned Counsel has also placed his reliance in DP khatian No. 437 which has also been marked as exhibit-D-1 and that of (মাঠ পর্চা) appertaining to khatian No. 721 which has been marked as Annexure-E to the supplementary-affidavit filed on 7-12-2013. 

 36. Anyway, I have very meticulously gone through all those documents but I don't find any iota of substance in those documents because from those documents it does not show the said khatians have finally been published in the name of the pre-emptor or that of the name of the pre-emptees. And in that regard, the learned Counsel for the opposite party has placed his reliance on the decision reported in 36 DLR 193 where it has been held that; 

 "In absence of final publication of record-of-right as provided in section 19 and 144 there cannot be any presumption as to its correctness." 

 37. It has already been held that, in absence of final publication of record of right as provided in section 19 and section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there cannot be any presumption as to the correctness. In such a view, it can safely construe that, until and unless a khatian is finally published, the pre-emptee cannot claim to have separated the holding, so that very decision is squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 41. So only point is left for the pre-emptee-petitioners that, the pre-emptor has ceased to be any co-sharer in the case holding but no documents haw produced which will suffice to prove the said assertion. Because, though in the written objection the pre-emptees claimed that, before being transferred 5 decimals of land by the vendors of the pre-emptor, he mutated his name in the khatian mentioning a certain mutation case number but nothing of that sort document has been produced to that effect. 

 42. Moreover, it has already been decided by our Apex Court that, mere mutating the name in the khatian will not deprive or will not cease the right of the pre-emptor in exercising its statutory right of pre-emption.

3. The case of the preemptors was that the land of C.S.
