parties:
Payari Mohan Das and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Rajjabernessa & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that one Pitambar Gope was the original owner in possession of Schedule 1(ka) land in rayati right and under him one Nida Gazi was in possession in korfa right in khatian No. 42. Before the last settlement operation the said Pitambar transferred the land of Schedule 1 (Ka) to Guru Das Dhupi and his brothers and during settlement operation the land was recorded in the names of the said purchasers. The aforesaid Pitambar died leaving his sons, Rajani Kanta Cope and Ramani Kanta Gope as his heirs in respect of the first Schedule land. Subsequently the rent in respect of first Schedule land became arrear and the landlord Chandi Charan Laha filed Rent Suit No. 3552 of 1931 in the court of Munsif, Comilla and obtained a decree and put the decree in execution in Rent Execution Case No. 3227 of 1934 and the said landlord auction purchased 15.98 acres of land and the sale was confirmed on 2-1-35 and the landlord also took delivery of possession therein through court. Thereafter the said Chandi Charan died leaving behind his sons Tarini Chandra Laha and others as heirs and by virtue of an amicable partition between the brothers, the first Schedule land fell exclusively in the saham of Tarini Chandra Laha. Due to the aforesaid auction sale, the korfa interest of Nida Gazi ceased to exist. The aforesaid Nida Gazi died leaving behind his mother, Johara, brothers, defendant No.1-3 and sister defendant No. 4. Thereafter the said Johara Gazi took settlement of 0.4 acre out of 0.19 acres of plot No. 54, .39 acres of plot No. 377, 0.10 acres of plot No. 384, 1.23 acres out of plot No.391, 0.27 acres of plot No. 392 and western .04 acres of plot No. 393 ie in all 2.43 acres at an annual rental of Taka 18 in the month of April, 1940. Thereafter the said Johara Bibi died leaving behind the defendant Nos. 1-4 as heirs. 

 4. The said Tarini Chandra granted settlement of 3.72 acres of land of various plots of khatian Nos. 41 and 42 to one Ruhini Lal Das by a registered kabuliyat dated 3-9-42. The said Tarini Chandra granted settlement of 4.51 acres of land of khatian No. 41 to one Durga Chandra Das and Shyama Chandra Das by a registered kabuliat dated 2-10-42. Thereafter Durga Chandra died leaving behind plaintiff No.3 and Shyama Charan died leaving behind plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 who had been possessing the same. The said Tarini Chandra granted rayati settlement of 2.43 acres of khatian No. 41 to one Bharat Chandra Das by a registered kabuliat dated 1-4-43 and delivered possession. Thereafter the said Tarini Chandra granted settlement of 1.46½ acres of land of khatian No. 41 to Mohini and Jagat, brothers of Bharat Chandra. The said Mohini Chandra died childless leaving behind her brothers, Jagat Chandra and Bharat Chandra who became the owners of his property. Jagat Chandra died leaving his only daughter Haribala and Bharat Chandra died leaving his only daughter Hemlata who became the owners in possession of the property left by their respective father. The aforesaid Tarini Chandra out of Schedule I land granted settlement of 0.65 acres of plot No. 16 and 32½ acres of plot No. 481 to Copal Chandra Das and also 0.77 acres of plot No. 464 to Abhoy Chandra Das on the basis of kabuliat. Thus Tarini Chandra ceased to have any interest in Schedule I land. 

 5. The lands taken settlement by Jahora Bibi was recorded in RS Khatian No. 46 but due to mistake 2.43 acres was recorded in place of 2.65 acres. Thus the said record of right was wrong and the defendant Nos.1-4 have no title or interest therein. The said lands are in possession of the plaintiffs. The lands of Rohini Das was correctly recorded in RS Khatian No. 98 who sold .44 acres land of plot No.543 of khatian No. 42 of Schedule 1(Ka) to Osman Ali by a registered kabala on 4-3-68. Thereafter the said Rohini sold .64 acres of plot No. 562 of Khatian No. 42 of Schedule 1(Ka) to Azimunnessa and her son Muslimuddin by a registered kabala dated 14-3-70. In RS Khatian No.97 an area of 4.15 acres of land settlement by Durga Charan and Symacharan was recorded in their names. In the said khatian in plot No. 393 an area of 1.07 acres of land belonging to the plaintiff has not been at all recorded and the plaintiffs being the owner are in possession of the same. 

 6. As the suit land of Schedule II has been wrongly recorded in the name of defendant's predecessor Johura Bibi in RS Khatian No. 46, the defendants falsely raised claim over the land and as such, cloud has been cast upon their title. It transpired that the defendants collusively created two mutation khatians in respect of plot No. 393. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land from the time of their predecessor for long over 12 years and subsequently the defendants illegally trespassed into the suit land on 24th Sraban, 1389 BS and thereby dispossessed the plaintiffs. 

 8. Their further case is that, Pitambar Cope was the owner in possession of Schedule 1(Ka) and belonging to khatian No. 41 and that in khatian No. 42 within the said khatian lands measuring 6.07 was taken korfa settlement by Nida Gazi by a registered kabuliat dated 20-11-17 and was paying rent regularly. There was never any rent suit, rent decree or auction sale as alleged in the plaint and all these are mere paper transactions. There was never any delivery of possession through court. The interest of Nida Gazi was not affected by the auction sale and Nida Gazi was never evicted from the lands of Khatian No. 42. The plaintiffs case of granting settlement by Tarini Chandra in favour of several persons by kabuliat are all false and collusive. The defendants are in possession of 1.47 acres of land in plot No. 393 described in Schedule II by inheritance. Taking advantage of the minority of defendants and old age of their mother Johara Bibi the plaintiffs predecessor Durga Charan in collusion with settlement staff got the lands belonging to and in possession of the plaintiffs in respect of plot Nos. 49/50/393/391/54/481 of Khatin No. 97 recorded in the names of Durga Charan and Shyma Charan. The said khatian is wrong and Johura Gazi never took any settlement of the lands of Khatian No. 42 and she was possessing the same by inheritance and on her death the defendants are possessing the same. The plaintiffs had never any title or possession in the suit land. The defendants are illiterate and the plaintiffs with ulterior motive created RS Khatian No. 98 in respect of the land of Khatian No. 42 and the defendants are not aware of any mutation of their names in respect of Khatian No. 97 which was collusively created by the plaintiffs. Their further case is that the plaintiffs falsely alleged that the defendants dispossessed them from the suit land on 24th Sraban, 1389 BS. The defendants did not dispossess the plaintiffs on the said date. The defendants instituted Tile Suit No. 16 of 1983 in respect of the suit land alleging wrong recording of the RS Khatian which is pending. 

 14. Mr Syed Mahmud Hussain, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that the land of Khatian No.42 measuring 6.07 acres of land belonged to Nida Gazi in korfa right and after his death his heirs the defendants have been in possession. He further submits that there was no Rent sale and the land of Khatian No. 42 was never sold in auction. He further submits that the plaintiffs case is that the land of Khatian No. 41 was sold in auction but no delivery of possession was taken through court in respect of the land sold in auction as claimed by the plaintiffs-petitioners. He further submits that in the sale certificate filed by the plaintiffs the suit plot No.393 does not find place. He further submits that no writ of delivery of possession has been filed in support of the plaintiffs contention that after auction purchase the landlord took delivery of possession through court. From the certified copy of suit register also it appears that no delivery of possession was taken through court after the alleged auction purchase. He also submits that as per law after auction purchase korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi which was an encumbrance was to be annulled under provision of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. But there was no such annulment. 

 15. Exhibit No.1, CS Khatian No.41 of Mouja-Bhowri, PS Chandina, District-Comilla shows that an area of 9.91 acres of land in 13 plots was recorded in the name of one Pitambar Cope under landlord Rajakunga Das Laha and others and under Khatian No.41 in Khatian No.42 an area of 6.07 acres of land in 12 plots was recorded in the name of Nida Gazi in Korfa right. CS Khatian No.41 shows that all the 13 plots recorded in the Khatian were sold out before or at least during CS operation by the recorded tenant to different persons and accordingly in all the 13 plots of land of Khatian No.41 the possession of the purchasers was recorded and this position is not disputed. 

 16. Plaintiffs-petitioners case is that landlord Chandi Charan Laha brought Rent Suit No.3752 of 1931 in the Court of Munsif, Comilla against Pitambar and obtained a decree, put the decree into execution in Rent Execution case No.3227 of 1934 and the landlord auction purchased 15.98 acres of land and the sale was confirmed and they took delivery of possession through Court. The defendant's case, on the other hand, is that there was no such Rent Suit and no auction purchase by the landlord and no delivery of possession was taken through court. Their further case is that the land of Khatian No. 42 which Nida Gazi possessed in korfa right was not sold in auction as Nida Gazi was not a tenant under Laha Babus. From the certified copy of sale certificate it appears that the suit plot No. 393 does not find place in the sale certificate. So it cannot be said that plot No. 393 was also sold in auction as claimed by the plaintiffs. No writ of delivery of possession was filed to show that after auction purchase, the landlord took delivery of possession through court. The certified copy of Rent suit Register Ext.6 shows that there is no note in the Register regarding taking delivery of possession in the land. There is also no evidence on record to show that the korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi was annulled as per provision of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act after the alleged auction purchase by the landlord. 

 17. Mr BK Das submits that Nida Gazi took korfa settlement of the lands of Khatian No. 42 for a period of 5 years and after the expiry of the period of 5 years the korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi extinguished and as such there was no necessity for annulment of the encumbrance after auction purchase by the landlord. In reply Mr Hussain, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that from the evidence of PW 1 Rai Horon Banik and PW 2 Md Jafar Ali it is clear that the korfa settlement of Nida Gazi continued till the date of alleged auction sale. PW 2 further stated that the landlord took delivery of possession in the suit land by demolishing the dwelling huts of the defendant ie the heirs of Nida Gazi. From this it is clear that Nida Gazi and after him, his heirs were in possession of the land of Khatian No. 42 after the expiry of the initial period of 5 years. So the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that after the expiry of 5 years the korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi ceased to exist does not stand. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties in support of his contention placed the case of Jagabandu Basak and others vs. Karim Mondal and others, reported in 8 DLR 366. In that case it was held that, if an under raiyat has been allowed to continue in occupation, his tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Until such steps have been taken in time he cannot be ejected from his land. In the instant case there was no case of the plaintiff-petitioners in the plaint that after expiry of the period of 5 years the korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi ceased to exist. Thus from the evidence on record it is proved that the korfa tenancy of Nida Gazi continued after the expiry of 5 years for which initially Nida Gazi took korfa settlement of the land of Khatian No. 42 and after Nida Gazi his heirs continued to possess. 

 19. Mr Hussain next submits that under section 160(c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act the under tenancy of Nida Gazi is protected for as per CS Khatian No. 42 there are homestead, tank, etc. in the land. So, the landlord was entitled to claim enhancement of rent only if the auction purchase by the landlord is proved. CS Khatina No. 42 shows that plot No. 391 is homestead and plot Nos. 54, 377, 384 are tanks. Sub-section (c) of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides that, "(c) any lease of land whereon dwelling houses, manufactories or other permanent buildings have been erected, or permanent gardens, plantations, tanks, canals, places of worship or burning or burying grounds have been made shall be deemed to be protected interest." 

 24. Mr BK Das next submits that the plaintiff-petitioners filed an application on 22-7-91 before the learned District Judge under Order 41 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure with annexure of registered deed of partition dated 1-5-41 praying for accepting the same as additional evidence for the purpose of showing that Chandi Charan was the superior landlord of the suit land and the application was fixed for hearing on 2-10-91. But ultimately, the appeal was disposed of without deciding the said application and this has caused prejudice to the plaintiffs. It is not disputed that Chandi Charan was the landlord in respect of Khatian No.41. The copy of deed of partition dated 1-5-41 was filed to show that by the amicable partition Tarini got the land of Khatian No.41 in his share and thereafter he settled the land to different persons including the plaintiffs. It is not disputed that Laha Babus were landlords in respect of CS Khatian No. 41. So, in my poinion, the non-consideration of this document by the court of appeal below did not cause any prejudice to the plaintiffs-petitioners.

lawyer:
Mr Miah Abdul Gafur with Mr Mahbubey Alam, Mr. Abbasuddin Ahmed, Mr. Aminuddin, Advocates ------ for the petitioner. 
Mr. Nurul Hoque with Mr. A K M Shahidul Huq, Advocates ------ for the opposite parties.
parties:
Musammat Nurjahan Begum and ors. ------ Petitioners

full_judgment:
2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, Narayangonj for permanent injunction against the defendants restraining them from illegally entering into the suit lands. The plaintiff’s case is that the suit land along with other lands under C.S. Khatian No. 261 of Mouza Fatullah originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal share. Sonaton Baroi died leaving leaving behind son Shyam Charan Baroi as his heir Ramananda Boroi died leaving 3 daughters. Mohan Mala Biswas, Hari Dasi Baroi and Seba Dasi Baroi as his heirs. By an amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton and Ramananda, the said heirs of Ramananda got the suit plot i.e. C.S. plot No. 393 along with northern half of C.S. plot No. 436 of C.S. khatian No. 261 and they have been in peaceful possession of the suit land and the northern half of the C.S. plot No. 436. The further case of the plaintiff is that the S.A. Khatian of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Shyam Charan which was corrected by compromise decree dated 15.1.75 in Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 of the second Court of Munsif at Narayangonj wherein the right, title, interest and possession of the heirs of Ramananda in the suit plot and the northern half of plot No. 436 was declared and established. While the said Mohan Mala and her two sisters along with their sons were owners in possession of the suit plot along with northern half of the plot No. 436, they enured into a registered agreement dated 4.7.74 to sell the said lands for a consideration of Tk. 25,000/- and received taka 21,000/- as earnest money and delivered possession of the said lands to the plaintiff. Subsequently on 18.2.75 the vendors of the plaintiff executed and registered a saf kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff on receiving the balance consideration of taka 4,000/- from the plaintiff. The plaintiff excavated a tank in the southern portion of the suit land and stacked earth on the northern portion of the suit land for the purpose of manufacturing bricks and has been rearing fishes in the tank. The plaintiff mutated her name in S.A. Khatian in respect of the suit land by mutation case No. 35 FA/75-76 dated 22.7.75 and has been paying rents for the suit land in her name. The name of the plaintiff was duly recorded in the present R.S. Khatian No. 612 of Mouza Fatullah in respect of the suit land. The defendants have/had no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land. The defendants tried to enter into the suit land in the middle part of the month of September, 1979 but could not succeed on account of timely resistance put up by the plaintiff. The defendants gave out that they would enter into the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit. 

 5. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner submits that the judgment of the learned appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal because the appellate court below being the final court of fact has not controverts the reasoning and discussion of the trial court inasmuch as the learned appellate court below has not considered and discussed the entire evidence oral and documentary on record and as such this error of law on the part of the appellate court below caused erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that 'the learned appellate court below misread the C.S. khatian No. 261 exhibit 3 C in asmuch as he failed to read the word “গং” after Sonaton Baroi and also failed to read the word “বরাত” in C.S. Khatian No. 76 and the total non-consideration of these material words vitiated the findings of the appellate court below. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned appellate court below erred in law in deciding the question of title of the suit plot in favour of the defendants by wrongly holding that the properties of the disputed C.S. Khatian 76 exhibit 3C belong to Sonaton Baroi, the predecessor of the defendants along although it has been held that the suit is not maintainable for its involvement of complicated question of title. The learned Advocate referring to exhibit 3B and 3C further submits that the learned appellate Court below erred in holding that the learned Munsif is not justified to observe that the land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares. The learned Advocate with much emphasis submits that the learned appellate court below failed to consider and discuss the various exhibited documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner such as exhibits 1,1A, 2-2A, 3, 3A, 3B, 4A, 5, 6, 6A and also the oral evidence of 5 P.Ws. and those have proved the plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land and as such there is erroneous decision in the matter by the appellate court below occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that exhibit IA, bainapatra and exhibit 3A, S.A. Khatian, exhibit 2-2A rent receipts, exhibit 3 R.S. khatian exhibit 4, 4A containing an admission of Satya Ranjan son of Randha Ballav about the possession and title of the plaintiff petitioner's vendors in the suit plot and evidence of P.Ws. clearly proved the plaintiff's possession and title in the suit land and as such the learned appellate court contrary to those evidence on record erred in dismissing the suit. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendants could not produce their alleged bainapatra dated 6.11.1963 showing their alleged possession since 1963 and that the defendants case of possession being self contradictory and that D.W.1 and 2 could not give the boundary of the suit plot inasmuch as D.W.1 and 2 are the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 respectively and as such the appellate court below erred in setting aside the decision of the trial court which decreed the suit considering the evidence and materials of the plaintiff vis-a-vis those of the defendants. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate, in support of his contention refers to and relies on the decisions namely (1991)11 BLD (AD)245,37D.L.R.79,PLD1976 (SC)784, 35DLR216 and 6 DLR 271. 

 6. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties submits that the correct position in that Sonaton Baroi was the sole 16 annas owner of the land of C.S. Khatian No. 261 as will appear on mere reading of the said Khatian exhibit 3C and in a suit for permanent injunction it is of paramount importance that the plaintiff must prove his title to the suit property and unless the plaintiff can show that he has some legal rights and the defendants have legal obligation not to disturb lawful possession of the plaintiff a suit for permanent injunction can not be maintained and in the instant case exhibit 3C clearly shows that the suit land solely belonged to Sonaton Baroi. The learned Advocate further submits that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are sons of two different persons and Ramananda Baroi was not a co-sharer of Sonaton Baroi and as such the question of amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi does not arise at all. He further submits that these two persons being stranger to one another the question of any amicable partition between their heirs and such possession on the basis of the said alleged amicable partition does not arise. The learned Advocate further submits that the so called amicable partition if any, was falsely created and the same appears to have been created near about the time when the plaintiff was creating her documents. The learned Advocate further submits that the Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 cannot be a legally tenable suit for correction of S.A. record twelve years after finalization of the said record in 1962 and the trial court failed to take notice of this aspect of the case. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that the compromise decree was collusive and untenable decree which cannot confer any right, title, interest and possession in favour of the heirs of Ramananda Baroi who was nobody having any interest in the suit land. The learned Advocate further submits that the story of excavation of the tank by the plaintiff is also a cock and bull story which the learned Munsif was hesitant in believing the same reading of the evidences of P.W. 3 and the trial court found major contradiction in evidence along with possession but gave his finding of possession in favour of the plaintiff petitioner without making any comment about the evidence of the D.Ws. which is not a legal decision on assessment of the evidence of both the parties as is called upon to do by the courts of facts and the trial court failed to follow the provisions of the Order 20 Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate further submits that the mutation in the name of the plaintiff in Mutation Case No. 35/PA/75-76 dated 22.2.75 was not done in a lawful proceeding after service of notices as required under the law. There was no record to show that such mutation was lawfully made, the same was done during pendency of the title suit between the defendants and Satta Ranjan Baroi and as such record is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The recording of the plaintiff's name in the R.S. record was consequential effect of the illegal mutation of the plaintiff's name. In view of the decree obtained by the defendants in Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 the intervening all acts are hit by the doctrine of lis-pendense. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial court misread the C.S. khatian as was rightly found by the learned appellate court below. Mr. Nurul Hoque further submits that the prima facie title of the plaintiff and her possession was not legal finding inasmuch as the khatian No. 261 cannot be construed to show that Sonaton and Ramananda were the joint owner and such contention would be violative of the provisions of section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate finally with much emphasis submits that in the instant case a complicated question of title is involved and the same cannot be decided without evidence in a properly framed suit and in that view of the matter also the learned appellate court below rightly dismissed the suit. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate has referred to and relied on the following decisions namely 1991 BLD (AD) 245, 10 DLR 193. 1982 BCR (AD). 

 7. Before I enter into the merit of this rule I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the trend of the earlier-judicial pronouncements that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima facie title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff only the he is entitled to a decree for permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodies the well known principle of Roman law that possession in prima facie proof of ownership and when, therefore, a person is in possession of the property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under section 110 of the Evidence Act the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who affirms that he is not the owner. Similarly section 9 of the Specific Relief Act also protects the possessory right of a person. Title cannot be pleaded in bar in a suit of this nature and the court does not adjudicate upon the title of the parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. It is thus, clear that even a tress passer can recover his possession if he is dispossessed from immovable property without his consent. If this be so then why a person who is already in possession of an immovable property claiming to be the owner will be required to prove his title to the property in order to protect his possession. In my opinion the correct legal position is that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff need not prove his title to the property as a condition precedent to succeed in an action for permanent injunction It is sufficient if the plaintiff can prove his prior and present possession of the suit land i.e. in a suit for permanent injunction possession is of paramount consideration and the fate of the suit veer round the proof of possession by the plaintiff. 

 17. It further appears from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below found that the suit plot No. 393 of C.S. khatian No. 261 of mouza Fatullah comprising an area of 1.10 decimals of land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone and this finding of the appellate court below is based on c.s. Khatian No. 261 exhibit 3C in respect of the suit plot No. 393 which speaks that the suit land belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone as a “রায়তী স্থিতিবান”. The learned trial court found that the land recorded in c.s. khatian No. 261 belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares and the learned appellate court below has reversed that finding observing that in exhibit 3C there is no mentioned that Ramananda Baroi is also 8 annas owner of that jote but this finding of the appellate court below cannot be sustained in law inasmuch as exhibit 3C the c.s. Khatian No. 261 itself shows that Sonaton Baroi and others are the owners and in the column of rent it is written ১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই Exhibit 3B the c.s. khatian 76 shows that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are the owners of the land recorded in that khatian. Of course, in khatian No. 76 plot No. 83 is recorded whereas the suit plot is recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 261. It is submitted by Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner, that বরাত mean reference and by referring to the relevant provisions of Technical Rules and Instructions of the Settlement Department, 1957 it has been shown that when tenant have land in different plots in different mouzas the full rent should be entered in one khatian only and cross-reference should be made in all the khatian and as such in the instant case the c.s. Khatian No. 76 and c.s. khatian 261 is to be read together and treated as one document and from this the trial court rightly arrived at a finding that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi were equal sharer of the said jote. He has referred to the definition of "jote" as contained in section 5 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. "Jote' does not necessarily mean the interest of a cultivator, or an occupancy holding; it is only a general term and may mean a raiyati, under raiyati or any sort of holding for the purpose of cultivation. It simply connotes a tenancy. So if exhibit 3B and 3C are considered together it appears that the finding of the trial court is at least correct with regard to the prima facie title of the predecessor in interest46of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land and the observation of the learned appellate court below cannot be maintained in view of the fact that in arriving at such a finding that Sonaton Baroi is the sole owner of the c.s. Khatian No. 393 is based on misreading of exhibit 3B as well as 3C because in exhibit 3C itself in column of owner it is written "owner is Sonaton Baroi and others and in the column of rent it is written “১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই ” and the learned appellate court has failed to take notice of the contents of exhibit 3C and 3B and totally misread exhibit 3C and therefore the finding of the learned appellate Court below that Sonaton Baroi is the Sole owner of the suit land is absolutely contrary to the materials and evidence on record. At least there is prima facie evidence to show that both Sonatan Baroi and Ramananda were 8 annas share of the land recorded in 2 Khatians namely C. S. Khatian No. 261 and 76. On top of that the R.S. Khatian also stand in the name of the plaintiff petitioner. It is submitted that this R.S. Khatian has been published in the year 1974 in the district of Narayanganj by virtue of section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This RS. Khatian also has a presumptive value and this R.S. Khatian has been published after conducting field survey. In that view of the matter also it can be said that the plaintiff petitioner has been able to prove his prima facie title and possession in the suit land. If these 3 documents are considered along with the oral evidence of all the P.Ws. and D.Ws. it appears that the finding of the trial court that the plaintiff has been able to prove her prima facie title and exclusive possession in the suit land cannot be assailed. I, thus, find that the finding of the appellate court below that C.S. plot No. 393 entirely belonged to Sonatan Baroi is erroneous and contrary to the materials and evidence on record. 

 20. Regarding physical possession of the suit land the appellate court below relying on the deposition of two D.Ws. and writ issued in pursuance of the Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1976 has arrived at a finding that at least the defendants have been able to prove symbolical possession in the suit land after successful termination of the Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 in their favour but in arriving at such a finding the appellate court below lost sight of the two c.s. khatians being khatian No.76 and khatian No. 261 and the R.S. khatian exhibit 3 and rent receipts exhibit 2-2A and the oral evidence of P.Ws. which conclusively proved the possession of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land. It thus appears that the finding of the learned appellate court below that the defendants have been able to prove at least their symbolical possession of the suit land does not inspire confidence and the finding of the trial court on that point is backed by sufficient materials and evidence on record both oral and documentary. 

 24. From my aforesaid discussion it is crystal clear that in a suit for permanent in-junction there is no scope to adjudicate upon the question of title of the parties although the court can incidentally can go to the question of title. In that view of the matter the court should be conscious in making any observation touching the merit of title of either parties. On a scrutiny of the trial court's judgment it appears that the trial court has made certain observations which are actually relevant in determining the question of title. It has already been found that title is of no significance in a suit for permanent injunction and as such the observation made by the trial court regarding title of the parties are unwarranted, uncalled for and must be expunged. So, the finding of the trial court that "It gives a strong presumption that they merely created a document of title to and possession over the suit land by filing the aforesaid execution case for delivery of possession" and the finding of the trial court that "On perusal of the documents it appears that as per C.S. Khatian both Sonaton and Ramananda are equal shares (8 annas each) in the land of suit khatian" are expunged.
