Abdul Rob Choudhury and ors ------Opposite party
full_judgment:
2. The common case of the petitioner in all the three miscellaneous cases is that he is the co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 of mouza Chandpur and lands recorded therein originally belonged to Shafi Kumar, Kali Kumar, Krishna Chandra, RajKumar, Nakshatra and Sharoda and that he is the son of Krishna Chandra and that opposite party No. 2 is also a co-sharer by inheritance in the aforesaid C.S. Khatian No. 803, that the opposite party No. 2 by three different kabalas sold some portion of the disputed plot to the opposite party No. 1 in the year 1972 and .did not serve any notice of such transfer to him and that the opposite party No. 1 is a stranger-purchaser, that he is in possession of some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. Thus he is entitled to pre-empt the disputed lands. 

 3.  The pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 contested the cases by filling written objection and alleging, inter alia, that the petitioner was not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property with regard to which two khatians under S.A. operation, namely Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 have been prepared and the disputed land has been recorded in new Khatian No. 845 and that the land recorded in Khatian No. 844 belonged to the petitioner. Thus after splitting up of the original khatian i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803 the petitioner is not entitled to claim himself as a co-sharer. tenant in the disputed khatian No. 845. The further cases of the opposite party No. 1 is that the land in dispute is a debuttor property and as such the petitioner is not entitled to claim any pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 4. The learned Munsif dismissed the pre-emption petitions upon holding that the vendors of opposite party No. 1, namely Phani and Khogendra, are the tenants in the separately recorded M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 845 at jama of Tk. 7/14 annas and the M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844 stands recorded in the name of the petitioner along with his other co-sharers. Thus the interest of the vendors of the opposite party No. 1 in their parent C.S. Khatiaa No. 803 was no longer in existence while the impugned transfer took place. The learned Munsif also declined to consider whether the parent Khatian No. 803 was legally spitted up into two khatians, namely, M.R.O.R. Khatian Nos. 844 and 845. Thus the learned Munsif  held that the petitioner has no locus standi to claim pre-emption in respect of the disputed land. 

 5. Against the judgment and order of the trial Court the petitioner preferred the above mentioned miscellaneous appeals and the lower appellate Court by the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeals and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court upon taking the same view that the parent khatian i.e C.S. Khatian No. 805 having been separated into two khatians and the disputed land having been recorded in the new khatian No. 845, the petitioner is not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed land. 

 6. Mr. S.K. Sinha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has raised two points for all the three Rules. Firstly, that the opening of two separate jamas under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by way of sub-division of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 801 having not been done in accordance with law, the Courts below committed an error of law in holding that on the basis of two separate khatians the pre-emptor, although is admittedly a son of the original owner, lost his right of claim to be a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property. Secondly, that the petitioner also claimed that he is the contiguous owner of the disputed land but the Courts below failed to consider his case as to whether he could prove his claim as the contiguous owner of the disputed land. 

 7. Mr.M. Shehabullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 contends that the parent jama was separated at the instance of the pre-emptor as well as his other co-sharers and on the basis of separate khatians, namely, Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 they have been paying rents in respect of the disputed land. Thus the Courts below legally held that the pre-emptor lost his right of claiming pre-emption as a co-sharer. The learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptor in his petition for pre-emption did not specifically plead that he is also a contiguous owner of the disputed land and nothing also transpires from the judgments of the Courts below that the pre-emptor also pressed his claim that he is entitled to pre-empt the land as contiguous owner. The learned Advocate in his affidavit-in-opposition has annexed true copy of the petition of miscellaneous case No. 128 of 1972 and in paragraph 8 of the said-affidavit it is stated that the petitioner did not claim his right of pre-emption as a contiguous owner too. 

 8. At the time of issuance of the Rules records were not called for. But on being asked the learned Advocate for the petitioner produced the certified copy of the depositions of the witnesses. Since nothing has been mentioned in the judgments of the Courts below regarding the oral evidence of the parties, for my personal satisfaction have perused the evidence of the witnesses of both The sides from the certified copies of the depositions. It is evident from the Annexure-1 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner has stated that he along with the vendor of the opposite party No. 1 is co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 and that he is in possession in some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. In the Schedule be has mentioned the original Khatian No. 803 as well as the present Khatian No. 845. The disputed plots are Plots No. 846 and 850 measuring the total area of 1.84 and, 69 decimals respectively. 

 9. Admittedly, two separate khatians under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been prepared in respect of the land of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803. The Courts below have observed that these two khatians are the modified record-of-right Nothing transpires either from the evidence 91 the parties or from the judgments of the Courts below that those khatians have been-finally published and accepted under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as final. There are two provisions under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act regarding preparation of the record-of-rights. Under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the notification of the Government under section 17 of the Act a draft record-of-right was prepared for the purpose of acquisition of the rent-receiving interest or under the same provisions the record of right that was prepared under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act would have been revised in respect of any district, part of a district or of any local area as the Government would deem fit and necessary; The particulars which are required to be incorporated under those draft record-of-rights have been mentioned in the rules framed for the purpose. A judicial notice can be taken that the draft or the revised khatians that were directed to be prepared under section 19 of the Act was not finally published since before coming into force of Part V or the Act, which came into operation in the Noakhali district on 1.8.63. After coming into force of whole of the Part V a radical change in the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was brought in, whereby in view of sub-section (8) of section 82 the words 'raiyati' or 'tenant' as well as 'rent' were to be deemed to have been substituted by the words 'milk' an 'land revenue'. Chapter V of the Act also brought in the incident of tenancy including the right of occupancy as well as devolution of interest by way of inheritance. In view of sections . 83 and 84 of the Act. Thus question of status of the malik as well as the co-sharer malik, as are to be read in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the, provisions of section- 82 (8) of the Act, gave a new dimension in the rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt by a co-sharer malik in respect of the transfer of any holding or portion thereof by a ma to any stranger. Section 96 has also brought a new right of pre-emption for the owners of the contiguous lands. Under section 19 provisions have been made only to prepare a draft record-of-right or to revise the re-cord-of-right prepared and finally published under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. After coming into force of Part-V and giving the raiyats of different natures to a single status of malik, the right to hold or occupy such land for agricultural or horticultural purposes on payment of revenue direct to the Government. The word 'tenant' as has been defined under section 2(27) of the Act lost is connotation as was initially defined. It is evident that in Part—V provision has been made under section 117 of the Act for amalgamation, consolidation or subdivision of holdings. In .case of amalgamation or consolidation of holdings under section 117 (1) (a), (b) the revenue officer either of his own motion or upon any application made to him in that behalf is entitled to amalgamate or consolidate the holdings. But so far the sub-division of holdings is concerned under section 117(1) (c) of the Act it has been made imperative that the sub-division of joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof can be made by the revenue officer only upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and no order for such sub-division shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and to be heard by him in the matter. It has further been provided under sub-section (3) of section 117 that that when an order under sub section (1) has been passed sub-dividing a joint holding, such sub-division may be demarcated on the ground and shown on the cadastral survey map. Thus the scheme of sub-division is very much clear for the purpose of adjudication that has been provided under Chapter XII of Part-V of the Act. 

 10. The modified record-of-right, as in evident from the provision of sec. 46 of the Act, was required to be prepared and considered for the purpose of final publication of the compensation assessment roll regarding acquisition of all kind of rent receiving interest under the Act. The record of right derives its presumptive value of correctness both under section 19 of the Act as well as section 144 of the Act. In the absence of any final publication of the record of right which have been prepared under the Act either under section 19 or under section 144, there cannot be any presumptive value of its correctness which is required to be rebutted. It does not a from the judgments of the Courts below that they considered as to whether this sub-division of the original jama was done upon the application of the pre-emptor or with notice to him as provided under section 117 (1) (c) of the Act. Preparation of the record-of-right under Chapter IV was for the purpose of acquisition of rent receiving interest whereas the purpose of preparation of the record-of right under Part-V, Chapter-XIV is for maintaining the proper and up-to-date settlement rent roll. It should be significantly noted that whenever the raiyat or under raiyat or any other raiyat as they had been under the Bengal Tenancy Act, alter coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 have been merged into a single status of malik having their equal rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt any land under section 96 of the Act. Thus in the absence of any material or evidence on record that such separation of original jama was done in accordance with section 117(1) (c) of is not at all safe to oust a co-sharer malik from exercising his vested right only on the basis of two M.R.O R. Khatians which were prepared initially for the purpose of realisation of rent pending final publication of record-of-right as has been contemplated under the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 11. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party that on the basis of two new khatians the vendors of the opposite party as well as the pre-emptor have been paying rent separately but it does not appear from the judgments of the Courts below that they had the opportunity of considering any materials regarding such payment of rent which would give some light as to the point of time since when they started paying rent. The Courts below have proceeded on the footing that so far the exercising of the right of pre-emption is concerned under section 96 of the Act on the basis of the claim of co-shareship in the holding, mere showing the payment of land revenue under two different numbers in the tenants ledger is sufficient to give a complete negation to any vested right of pre-emption. There cannot be doubt, of course, whenever all the co-sharers of the original C.S. Khatian amicably, split up the jama for the purpose of facilitating payment of land revenue that can be construed as very much identical to the amicable partition amongst such co-sharers. In such a case by their conduct amongst them-selves the co-sharers would dis-entitle them-selves from claiming any benefit of a joint tenancy in view of the doctrine of estoppel, as has been provided under section 115 of the Evidence Act. " 

 Moreover, the pre-emptor in the application for pre-emption has asserted that he is in possession in a portion of the disputed plots in his maliki right and two of his witnesses, namely, P.Ws. 2 and 3 have deposed that the pre-emptor has the land contiguous to the disputed plots. Thus it was also the duty of the Court below to consider as to whether the pre-emptor is a contiguous owner of the disputed plots, since it is not the case of either of the party that such sub-division was finally effected under section 117(3) of the Act. I do not find any light from the judgments of the Courts below as to whether the land of the plots under pre-emption has also been recorded in the other M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844. In support of the contention, Mr. M. Shebabullah. the learned Advocate has referred to a decision reported in 29 DLR. 153 in which the original C.S. Khatian was split up into four different khatians and in respect of such split up khatians pre-emption was sought for by the owner of the other khatians, where it has been decided that since those khatians were amicably allowed to be prepared out of the parent khatian, the pre-emptor and his other co. sharers virtually waived their right to claim co-sharership into the disputed khatians. Since I do not find any material that in the instant case the two khatians were allowed to be prepared amicably by the co-sharers, in my opinion, the decision reported in 29 D.L R. is distinguishable on facts. Mr. S.K. Sinha, learned Advocate in support of his contention has also cited a decision reported in 33 D.L.R. (A. D.) 323 in the case of Md. A. Rouf and others vs. Mahmuda Khatun and others. He has also referred to another case reported in the same volume of 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. from the decision reported in 3 D.L.R (A. D.) it is clear, so far as the sub-division of the original holding is concerned under section I l7(1)-c) of the Act, that it is mandatory to notify all other co-sharers before passing order for such subdivision. In the instant case since no material is available from the judgments of the Courts below that such sub-division of holding was done either amicably or by an application under section 117(1)(c) of the Act, I am afraid to come to any definite conclusion that the pre-emptor has either lost his right of pre-emption as a co-sharer or his interest in the original jamal still exists. In such view of the matter I am of the opinion that for the interest of justice the applications for pre-emption should be heard by the trial court afresh.

lawyer:
M. Fazlul Karim With Nurul Islam Chowdhury ----- For the Appellant. 
Sharifuddin Chaklader ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Abdur Razzak ----- Appellant
Vs.
Rabeya Khatun ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs case in short is that the land in suit previously belonged to one Wahed Ali who executed a deed of gift in the year 1925 A.D. in favour of his sisters sons Thanda Mia and Omra Mia defendant Nos. 2 and 5 respectively and delivery of possession of the same to them. The defendants Nos. 1 and 5 since the gift continued to remain in possession of the suit land and the said property was recorded in C.S. record of right in the name of both the defendants in 4 annas share each of the entire land being the gifted property. The remaining 8 annas share of the property was recorded in the names of his 2 daughters namely Ambia defendant No. 3), Rabya Khatun (defendant No. 1) and his wife. When defendant Nos. 1 and 5 had been in possession of the gifted property the plaintiff purchased the 4 annas of defendant No. 5, Orma Mia by a registered sale deed in the year 959 A.D. vide Ext. 1 and his name had been recorded in the S.A. khatian to the extent of his purchase. But as there was difficulty in possessing ejmali he demanded partition, but being refused he brought the suit for partition and for separate saham of his purchased share. 

 12. The principle thus enunciated was followed in the case of Mst. Khan Bibi Vs. Mst. Sufia Begum, reported in P.L.D. 1969 Lah. at page 388, Lad Jan Vs. Mohammad Shaft Allan, reported in I.L.R. 34 All at page 478. Following those authorities as quoted above I find that the finding of the court of appeal below to the effect that the said condition reserving the usufruct for the life time of the donee and control over said usufruct would make the gift a contingent gift purported to take effect in future and thus a void gift is wholly erroneous as in the said document (Ext. A (1) there is nothing to how that the possession or dominion over the corpus of the said property was also reserved or postponed to a future date. That the said was not the intention would be evident by the entry in the records of right of the entire gifted property of the donor in the name of the donee namely, Thanda Mia and Omra Mia in the R.S. Records. The said R.S. khatian was prepared in the year 1929 and completed in 1930 immediately after the deed of gift was executed and registered in 1925 without any objection from the donor. An entry in the khatian is not an evidence of title by itself but it is an evidence of possession and a strong presumptive evidence of title also (Ref: 30 D.L.R. (S.C.) 81 and following the principle as enunciated by the Privy Council in the case referred to earlier the donee would be considered to be in constructive possession of the said gifted property and would be construed that the said gift was in fact followed by possession as evidenced by the entry in the C.S. khatian in the names of the donee. There is evidence on record that the donor died long before and the defendants donee had been in possession of the suit land since after the death of Wahed Ali. 

 13. The court of appeal below however took notice of the fact that the name of the plaintiffs vendor was recorded in the R.S. khatian and having taking notice of the said the learned court took the view that through the said was recorded as such the said entry was absolutely void and without basis as the gift itself was void ab initio. If the deed of gift was a valid one, the said entry perhaps could have been taken into consideration by the court of appeal below, in proving prima facie the plaintiffs vendors possession of the gifted suit land, to the extent of his 4 annas share. 

 14. The construction of a title document is a question of law. Findings of fact arrived at by misconstruction of a document are liable to be set aside in second appeal but only when the said document was a document of title and was the foundation of a suit, being in the nature of a contract or a document of title and hence the construction of a kabuliyat or the construction of an entry in a khatian used as a document of title or the construction of a deed, purporting to be a deed of gift would amount to a question of law (Refer 120 I.C. at page 557). In the instant case the court of appeal below arrived at the finding of fact to the effect that the gift was not a void gift as it purported to take effect in future by reserving the usufruct was arrived at on a misreading and misconstruction of the document of gift and upon a wrong view of the law, causing an error of law affecting the merits of the case and thus it needs to be set aside. The finding of the court of appeal below as to possession was also arrived at only on a consideration of the fact that as the gift was void there could not be any question of possession on the strength of the gift which was again erroneous as it was arrived at without taking into consideration the presumption of correctness attached to an entry in the R.S. khatian and without taking into consideration the evidence as to the possession of the plaintiff evidenced by the entry in the R.S. khatian and the evidence on record and without taking into consideration the legal position that even a possession under a document of title which subsequently proved to be a void document, would create a title in favour of the possessor if possessed for a period of more than 12 years, by adverse possession. On the premises above I find enough substance in this appeal and the said need to be allowed.

lawyer:
B.N. Chowdhury, Advocate, instructed by A. Rab-II, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant. 
M.H. Khandker, Sr. Advocate, instructed by Daliluddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent No.1. 
Ex-parte ----- Respondent No. 2-5.
parties:
Lal Meah, being dead his heirs Momena Khatun & ors ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Haji Md. Ibrahim Meah and ors ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J. This is a Defendant's appeal by special leave arising out of a suit for recovery of possession of the suit land upon declaration of the plaintiffs title therein. The suit land is R.S. Plot No. 158 of mouza Madar Bari, Chittagong recorded in Khatian No. 234. Plaintiff says that the suit plot was recorded in raiyati right of Abdus Subhan. Plaintiff took, long lease of the land from the heirs of Subhan. This land is to the contiguous east of other lands of the plaintiff. They were wrongfully taken possession of by the defendants but the plaintiff succeeded in obtaining a decree for their eviction in Title Suit No. 5 of 1947. Out of spite for eviction, the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff by dismantling collie huts on the disputed lands 10 May, 1955. Hence the suit. 

 4. On appeal by the plaintiff the first appellate Court found that the defendant's claim of title on the basis of Ext. B, Kabuliyat standing in the name of Ramzan did not subsist. He referred to two judgments, one in Title Suit No. 5 of 1941, and the other S.C.C. Suit No. 290 of 1941, Ext. 7(a) and 11. He also referred to Ext. F, written statement of Abdul Majid, father of defendant No. 1. Along with them, he considered Ext. 10, Khatian No. 234, relating to the suit land, and came to the conclusion that from these papers it was established that Ramzan's 5 years tenancy on the basis of Ext. was terminated by his superior landlord, Moifula Khatun, who in her turn settled the land with other tenants. The decisions of the aforesaid suits were binding on defendant No. 1 regarding this claim of title, As. regards plaintiff's title he differed with the, trial Court on the presumptive value of Khatian and treated it is evidence of title as well. He thereafter considered the oral and documentary evidence of both the plaintiff and defence on possession. He considered Ext. A to A4 Municipal demand register, Ext. C to C-7 the Municipal Tax receipts, Ext. G and G-l sale deeds, Ext. D and Ext. E filed by Defendant No. 1 and hold that they did not establish adverse possession of the defence on the suit land. He held so, after rejecting the second pleader commissioner's report. Earlier, a pleader commissioner's report had been rejected. The reason for rejecting the second report was that it was not prepared by surveying the land or with reference to the Municipal map. He disbelieved the defence witnesses but believed the plaintiff's witnesses, and found that the plaintiff succeeded in proving his dispossession in 1955 He hold that defendant No. 1 erected pucca and katcha structures on the land after dispossession of plaintiff. He also held that the plaintiff's suit was not barred by limitation. He reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the suit. 

 7.The points referred to in the leave order, though mentions question of title, and possession separately, yet in facts of the present case, the two questions are interdependent arid should be treated as such. It is to be remembered that the suit plot viz., R.S. 158 of Khatian No. 234 is part of the Kabuliyat land of Ramzan, grandfather of the appellant. We are to proceed with the questions of title and possession, keeping this basic fact in view. Both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 claim tenancy right in the land. They also claim possessory right over the land, defendant No. 1 claims expressly adverse possession, and plaintiff by implication, in tracing his title from Subhan. Plaintiff, however, came with the. story of possession followed by dispossession and is seeking eviction of defendants from the suit land. It is well settled that when a defendant is in possession, he could be evicted only by person having a better title than he. In such suit, plaintiff can only succeed by proving his better title over suit land. Has the plaintiff succeeded in doing so in the present case ? 

 9. Plaintiff claims a derivative title from Subhan. According to him Subhan held the suit land in rayati right which was inherited by his heirs, two sons and wife, and they, by a patta, Ext. 4 dated 28-7-54, settled the land with him. Plaintiff in 1955 purchased the superior rayati right of his lessors, and thereby succeeded to the sixteen annas title of Subhan in the suit land. No doubt plaintiff.has produced the Patta Ext. 4, and the Kabla received from the heirs of Subhan one in 1954, and the other in 1955. The question is not the validity of the patta, but whether the lessors of the plaintiff had any transferable right. That again depends upon the fact whether they inherited any such transferable right from their predecessor, Subhan. Is there any evidence to show that Subhan held any tenancy right as claimed by the plaintiff ? The plaintiff except making his own bare assertion, and reliance on R.S. Khatian, Ext. 10, has adduced no evidence, oral or documentary. Plaintiff being a transferee from the heirs of Subhan, has not and cannot claim direct knowledge of the creation of tenancy in favour of Subhan. He could, however, lead evidence to prove the creation of tenancy. That he has not done. His case of title rests on the alleged presumption of correctness of settlement records. 

 10. The High Court has taken a view that although, an entry in the record of right would indicate the possessory right of the person whose name appears therein, but this also lends support to the claim of title made by the plaintiff. It seems to us, that this view of the High Court does not state the correct view of law on the presumption arising from the record of right. Both the learned counsel have on this point, cited a number of decisions. Apart from the cited decisions, there are a large number of authorities on this point, Some of them may be mentioned. Rani Harshamukhi Vs. Kshitindra, 47 C.W.N. 662, Anup Mahto Vs. Mita Dusadh 38 C.W.N. 365 (P.C.), Sri Nath Rai Vs. Pratap Udai Nath Sahi Deo, 28 C.W.N. 145 (P.C.), Pankajini Debi Vs. Suair Dutta 60 C.W.N. 793, Munnalal Vs. Mst. Kashibai 51 C.W.N. 175, Narendra Vs ( Rajendra 45 C.W.N. 654 ; Rai Kiran Chandra Roy Bahadur Vs. Srinath Chakrabarti 31 C.W.N. 135, Kumar Rai Vs. Baraboni Coal A.I.R. 1935 Calcutta 368, Jemarat Ali Vs. Rahman Sardar 17 D.L.R. Dacca 589, Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 392. 

 11. Not all the cited authorities are. directly on the question before us, nor do we feel the necessity of referring to all of them in detail. From the cited decisions, we find that the preponderance of the judicial opinion is that the presumption of correctness arsing from the record of right under s. 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act raises a presumption of possession in favour of person whose name is recorded therein at the time of its final publication. No forward or backward presumption arises from correctness of record of right. For drawing backward presumption there must be some evidence. Forward presumption however is not available from the s. 103B of Bengal Tenancy Act, but a presumption of continuity may be drawn under s. 114 (d) of the Evidence Act. This forward presumption becomes weaker with the passage of time, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. 

 13. We may now turn to the facts of the case. R.S. Khatian of the plot, Ext. 10, shows a tenancy was recorded in the name of Subhan under, Moifula Khatun. The record of right was published some time in 1927. Initial presumption of correctness of recording of possession of 1927 in favour of Subhan is there. Barring Khatian, the plaintiff has led no evidence on the creation of tide of Subhan. Plaintiff leading no evidence, either oral or documentary, cannot use the Khatian as evidence of title in favour of Subhan. The High Court was wrong in presuming title in favour of Subhan barely relying on Khatian. Bereft of this Khatian, there is no evidence of creation tenancy in favour of Subhan. The plaintiff has failed to prove that the heirs of Subhan acquired any transferable right to confer upon plaintiff by patta Ext. 4 Plaintiff has therefore valid to make out a valid title in his favour on the basis of Patta, 

 16. Defendant No. 1’s claim both as regards title and adverse possession has failed; still then for the plaintiff to succeed, he has to make out a title in his favour. Though the plaintiff has failed on the acquisition of his title from Subhan's heir on the basis of Patta Ext. 4 yet prescriptive title of his predecessors may nonetheless subsist by continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs Plaintiff's registered patta Ext. 4 as a genuine document remains unchallenged, and so, if, he can show possessory title of his predecessors for the prescriptive period, he can still succeed in showing the acquisition of title in his favour. It appears, that this question bas not drawn the attention of either the First. Appellate Court or the High Court since they found title for plaintiff on the basis of patta But that finding having failed, this question assumes importance, and has now become decisive. It will be open to plaintiff to show the continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs, either direct or constructive on the Suit land for the prescriptive period before the grant of Patta in his favour. We feel that a determination of this question is necessary for complete adjudication of dispute between the parties. It is a mixed question of law and fact. We think therefore, the case should be remitted to the First appellate Court for decision of this narrow question; whether Subhan and his heirs were in possession direct or constructive at least from 1927, the year of publication of the Khatian till the Patta in 1954 was granted in favour of the plaintiff. Alternatively the plaintiff can show Subhan and/or his heirs were in possession for over the prescriptive period of 12 years prior to the grant of Patta on 28-7-54. Plaintiff, succeeding in establishing any of the alternatives, will be entitled to a decree for eviction on declaration of his title, as all other relevant questions have concurrently been held by the appellate Courts below in his favour. In this view of the matter, we refrain from making any observation on this question. The Court shall proceed to decide on the evidence already on record.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed A.B. Mahmud Husain
Mr. Justice A. F. M. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury

lawyer:
A. F. Hasan Arif; Senior Advocate, instructed by Mrs. Mahmuda Begum, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants 
Goutom Kumar; D.A.G instructed by Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Md. Abdul Matin Kazi and others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts for the disposal of the appeal, in short, are that the appellants instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of their title in the suit covering an area of 1.20 acres of C.S. Plot No. 1 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 53 of Mouza Kakrail., Police Station Ramna, (former Keranigonj) Dhaka alleging, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands measuring 48.90 acres of said Plot and Khatian corresponding to S.A. Plot No.64 and S.A. Khatian No. 26 originally belonged to Bhawal Zaminder Rajkumer Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury who settled the suit land to Ashraf Ali Kazi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs executing a pattannama on 05.02.1905. Said Ashraf Ali Kazi took over possession of the suit land and paid rent to the Zaminder. In C.S. operation, the suit land along with other lands of the disputed jam, was recorded in the name of Public Works Department under Bharat Samrat. Against the said record of right Ashraf Ali Kazi filed objection to get the same corrected and got an order on 24.05.1925. In S.A. operation the same was again recorded in the name of Public Works Department. On 12.01.1992, the plaintiffs discovered the pattannama, rent receipts and mutated C.S. Khatian in an old box in their house. On 08.03.1992, they collected the certified copies of the S.A. and C.S. Khatians and confirmed about the erroneous preparation of S.A. record of right. Thereafter, they filed this suit. 

 3. The defendant-respondents contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the that the suit land along with other lands covering 48.90 acres originally belonged to Public Works Department under Bharat Samrat. Accordingly, the same was recorded in C.S. Plot No. 1 and khatian No. 53. Subsequently the Deputy. Commissioner, Dhaka took over possession of the suit land. The story of settlement of the plaintiffs from Bhawal Rajkumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury is false and the document produced by the plaintiffs are forged and fabricated. The C.S. Khatian had not been corrected at the instance of the plaintiffs' predecessor. The corrected Khatian produced by the plaintiffs is forged. The Government has been possessing the suit land. The Government started to construct buildings in the suit land for residential purpose of higher Government Officials. The S.A. record of right was duly prepared in the name of the Government. The suit should be dismissed. 

 6. Mr. A.F. Hasan Arif, the senior Counsel 'appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-appellants got the suit land by way of settlement in the year 1905 and produced more than 30 years old pattannama (exhibit-1) . The plaintiffs paid rents to the Zaminder vide Exhibit-2 series and they got the C.S. Khatian corrected vide exhibit-3 series and had been possessing the suit land more than 87 years. The third Judge of the High Court Division has committed an error of law in disbelieving the pattannama, corrected C.S. Khatian and rent receipts. He submits that the findings of the third Judge of the High Court Division regarding authenticity of exhibit-1 made in an old British Indian Stamp of 1905, and the rent receipts (exhib-it-2 series), the corrected C.S. Khatian (exhibit 3 series) and exhibit-4, the volume book of Government containing C.S. Khatian are erroneous. He further submits that since price of the land was Tk. 15/- only as it appears in the pattannama, the same was not required to he registered under section 17 of the Registration Act. 

 7. Mr. Goutom Kumar, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the High Court Division on vivid discussions on the materials on record came to the conclusion that the pattannama, rent receipts of the Zamindar and corrected C.S. Khatian are forged and fabricated documents. He submits that Mr. Justice Md. Abdur Rashid rightly directed to prosecute the plaintiff-appellants initiating proceeding under Section 476 read with 195 (1) (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on allegation of forging those documents. He submits that the plaintiffs had no title-and possession in the suit land. The Government, constructing the buildings in the suit land; has been possessing the same. The instant suit was not at all maintainable without the prayer for recovery of khas possession. 

 9. The case of the plaintiffs is that their predecessor Ashraf Ali Kazi took settlement of the suit land on the basis of pattannama dated 05.02.1995 (exhibit-i). P.W.1 Abdul Matin Kazi, who was about 67 years old at the time of adducing his evidence on 19.08.1994 (that is, he was born after 22 years of alleged execution of the said pattannama) in his evidence, inter alia, said, এই সেই পত্তন নামার মূল কপি প্রঃ- ১ হিসাবে চিহ্নিত। কোর্ট দাখিল করিলাম। বিবাদীপক্ষে এই মর্মে আপত্তি যে, লেখা অষ্পষ্ট ও ছেড়া প্রঃ ১টি। নোটারি পাবলিক কর্তৃক প্রত্তন নামার সত্যায়িত টাইপ কপি দাখিল করিলাম। প্রঃ ১(ক) আপত্তি সহকারে”। The is, exhibit-1 and 1(Ka) had been admitted in evidence with objection. The plaintiffs examined P.W.2 Sailendra Nath Sarker, a man of 78 years old, to prove the pattannama. In his cross-examination he said " ১নং প্রদর্শনী পড়তে পারব না।" From his evidence it appears that this witness was horn sometime in 1916, that is, after 11 years of the alleged execution of the pattannama. In order to substantiate the contents of the pattannama, the plaintiffs produced a notarized copy of the said pattannama exhibit-1(ka) P.W. 2 admitted that contents of the exhibit-1 are not readable. The plaintiffs did not examine the writer of the duplicated pattannama nor they examined the notary public, who notarized the same. In such view of the matter, Ext.1(Ka) could not be relied on. In the case of Harihar Prashad Vs. Desnarain reported in AIR 1956 SC 305 it was observed that the presumption enacted in Section 90 of the Evidence Act can be raised only with reference to original documents not to copies thereof. Furthermore, it appears that from Ext.1(Ka) that Ext.1 had been executed by Sree Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya on behalf of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury. The P.W. 2, who claimed to be the Tahsilder of Bhawal Estate and joined in the said Estate in 1346 B.S., did not say in his evidence that Sree Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya was the Manager of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, the Zaminder of Bhawal Estate. The plaintiffs failed to produce any other evidence to prove that Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya was the manager of the Estate. 

 10. Submission of Mr. Arif is that since the Ext. 1 Pattannama is an old document of more than 30 years and had been produced from proper custody, the court would presume that the signature and every other part of Ext.1 is that person's hand writing and, the same had been duly executed by the person by whom it purports to be executed as per provision of Section 90 of the Evidence Act. The spirit of section 90 of the Evidence Act is that if private documents not less than thirty years old are produced from proper custody and are on their face free from suspicion, the court may presume at they w have been signed or written by the persons whose signatures they bear or in whose hand writing they purport to he, that they have been duly attested and executed, if they purport so to he Section 90 only lays down that the court may presume that document purporting to be 30 years old are genuine. That it must not presume them to be so. Supreme Court of India in the case of Sri Lakhi Baruah Vs. Sri Padma Kanta Kalita reported in AIR 1996 SC 1253 observed that Section 90 of the Evidence Act is founded on necessity and convenience because it is extremely difficult and sometimes not possible to lead evidence to prove handwriting, signature or execution of old documents after lapse of 30 years. In order to obviate such difficulties or improbabilities to prove execution of an old documents section 30 has been incorporated in the Evidence Act, which does away with the strict rule of proof of private documents. Presumption of genuineness may he raised if the document in question is produced from proper custody. It is, however, the discretion of the Court to accept the presumption flowing from Section. The presumption is permissive and accordance no the circumstances of each case the court may or may not raise it. That is, such presumption discretionary and so where a document is suspicious on the face of it or mutilated, the court may refuse to make presumption. It is not obligatory on a court to raise the presumption. The language being "may" when the person who has been examined as P.W.2 to prove the Ext.1 himself has said “১নং প্রদর্শনী পড়তে পারবো না"; then why the court will rely upon such document .At the time of making exhibit the defendant raised objection saving, লেখা অষ্পষ্ট ও ছেড়া প্রঃ ১টি। In such circumstances, the provision of section 90 ought to be applied with more care and great caution because nothing can he more easy than, for an unscrupulous ours person, who is wrongfully in possession and wants to make out a title to it to forge such document in his favour more than 30 years old and produce it as the proper custodian relieving himself of the necessity of proving its execution. The Ext. 1 patina must not be presumed to he genuine merely from its being ancient. Some other evidence were required to be given of the early existence and publicity of Ext. 1 . Neither C. S. khatian nor S. A. khatian had been prepared on the basis of Ext. 1. 

 11. In order to show the existence and publicity of Ext.1 or in other words to prove the story of their settlement dated 11.02.1905 and rebut the presumption under Section 103. B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, which is available in favour of the Government since C.S. record of right was prepared in favour of the Government ( Ext. A), the plaintiffs produced Ext .2 series, the Zamindari dakhilas and alleged corrected khatian Ext. 3 series. It is the claim of the plaintiffs that against C.S. Khatian their predecessor Ashraf Ali Kazi filed Objection Case No. 327H/1932 and got his name corrected in the Zamindery Sherista and obtained certified copies of the corrected Khatian from Zamindery sherist- Correction of the entry in Khatian filing objection in the Zamindery Sherista is totally illegal. As per provision of Section 108A of the Bengal Tenancy Act, which was transferred as section 115B, by the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1928, only the Revenue Officer specially empowered by the Government on application or of his own motion, within two years (earlier time limit was for 12 months) from the date of certificate of the final publication of the record of right under sub-section (2) of Section 103A, correct any entry in such record of rights which he was satisfied had been made owing to a bonafide mistake. That is, Revenue Officer was legally authorized to correct the Khatian nobody else. The concerned volume regarding P.S. Khatian was called for to ascertain the authenticity of Ext. 3 series which was marked as Ext. 4 . T. Islam, J examined Ext. 3 series, the corrected Khatian produced by the plaintiffs and relevant volume book of C.S. khatian Ext. 4 thoroughly. Such examination, as it appears from his observation that the same was made most carefully which is praise-worthy. 

 "I have gone through Ext. 4, which is the volume of Mouza 282 Kakrail produced before the trial court. In C.S. Khatian Nos. 1, 2, 9-10, 13, 24, 53 and 55 as contained in Ext. 4, on the top of the front page at the left hand side under the heading  উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words "ভারত সম্রাট" have been printed and out of the above Khatian at the right hand side of the Khatian Nos. 1, 2, 9-10, 13-24 under the heading উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে বিস্তারিত দখল the names of different persons were printed and in the remaining C.S. Khatian Nos. 53 and 57, under this very heading at right hands side, public works Department and District Board respectively, both on behalf of Bharat Samrat were printed. In C.S. Khatian Nos. 3, 4, 5, 6 and 17 as contained in Ext. 4 similarly under the heading উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the word পত্তন রাজেন্দ্র নারায়ণ রায় ৩নং কুমার রবিন্দ্র নারায়ন রায় চৌধুরী ওয়ারিশগণ পক্ষে কোর্ট অফ ওয়ার্ড were printed and out of the above khatian under the heading অত্র স্বত্ব/অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল of C.S. Khatian Nos.  4,5 and 6 the names of different persons were printed and in C.S. Khatian Nos. 3 and 7 only, and this heading " কুমার রবিন্দ্র নারায়ন রায় চৌধুরী ওয়ারিশগণ পক্ষে কোর্ট অফ ওয়ার্ডস’"Were printed. 

 In C.S. Khatian Nos. 31-32, 33Ka, 34-35, 39-40, 43, 46-47 and 47Ka as contained in Ext. 4 under the heading উপরিস্তস্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words পত্তনী কালীন নারায়ন রায় ৩০নং দখল কুমার রবিন্দ্র নারায়ন রায় চৌধুরী ওয়ারিশগণ পক্ষে কোর্ট অফ ওয়ার্ডস were printed and under the heading অত্র স্বত্ব/অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্���ারিত দখল the name of different persons were printed and in C.S. Khatian No. 8, as contained in Ext. 4 under the heading উপরিস্থ স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words মিরস জামাল, ৭নং রবিন্দ্র নারায়ন রায় চৌধুরী ওয়ারিশগণ পক্ষে কোর্ট অফ ওয়ার্ড were printed and under the heading অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the name of Sheikh Abdul was printed. 

 In C.S. Khatian Nos. 30, 51Ka and 51 Kha as contained in Ext. 4, under the heading অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the words সিকিম তালুক রামকৃষ্ণ দত্ত were printed and out of the above Khatians, in C.S. Khatian No. 30 under the heading অত্র স্বত্ব/অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the words কুমার রবিন্দ্র নারায়ন রায় চৌধুরী ওয়ারিশগণ পক্ষে কোর্ট অফ ওয়ার্ডস were printed and in Khatian No. 51 Ka and 51 Kha under the above heading of অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the names of other persons were printed. 

 In C.S. Khatian No. 25-27 and 51 as contained in Ext. 4 under the heading উপরিসত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words and also the names of 13 co-sharers of the Zamindari were printed and under the heading অত্র স্বত্ব/অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the name of different persons were printed. 

 Thus in the Khatians mentioned above on the front page on the top at left hand side under the heading উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/ পরিচয়ে the names of Zamindars were printed and at the right hand side under the heading অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the name of tenants/riots were printed and at the over leafs of some of the above Khatians, the names of the possessors were printed. 

 Regarding C.S. Khatian No. 53 as contains in Ext. 4, as it appears at left hand side under the heading উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words উপরিস্ত স্বত্ব/পরিচয়ে the words ভারত সম্রাট were printed and under the heading অত্র স্বত্ব/ অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল the name of Public Works Department on behalf of Bharat Samrat, have been printed and it is only at the over leaf, Kumar Rabindra Narayan himself was shown as mere possessors of 48.90 acres of land in C.S. Plot No. 1 as stated earlier, in C.S. Khatian Nos. 3-7, 8, 30, 31, 32, 32 Ka 33, 34, 39; 40, 43,47, 51Ka and 51 Kha of Ext. 4 in most of the cases the Court of words of the heirs of Kumar Rabindra Narayan have been shown as Zamindars and in few cases the above court of words have been shown ryot under the heading" অত্র স্বত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল and is none of the above Khatians Kumar Rabindra Narayan himself was not shown as Zamindar or tenant. It thus appears that on 23.04.1917, when the above C.S. Khatian were finally published, Kumar Rabindra Narayan ceased hold any interest in any of the above Khatians and instead the court of wards of his heirs were shown as Zamindar and tenants. 

 Accordingly how in C.S. Khatian No. 53 as contained in Ext. 4 Kumar Rabindra Narayan could be shown as possessor and like wise how in Ext. 3 also Kumar Rabindra Narayan himself could be shown as Zamindar." 

 14. Mr. Arif failed to satisfy this court making any submission to discard aforesaid findings referring any material on record. The aforesaid findings arrived at by the last court of facts are based evidence. Since Kumer Rabindra Narayon was neither landlord nor tenant in the land recorded in Khatian No. 53 and plot No. 1 no one, claiming himself as manager of Kumer Rabindra Narayon Chowdhury, had any authority to settle the same on his behalf. He was not a person immediately under whom the tenant holds and no tenancy had been established pursuant to Ext. 1 in re sport of the suit land. 

 15. The C.S. record of right was prepared in the name Public Works Department under Bharat Samrat. Such record of right is evidence of the matter referred to in the entry and should be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. Since such presumption being a statutory one could not be taken away mere by allegation that the same is incorrect. The burden of proving that such entry in the record of right is incorrect is on the party who alleges it. In this case the plaintiffs failed to rebut the presumption by adducing evidence. The documentary evidence produced by the plaintiffs are found to be forged and fraudulent one by the Court of facts. 

 16. The plaintiffs stated that their predecessor Ashraf Ali Kazi died sometime in 1948. It has also been stated in the plaint that in 1992 the plaintiffs allegedly got the papers produced in the Court in an old box. The plaintiffs did not produce any materials in support of their claim to deal with the property, at least, from 1948 to 1992. They did not take any step to record their names in the khatian and to pay rent to the Government. It is totally unacceptable proposition' that one, who is allegedly in possession in the land and structure thereon within Dhaka City Corporation, would not take any step to record/ mutate his name in the khatian, pay rent, municipal taxes, WASA, Gas bills etc.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 599 of 1998.
lawyer:
For the petitioner: Mr. M. A. Sobhan Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record. 
Respondent: Not represented.
parties:
Taleb All Pramanik and others ------ Petitioners.
Versus
Serajul Haque Mondal and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The suit is one for declaration of title to 2.33 acres of land recorded in C.S. Plot No. 9 and 10 of Khatian No. 4 fully described in the schedule to the plaint. The case of the plaintiffs is briefly this: One Salimuddin had raiyati interest in the disputed plots. Majitullah, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs had Korfa interest under Salimuddin. The raiyati of Salimuddin was auction sold for arrears of rent in 1934. Mobarak, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants, auction purchased the holding. He did not annual the Korfa interest of Majitullah but recognised him as a tenant. In the M.R.R. Khatian the suit plots had, however, been wrongly recorded in the name of the defendants. 

 3. Defendant No. 1 (Respondent No.1) contested the suit. His defence on the other hand, is that Majitullah surrendered his Korfa interest in favour of Salimuddin and continued to possess the land as bargadar under him executing registered kabuliyats. The interest of Mobarak who auction-purchased the holding devolved upon the defendants by way of inheritance. Mobarak sold 1.68 acres to Miazan, one of sons of Salimuddin. Accordingly their names were correctly recorded in the M.R.R. Khatian. The defendants have had been in possession of the disputed lands and the plaintiffs have no right, title or interest therein. 

 8. On behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners it is argued that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has failed to notice that the presumption of correctness of the entries in the C.S. Khatia.1 under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act had not been rebutted. 

 9. it is no doubt true that an entry in the C.S. Khatian must be presumed to be correct unless the contrary is proved, but when the matter is investigated by the Court on the evidence adduced by the parties on the point in controversy, the entry loses its significance. In the instant case, the lower appellate court, after a detailed discussion of the evidence of the parties came to the conclusion that after the auction sale of the raiyat interest of Salimuddin in 1939 there had been a change in the status and possession of the parties. Therefore the presumption of right, title and possession on the basis of C.S. Khatian did not hold good any more.

full_judgment:
3. In Writ Petition No. 2678 of 2005, wife, and sons and daughters of one Abdul Khaleque Khan are the petitioners. Their common case is that 1.54 acres of land of CS plot No. 163 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 of Mouza Keraniganj, then Tejgaon, at present Dhanmondi, originally belonged to respondent No. 2, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards for and on behalf of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and his sons in sixteen Annas permanent Jamindari rights and CS Khatian was accordingly, prepared in their names. In 1336 BS, said land was settled with one Radha Sham Banik by a registered deed being No. 910 dated 25-4-29 AD, who possessed the land by payment of rents up to 1953 BS, Annexure A. 

 5. After the wholesale acquisition under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, in short, the SAT Act, rent receiving interest of aforesaid land receiver was acquired and Rahima Dad Khan became 'Malik' directly under the Government and his name was accordingly, recorded in Review Khatian in 161 and 164 dated 24-1-1959, Annexures D and D1. 

 8. Then, by various registered deeds of gift during 1984 and 1985 some lands were transferred and possession was handed over to the petitioners amongst themselves, Annexure I series. Transferee petitioners got their names mutated and possessed the case land by payment of rents upto 1410 BS, Annexure J series. On the basis of their possession, RS record of rights were also prepared in their names and finally published in respect of RS Plot No. 1229, 1258, 1261, 1266, 1259 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 386, Annexure K. 

 10. Under the present Mohanagar Survey 0.3864 acres of land out of case land was recorded in the name of Abdus Samad Khan (petitioner No. 3); 0.3864 acres of land in the name of Abdus Salam Khan (Petitioner No.2); 0.3864 was recorded in the name of Abdus Sadek Khan (Petitioner No.4); 0.3160 was recorded in the names of Mrs Romisa Khanam (Petitioner No.1); 0.0712 acres of land was recorded in the name of Shaheda Khanam (Petitioner No.6) and 0.1620 acre in the names of Sanjida Khanam and Shahela Khanam (Petitioner Nos. 7 and 8) as the Tasdik stage correctly. 

 11. Against such draft record-of-rights, respondent No. 2 filed objections under Rule 30 of the Rules, 1955 being case Nos. 248, 249, 254 and 255 of 1999. The Objection Officer heard them together and rejected each of them by his order dated 17-1-1999, Annexure N. 

 13. Then, respondent No. 2 made an application before the settlement officer at Dhaka against the aforesaid appellate order and other orders disposing of 25 similar appeals for rehearing. The Appeal Officer took up hearing of 39 appeals, which were sent by the Settlement Officer by his memo dated 18-11-02 including rehearing of 13 appeals including those against the petitioners for analogous hearing. By the impugned order dated 10-2-03 the Appeal Officer set aside his earlier order dated 5-12-1999 and allowed 32 appeals in part directing to record the name of Court of Wards in place of the petitioners and others and to record the petitioners and others in column 9 as জোড় দখল that is forceful possession and forwarded the same for approval of the Settlement Officer. The Settlement Officer approved the said appellate order by his countersignature. 

 14. By filing a supplementary affidavit, the petitioners annexed photocopy of registered deed of Dak Pattan dated 25-4-29, the record of said Radha Shayam Banik, the gazette notification being No. 2773 LR dated 26-2-52 published in the Dacca Gazette Extraordinary dated 24-3-52 and No. 3126 LR dated 27-2-56 published in the Dacca Gazette Extraordinary dated 29-2-56 as Annexures R, RI and S, SI. 

 15. Of the respondents, respondent No. 1 represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land and respondent No.2, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards represented by a manager appeared and filed affidavits-in-opposition. In the affidavit of respondent No.1, it is stated that said respondent No. 2 made an application to the Settlement Officer for cancellation of the order passed by the Appeal Officer under Rule 31 of the Rules, 1955 and for rehearing of the appeals. The Settlement Officer accordingly cancelled the aforesaid appeal order under Rule 42 of said Rules, 1955 and appointed Mr Moshiur Rahman (respondent No. 7) Appeal Officer and Charge Officer by his memo dated 18-12-02 for disposal of the appeals afresh. Respondent No. 8 Appeal Officer heard the appeals and allowed the same and asked to record the name of respondent No.2, which was approved by the Settlement Officer on 6-3-2003. The Appeal Officer decided the appeals in accordance with the guidelines issued by respondent No.3, Secretary vide his letter dated 10-10-02. 

 16. The petitioners managed to record their names in respect of the case land. As per direction of the Ministry of Land issued time to time, the Directorate of Land Records and Survey updated the maps and records of the land in the country. The petitioners did not acquire any right or title on the basis of the documents annexed to the writ petition from said Court of Wards Estate, which was holder of intermediary interest. 

 19. After the land in question was recorded in the name of the petitioners, respondent No. 2 on behalf of the government filed objection under Rule 30 of the Rules, 1955, which was rejected. Then he presented appeal under Rule 31 of the aforesaid Rules, which was also rejected. Then, upon an application respondent No. 2, the Settlement Officer under Rule 42 of said Rules set aside the appellate order and asked the Appeal Officer to hear and dispose of the appeals afresh as per law and rules. Accordingly, the appeal were heard and allowed. 

 20. The present Rule was obtained after two years of the impugned order. In the meantime, new record was finally published in the Gazette. In sup- port a copy of attested Khatian No. 194 was annexed as Annexure- Y (4) but no Gazette could be produced. After final publication of the record-of- rights, an aggrieved person may institute a suit before the Land Survey Tribunal created under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the Act IX of2004 and the writ petition is not maintainable. 

 21. It is further stated that petitioner No. 1 already instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 96 of 2005 for permanent injunction in the First Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Dhaka and ultimately, has withdrawn the same with leave of the Court. Respondent No. 2 also instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 188 of 2006 in the Fourth Court of Joint District Judge at Dhaka for a decree declaring the SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights void, illegal, collusive, baseless and also that respondent No.2 is the owner in possession of the case land. 

 23. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioners, took us through the writ petition and submitted that having regard to the facts that after the transfer of the land by the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards by a registered deed of lease to Radha Shayam Banik in 1929 and successive registered transfers thereafter, the petitioners acquired the land in question by purchase and gift in 1960 and that SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights were prepared and finally published in the names of the petitioners and the petitioners possess the land by construction of building and living therein on payment of rents and taxes to respective authorities including the government, impugned order of respondent No.8, the Appeal Officer at the behest of respondent No.7, Settlement Officer allowing the appeals in part of respondent No.2 in the record-of-rights in the Mohanagar Survey must be held to be illegal, unauthorised and without jurisdiction. 

 24. He submitted that after the wholesale acquisition under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 of the receiving interest of said Bhawal Raj Court of Wards and Radha Shayam Banik, the petitioners became 'Malik' directly under the Government, which is evident by the gazette notifications, Annexure Sand S(1) to the writ petition and long continuous possession by the petitioners admittedly evidenced by SA record-of- rights and RS record-of-rights, respondent No.2 has got no right or interest in the land and objections raised by respondent No.2 against the draft record of rights.in Mahanagar Survey were all through rejected but at the behest of respondent No.7, Settlement Officer, the Appeal Officer most illegally allowed the appeals after rehearing of them and termed such lawful possession of the petitioners as 'Possession by Force'. 

 25. He submitted that in view of section 8A of the Court of Wards Act, 1879 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972, respondent No.2 has got no right to challenge the record-of-rights of the land which already stood acquired under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 Annexure-S and after publication of the Compensation Assessment rolls finally published under section 46E(3) of said Act, Annexure S I. In support, he cited Bangladesh vs Sree Sree Modan Gopal Jeo Begraha 33 DLR (AD) 13 and Anwara Begum vs Noorjahan Begum 27 DLR (AD) 109. 

 27. Lastly, he submitted that after the final publication of the record-of-rights both after SA survey and RS survey in the names of the petitioners and receipt of rents from the petitioners, the Government or the Revenue Authority is stopped from challenging the rights of the petitioners in the land. In support, he cited Osimuddin vs Bangladesh 1 BLC 375 and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs AKM Latiful Karim 1 BLC 567. 

 29. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances, the only issue that is facing us is, whether the impugned order passed by the Appeal Officer under Rule 31 of said Rules, 1955 in rehearing the appeals and allowing them in part is valid in law and directing to record the name of respondent No.2 in the record-of-rights and treating the possession of the petitioners as 'Possession by force'. 

 30. It is not disputed that the record-of-rights prepared under section 143 and revised under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 were finally published in the names of the petitioners in respect of the land in question. After final publication, under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act XXVIII of 1951), every entry in such record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. Such record-of-rights becomes binding upon all parties including the Government. The provisions for correction of such record-of- rights are now omitted. 

 31. It is also not disputed that in the recent Mahanagar Survey, the lands in question were recorded in the names of the petitioners and after the draft record-of-rights was published respondent No. 2 filed objections against such records under Rule 30 of the Rules; 1955. The Government however, did not file any objection to such draft record-of- rights. Objection Officer rejected all such objections. Then, respondent No. 2 filed number of appeals against rejection of all objections under Rule 31 of the Rules, 1955. The Appellate Officer dismissed all the appeals. 

 32. Then, after dismissal of the appeals by the Appellate Officer, respondent No. 2 on 14-7-2002 made an application to the Settlement Officer at Dhaka for hearing of the appeals under Rule 42A of the Rules, 1955. Under the signature of the Secretary of the Ministry of Land a circular was also circulated in respect of recording of the Government Khas land and land of Court of Wards. In the circular, the revenue authority is directed to examine the SA and RS record-of-rights by following the CS that is Cadastral Survey, record-of-rights in respect of recording the Khas land and the land of the Court of Wards. It is also stated that in case where SA record and RS record was not prepared in accordance with the rules and/or decision of the appropriate authority, it would not be proper in the present survey to have the reflection of continuity of SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights only. In such cases, the CS record shall have to be followed in the preparation of the Khatians and maps. Copy of said application and circular are annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition of said respondent No. 2 in Writ Petition No. 1512 of 2006. 

 35. It is already noted that after final publication of a record-of-rights and revised record-of- rights, every entry in such record-of-rights shall be presumed to be correct until such presumption is proved by evidence to be incorrect. The presumption arising out of such record-of-rights is of course rebuttable, which could only be possible in a properly constituted suit. It is also true that such presumption arising out of a record-of-rights relates to the time when it was prepared and with the passage of time, as the state of things starts changing and such presumption also loses its weight. But it must be remembered that a finally prepared and published record-of-rights takes precedence over the last record-of-rights. Moreover, the entries made in the CS record-of-rights which was prepared from 1917 to 1922 cannot be expected to be the same in 2002 and to override the SA record-of-rights and revised record of rights. 

 37. With regard to the second question, it is needless to say that an appeal is the creature of a statue and right to appeal therefore cannot be assumed by any authority under any law unless it is so provided. In the scheme of revision of a record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there are various stages laid down in the Rules, 1955. 

 38. After completion of attestation, the Revenue Officer shall under Rule 29 publish the draft record-of-rights for public inspection. Under Rule 30, the Revenue Officer shall decide summarily in presence of the interested parties any objection regarding ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land. Any person aggrieved by such an order on any objection made under Rule 30 may appeal to the Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer or of Assistant Settlement Officer commonly known as Appellate Officer within 30 days from the date of order appealed against. Any order passed on such appeal appears to be final as no further appeal or revision is provided therefrom. 

 39. After disposal of the objections under Rule 30 and appeals under Rule 31 and correction of the draft record-of-rights in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, the Revenue Officer shall proceed to frame final record-of-rights under Rule 31 and then, publish the final record-of- rights under Rule 33. Under Rule 34, the Revenue Officer shall within sixty days of the final publication make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof, etc. And the Government by a notification in the official gazette may declare with regard to any specified area that the record-of-rights has been finally published for every village included in such area and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. 

 40. Chapter VIII of said Rules, 1955 deals with general power of Revenue Officer in revising record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Rule 42 gives special power to a Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer to direct at any time before the publication of the final record-of-rights that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district or local area shall be cancelled and the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. Similarly, such Settlement Officer is empowered under Rule 42A upon an application or receipt of an Official Report to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in record- of-rights before final publication, and after consulting the relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, to direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to an appeal. At the same time, the Revenue Officer shall make the correct entry after hearing the parties and record his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. But none of such powers under Rule 42 or 42A of the Rules, 1955 appears to empower such Settlement Officer to sit and/or act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 and set aside such appellate order or direct the Appellate Officer to hear an appeal afresh in respect of a particular holding. Nor the Appellate Officer is empowered to rehear an appeal which was finally disposed by him. The Settlement Officer therefore most illegally cancelled the appellate orders and compelled the Appellate Officer to hear the appeals afresh. 

 41. It appears from the impugned order that the Appellate Officer allowed 32 appeals in part mainly on the view that the transfers of the Court of Wards in the light of the circular dated 10-11-2002 issued by the Secretary of the Ministry of Land did not appear to him in continuity of the CS record-of-rights. Upon such view, he directed to record the name of the Court of Wards in the recent record-of-rights and the possession of the petitioners as 'Possession by force. 

 42. It is not disputed that the petitioners possess their respective lands for more than 40 years on payment of rents to the Government. Possession of the petitioners are based on registered transfers firstly by the Court of Wards to Radha Shayam Banik in 1929 and ultimately to the petitioners. On the basis of such long and continuous possession the names of the petitioners were recorded in the recent Mahanagar Survey and all objections on behalf of respondent No.2 were rejected under Rules 30 and 31 of the Rules, 1955. 

 43. Such conclusion of the Appellate Officer as arrived by the impugned order therefore, must be held to be based on surmise and conjecture and more precisely on the instructions of the Secretary vide circular dated 10-11-2002. He fell in serious error in law in holding that possession in the lands in question, mutations after transfer of the lands, SA record-of-rights and RS record-of-rights as finally published in the names of the petitioners did not reflect the state of things as recorded in the CS record-of-rights. 

 44. In revision of a record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the particulars to be included, amongst others, are enumerated in Rule 26 of the Rules, 1955. Such particulars relate to the present state of things and not to the things which existed in 1922. Moreover, it is neither possible nor expected for such a recording officer to transfer title since 1922. Practically, such record-of-rights is to be prepared on the basis of present possession duly backed by documents of title only. It must be remembered that such record-of-rights does not confer any title though it is a very good evidence of possessory rights. The Appellate Officer definitely failed in the discharge of his duty in not considering the registered documents in support of transfers of the lands in question since 1929. Which carries statutory presumption of correctness and also the statutory presumption under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 attaching to the finally published SA record-of- rights and RS record- of-rights in the names of the petitioners. 

 45. In the famous case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury vs Kamir MandalI7 DLR (SC) 392, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held on such statutory presumption arising out of section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (Act VIII of 1885) : 

 "The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this, that the entry in the record of right represents the correct state of affairs On the date that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is the presumption value. This is a matter, therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof." 

 47. Respondent No.2 is stated to be Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate represented by manager with office in 141-143 Motijheel Commercial Area at Dhaka. As said respondent filed objections against the draft publication of the recent record-of- rights, it was so impleaded in the Rules. Section 5 of said Act clearly states that the Board of Land Administration shall be the Court of Wards for the territories to which the Act extends. Besides such Court of Wards, no other Court of Wards could be conceived in the Act. We also could not find the existence of such Act in the Indian Code. The Act might have served out the purpose. Disqualification of the proprietors of the estates both in respect of property and person ceased to exist long ago. 

 50. He submitted that after acquisition of rent receiving interest of the concerned estates, the tenants of the Bhawal Raj Estate were no more tenants under them and became "Malik" directly under the Government. Article 143(c) of the Constitution is not applicable in the case of present record-of-rights and the circular dated 10-11-2002 is illegal and any action taken thereupon must be set aside. 

 57. The Government must know its limitation and may be therefore, filed no objection to the publication of draft record-of-rights. Some manager on behalf of the Bhawal Raj Estate filed the objections and appeals. Every time, we were told, whenever revision of record-of-rights commenced, so-called manager put up objections against such record-of- rights. If the objections of such manager are heeded to then few record-of-rights in the city of Dhaka would be immune from such objections. 

 58. On the technical ground on maintainability of the writ petition, when confronted, MTH Khan failed to produce any gazette notification of final publication of the recent record-of-rights. He said due to the pendency of the Rules, the record-of- rights could not be finally published. Under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, when the Government would establish the Land Survey Tribunal only after final publication of last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144 and after establishment of such Tribunals, any suit challenging correctness of the last revised record-of-rights shall lie in such Tribunal.

4. Respondent No. 10 tried to kill time on this or that plea and ultimately, the case was fixed for hearing on 23.11.1998. Meanwhile, respondent No. 10 filed another application on 27.08.1997 before respondent No. 5, the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj with the prayer for adding 9 (nine) acres of land or 48 plots of Patleechak mouza and 26 acres of land of 106 plots of Moizpur mouza, in total 35 acres of land, to Darikhanjanpur mouza. On 18.11.1997, the petitioners filed a written objection before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamganj, respondent No. 6 opposing the prayer and stated in detail of the attempts of respondent No. 10 on different time for addition of certain plots from 2(two) different mouzas to be merged with Darikhanjanpur mouza. The office of respondent No. 5 rejected the said application for  addition of the said lands to Darikhanjanpur mouza by order dated 14.06.1998 considering the facts and circumstances of the case and all possible complicacies in respect of addition of the said two mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza.
