Against the said rejection, respondent No took an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner, Sylhet being Revenue Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 1998 who by order dated 14.12.1998 stayed operation of the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamganj and in addition opined that "proposal shall go to survey, and Settlement Dept for final decision." Accordingly, respondent No. 4 by his order dated 25.07.1999 sent the case records to the Director General of Land Records and Surveys Directorate, Tejgaon, for taking necessary action. The clever respondent, in the meantime, managed to obtain an order from the office of respondent No. 1, Secretary, Ministry of Land under the signature of respondent No. 2 vide her office Memo No.  ভূঃমঃ/শ-২ (মৌঃ নাঃ পঃ)-৫/৯৯/৪৩৭ dated 27.08.2000 of the administrative approval for addition of said 9 acres of land of 48 plots of Patleechak mouza and 26 acres of land of 106 plots of Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur mouza; hence, the petitioners filed the writ petition impugning the said memo. 

 5. It was further contended by way of submission that the office of respondent No. 1 "Passed administrative approval Notification" under the signature of respondent No. 2 vide her office Memo No.  ভূঃমঃ/শ-২ (মৌঃ নাঃ পঃ)-৫/৯৯/৪৩৭ dated 27.08.2000 without serving any notice upon the petitioners and was beyond jurisdiction as he was not empowered under rules 321 and 322 of the Bengal Survey and Settlement Manual, 1935(hereinafter referred to as the manual, 1935). The procedure laid down in rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 were also not complied with by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 before issuing the impugned notification. The application of respondent No. 10 for addition of some plots from two different mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza was rejected twice by the office of respondent No. 5 under the signature of respondent No. 6 after considering the facts and circumstances of the case against which respondent No. 10 did not approach the immediate higher authority, but taking the advantage of political influence managed to obtain an administrative approval in this regard from respondent Nos. 1 and 2 who approved the some beyond jurisdiction. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 passed the order of approval without giving any opportunity of hearing to the petitioners and others. Moreover, respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were not the proper authorities under rules 321 and 322 of the manual, 1935 to give the administrative approval. Respondent Nos.1 and 2 passed the order of approval without taking into consideration of the facts and circumstances of the ease and the possible complicacy of laws where the Government will not be benefited, in any way, and will not cause any loss or injury to respondent No. 10, rather maps of three mouzas must be amended and the people of those three mouzas will suffer irreparable loss and injury about their record-of-rights, mutations, rents. In the present survey, the lands of those curtailed plots have been recorded under the previous Patleechak and Moizpur mouzas in the names of the petitioners and others by the survey authority and the attestation khatian has been prepared in their names, but respondent No. 10 did not raise any objection anywhere against such survey or attestation till today. The impugned order of approval was passed by the respondents for addition of certain plots from two different mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza on some unfounded, vague, illegal and arbitrary cause. The impugned notification was void, illegal, beyond jurisdiction and was the result of colourable exercise of power and as such, was liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and was of no legal effect. 

 8. It was stated by way of submission that the respondent filed two applications before the Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate on 15.01.1996 for correction of mouza map/change of mouza map which were numbered as Miscellaneous Case Nos.1661 and 1662 of 1996. On 16.09.1996, the Zonal Settlement Officer sent the said report of the Assistant Settlement Officer to the Director (Land Record), Land Records and Surveys Directorate at Tejgaon for necessary action. The Director General of Land Records and Surveys Directorate by his letter dated 16.03.1997 asked the Zonal Settlement Officer to inquire and report whether there was any necessity to include the said lands with village-Darikhanjanpur. On 01.06.1997, the said Chairman issued a notice for holding meeting on the decision about correction of the mouza map/change of mouza map and he on 18.06.1997 filed an application before the Thana Nirbahi Officer for correction of the mouza map/change of mouza map stating that there was no obstacle to the inclusion of the lands with Darikhanjanpur village. On 03.10.1997, the Thana Land Officer (Kanangu) submitted a report on correction of mouza map/change of mouza map to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Jagannathpur in reply to his letter dated 04.09.1997 giving his opinion in favour of said inclusion, Then the Assistant Commissioner (Land) addressed a letter to the Thana Nirbahi Officer on 07.10.1997 concurring with the opinion of the Kanangu. The Thana Nirbahi Officer by his letter dated 07.10.1997 forwarded the opinion of the Kanangu along with that of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj. Then, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamganj by letter dated 22.10.1997 vide Memo No.  S. A./22/ Record/2/97/3073 wanted to know from the Assistant Commissioner (Land) why it was necessary for correction of the map as stated in his report. The Assistant Commissioner (Land), Jagannathpur was asked to report through the Thana Nirbahi Officer after holding investigation 

 9. Pursuant to the said order of the Divisional Commissioner, he sent letter to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate, Tejgaon on 08.02.1999 for necessary action. Copy of the said letter was also communicated to the respondent. 

 10. Thereafter, the Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet Zone, wrote a letter to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj under Memo No. 33/29/P:/874 dated 15.06.1999 for his opinion regarding correction of mouza map/change of mouza map. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Sunamganj consented to the matter vide his Memo No.  S.A./3(11)/8/ 98/2520. Again the Zonal Settlement Officer by order dated 13.05.1999 asked the Charge Officer-2, Md. Abul Kashem, to inquire into the matter on the spot and report. Then, the Zonal Settlement Officer addressed a letter to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj seeking his opinion in the matter. Whereupon the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) gave his opinion that on the application of the respondent, steps could be taken in the light of the decision of the Divisional Commissioner, Sylhet. Then, the Zonal Settlement Officer sent the records of Miscellaneous Case No. 01 of 1999 and other papers to the Director General, Land Records and. Surveys Directorate at Tejgaon for proper steps. The Superintendent of Police, Sunamganj by a letter dated (13.10.1999 addressed to the Zonal Settlement Officer gave his opinion that necessary steps could be taken in the matter on the basis of opinions of the Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and the Union Parishad Chairman. Then, the Director General of Land Records and Surveys Directorate addressed a letter to the Secretary, Ministry of Land on 18.01.2000 for administrative approval for inclusion of the aforesaid lands of Patleechak and Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur under rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 and rule 27(2) of “ইবিটি রুলস, ১৯৫৫”. On receipt of the said report of the Director General of Land Records and Surveys Directorate, a Senior Assistant Secretary; Ministry of Land by a letter dated 17.04.2000 sought for an explanation from the Director General as to why such change of mouza map was necessary as no explicit reason was given in the letter fin the proposed change. Then, the Director (Survey) by his letter dried 08.08.2000 informed the Ministry that fie local people, the Thana Nirbahi Officer the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj and the Superintendent of Police had got no objection if the proposed lands were included with Darikhanjanpur mouza. He also opined that approval could be given to the proposed change of the mouza map to which the Director General also concurred. 

 14. Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, who was appointed as amicus curiae, has filed a written submission. In his written submission, lie has given the history of the origin, meaning and legal basis of mouza, legal basis for fixing and re-fixing the exterior boundaries of mouza. He has tried to examine the legal status and force of the Manual, 1935. In connection with this, he has dealt with the English word `village', which bears similar meaning of the Bengali words 'Gram' or `Gaon'; he has also tried to trace back the history of settlements in villages right from the period of Menu, introduction of 'Soubha during the time of Akbar, the great Mughal Emperor, division of `Soubhas' of Bengal into the Circars or Sircars, the Circus into Purgunnas and the Purgunas into turfs, kismuts and villages or mouzas, the purpose   of creation of Village. The gradual history of `Khudkhast Rayot', that is, cultivators of lands residing in the same village, 'Paikast Raoyot', that is, those cultivating lands coining from nearby villages, the creation of Zemindars and the collection of rents by them from Raiyats through the instruments called `Sunnud' and to pay revenue to the royal treasury either directly or through Subedars, Dewans and Nahabs etc, the existence of some middle-interest-holders called Talukdars under the Zemindars, Talukdars who used to pay revenue to the Subcdars or Nawabs directly   like the Zemindars. The purchase of Talukdari of Calcutta, Sootanooty and Gobindpore by the East India Company in 1698, the acquisition of zemindary of 24 pergunnas by the said company as a grant on 23rd June, 1757, obtaining of grant of Dewani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from Shah Alam, the emperor of Delhi on 12th August, 1765 by the East India Company, the collection of rent by the East India Company as rent collector; the decision of the East India Company on the 16th of August, 1767 to appoint Supervisors to superintendent the collection of rent and administration of justice; proclamation issued by the East India Company on 11th May, 1772 to form Revenue Council to take charge of the office of ,the Dewani, passing of Regulation on 14th May, 1772 to appoint Rent Farmers for 5 years for each pergunna, abolition of the post of Supervisors and the appointment of collectors as officers to collect rent and to prepare rent roll, making of settlements from 1777 to 1789 on yearly basis for collection of rent, abolition of Revenue Council on the 12th day of June, 1786 and in its place establishment of Board of Revenue, passing of Regulation for Decennial Settlement on the 10th February, 1790, direction upon the collectors to assess `Jumma' (amount or rent to be paid by the Zemindars) for their estates. Passing of Bengal Regulation No. 1 on 22nd March, 1793 providing for permanent settlement of estates to Zemindars and independent Talukdars at yearly Jumma assessed under the decennial settlement. Making provisions for preparing Quinquennial Register of Revenue paying estates in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in which several particulars were to be recorded like present and future proprietors, 'jumma' etc by Regulation XLVII of 1793, preparation of Quinquennial registers and maintenance thereof mentioning Chauhaddi and Mouzas, undertaking survey   over whole of the permanently settled area in 1840 as an administrative measure which continued for 35 years, with the object to fix the outer boundaries or the topography of the different estates and mouzas. At the preliminary stages of such survey, boundary marks were fixed with mud-pillars commonly called Thaks and those recorded in the field hooks, field hooks were supplemented by a Roadad (Memorandum) and subsequently taking of more accurate and scientific survey called the Revenue Survey and preparation of maps accordingly. The enactment of the Survey Act, 1875 defining mouza as synonym of village, according to the said Act mouza included every village, hamlet, tola and similar subdivision of an estate, pergana or village by whatever name such subdivision may be known. The enactment of the Bengal Tenancy Act in 1885, shortly, 'the B.T. Act' with the principal object to give certain protection to the raiyats and the under Raiyats. So, mapping   of raiyati holdings and preparation of detailed record-of-rights became necessary. Chapter X of the B. T. Act made provisions   for preparation of record of rights. This Act did not take the term 'Mouza' instead it took the word 'village'. Section 3(19) of the B. T. Act defined 'village' as the area defined, surveyed and recorded as a distinct and separate village in the general land revenue survey which has been made of the province of Bengal, or any survey made by the Government which has been adopted by notification in the Calcutta or Eastern Bengal or Assam Gazette or which may he adopted by notification as the Calcutta Gazette as defining village for the purpose of this clause in any specified area; and, where a survey has not been made by, or under the authority of the Government, such area as the Collector may, with the sanction of the Board of Revenue, by general or special order, declare to constitute a village provided that, when an order has been made under section 101 directing that a survey be made and a record-of-rights prepared in respect of any local area, estate, tenure or part thereof, the Government may, by notification in the Calcutta  Gazette declare that in such local area, estate. tenure or part thereof "village" shall mean the area which for the purposes of such survey and record-of-rights may he adopted by the Revenue Officer with the sanction of the Board of Revenue accorded under the provisions of section 115A as the unit of survey and record. 

 15. According to Mr. Siddique, section 101 of the B.T. Act empowered the Government to order survey and preparation of record-of-rights. Section 115A in Part-IV of this chapter provided for demarcation of village boundaries. Section 115A of the B.T. Act provided that in the demarcation of village boundaries for the purpose of making a survey and preparing a record-of-rights under this chapter, a Revenue Officer shall, so far as is possible, and subject to the provisions of the Bengal Survey Act, 1875, preserve. as the unit of survey and record, the area contained within the exterior boundaries of the village maps of the revenue survey, or other survey, if any, adopted under clause (19)(b) of section 3 as defining village; and, where village maps prepared at such revenue or other survey exist, he shall not, adopt any other area as such unit. Rules were framed under the B.T Act. Such Rules framed on 26 March, 1929 dealt with the procedure for survey and preparation of record-on-rights. Part-II consisting of rules 46 to 59 dealt with the procedure in the preparation of record-of-rights. Rule 46 provided for the process.  Rule 47 provided for Traverse Survey. Rule 49(1) provided that a large-scale map showing features etc. of the country shall be prepared for each village as contemplated in section 115A of the Act as the unit of survey and record. Rule 49(2) provided for 2 situations for making a proposal for determination of the area to be adopted as the unit of record and survey. First one is that external boundaries of the previous survey is unsuitable as a unit of survey and record and the second one is that there was no previous survey. Either of those two situations being present, the Settlement Officer shall ascertain the opinion of the land lords and tenants and than submit proposal to the Board of Revenue. If the Board of Revenue sanctions the proposal, it shall submit a copy of its order to the Government for notification. After publication of notification under section 3(19) (b) of the Act, the area shall constitute a village for survey and record. 

 16. It has further been submitted by Mr. Siddique that The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter   referred to as the Act, 1950) which was passed by the East Bengal Legislative Assembly, after assent of the Governor General as Act, XXVIII of 1951 was published   in the Dacca Gazette on the 16th May, 1951, the Act has provided provisions for acquisition of all rent receiving interest, preparation of fresh rent roll, compensation assessment roll and fresh record-of-rights. Section 17 has authorized the Government to make an order for preparation of such record-of-rights. Section 18 has provided for prescribing the particulars to be included in such record-of-rights and section 18 has provided for draft publication, objection, appeal and final publication of such record-of-rights. He has also pointed out that the State Acquisition Rules, 1951 were framed under Part-IV. Rules 17 to 38 of Chapter-IV of the said Rules have provided for preparation and publication of record-of-rights and procedure for traverse survey and Cadastral survey have been provided therein. 

 17. Mr. Siddique has further pointed out that sections 32 to 46 in Chapter-V of the Act, 1950 have provided for preparation of compensation assessment roll and acquisition of rent receiving interests. Section 46 has provided for modification of the record-of-rights prepared under Chapter-IV by eliminating the entire chain of interest or rent receivers and then for reprint and distribution of the record-of-rights. Section 144 and subsequently added section 144A (inserted by amendment, 1967) of the Act in Part-V, Chapter XVII has provided for revision of the record-of-rights and a presumption of correctness has been attached to the revised record-of-rights. Section 152 has empowered the Government to make rules for Part-V. He has further pointed out that in exercise of power under section 152 of the Act, 1950 the Tenancy Rules, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as the Rules, 1954), was framed. Section 144 of the Act, 1950 has given power to the Government to make an order to prepare or revise the record-o f-rights in accordance with the Rules. Chapter-VI consisting of rules 26-35 of the Rules, 1954 has provided detailed procedure for revision of record-of-rights, rules 27 and 27A thereof have laid down almost the same procedure as was made by rule 49 of the Rules made under the B.T. Act. 

 (a)That the Government has ordered under section 101 of the B. T. Act or under section 17 or 144 of the Act, 1950 that a survey be made and/or record-of-rights be prepared or revised; 

 (c)The external boundaries of the village or mouza are unsuitable as a unit of survey and record. 

 19. Ile has further submitted that a plain reading of Chapter-X of the B. T. Act and Part-IV of the Act, 1950 makes it clear that once the Government orders for survey and/or preparation of record-of-rights, revenue officer/settlement officer starts from traverse survey and exhausting a long and complicated procedure, the entire process ends with final publication of the record-of-rights and delivery thereof to several persons and offices. After final publication, the executive branch of 1 the Government becomes functuous Officio with respect to the concerned survey and record-of-rights. C.S. record-of-rights in every district of Bangladesh excluding greater Sylhet district was prepared under Chapter-X of the B.T. Act. But, in except, a very few cases, external boundary of each mouza was kept unchanged. Again the Government had ordered for preparation of record-of-rights under section 171 of the Act, 1950 following which fresh survey was made, map for each roust, was prepared either afresh or adopting the map prepared under the B. T. Act. Any mouza map prepared under, the B.T. Act adopted for preparation of record-of-rights ordered under section 17 of the Act, 1950 contains a printed endorsement to that effect. It is only mouza map that shows plots and area of land covered by the plus Record-of-rights are prepare mentioning plot number and area of lands on the basis of and with reference to the mama map. So, final publication of the record-of-rights includes by implication final publication of the mouza map as well. Thus map of a mouza showing exterior boundary of the village/mouza, be it under the B. T. Act or under Part IV of the Act, 1950 is now a part of history, which cannot he changed. 

 20. Mr. Siddique has lastly submitted that record-of-rights prepared under Part IV of the Act, 1950 for the entire of present Bangladesh was finally published by 1962-63 and in Sylhet, in 1963. In 1967, by amendment section 143A was inserted in the Act, 1950 which was repealed in 1975. In section 143A, provision was made for applying to the civil Court for correction of the record-of-rights under Part-IV. It further makes the legislative intent clear that once a record-of-rights is finally published, it goes Out of the administrative/executive domain of the Government, to alter it. Only a pronouncement by the Court can say whether it was correct or wrong. Section 80 in Part- V of the Act says that from the date of coming into force of Part-V, the enactments specified in the schedule shall be repealed. The schedule shows that both the B. T. Act and the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 along with several other statutes have been repeated. The present case has arisen out of a boundary dispute of three mouzas under police station-Jagannathpur within district-Sunamganj, it was in the district of Sylhet till 1984 and Sylhet was not a part of Bengal before partition of India in 1947. Rather it was a part of Assam. The Assam Land and Revenue Regulation was passed in 1886. The Sylhet Tenancy Act was enacted in 1936. Provisions lie survey and preparation of record-of-rights were also there. But no survey was made and no record-of-rights was prepared there before the Act, 1950 came into operation, as was done in the rest of Bangladesh. Mauza map prepared in the greater Sylhet district in course of preparation of the record-of-rights as ordered under section 17 of the Act, 1950 became final with final publication of the record-of-rights (S.A. Khatian) in 1963. The executive branch of the Government lost all of its administrative powers to alter/correct/modify the map and the record-of-rights finally published in 1963. In between 1967 to 1975, r the civil Courts were vested with limited power to direct correction of finally published record-of-rights. But that did not include correction/alteration of exterior boundary of a mouza. Rules 1 and 2 of the Manual, 1935 state that it is a compilation of the principal rules of procedure relating to surveys and settlements. Survey and settlement operations or survey operations alone are/were conducted under different Regulations and Acts. But the rules of procedure   and the technical rules relate primarily to surveys and settlements under the Settlement Laws, the B. T. Act and the Bengal Survey Act. Thus it is clear that the rules of the Manual, 1935 do not have; force of law. Rule 321 or 322 or any other rule of the said Manual does not authorise the Government to alter the exterior boundaries of any mouza shown in the S.A. map after final publication of S.A. khatian in 1962-63. Now, Part-V of the Act, 1950 having already come into effect the Government has power under section 144 thereof to make an order to prepare or revise the record-of-rights for any area of such an order is made, than and then, only Settlement Officer can start a proceeding under rule 27A of the Rules, 1954 (1955) for alteration of the exterior boundary of a mouza strictly following the requirements of that rule and a successful completion of the process would permit preparation of a new mouza map including or excluding any land which was not there in the S.A. map of that mouza. Any other action to change exterior boundary limits of any mouza like the present one is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 (b) after rejection of the application of respondent No. 10 twice by the Divisional Commissioner and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) (in both cases it would be the Deputy Commissioner, the application was heard by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and the order was communicated under his signature), the Chairman of Patleechak Union Parishad informed the Thana Nirhahi Officer that the people had no objection if the said lands were added with `Darikhanjanpur' village and on such report the Zonal Settlement Officer, the Thana Nirhahi Officer, the Additional Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police acted and ultimately the Director (Survey) of the Land Records and Survey Directorate recommended for administrative approval for inclusion of those land with Darikhanjanpur village. 

 (d) There was no answer to the query of the Government as Made by letter dated 17.04.2000 as to why such change of the mouza map was necessary in any of those opinions. Even the Director General of Land Records and Survey Directorate dated 08.08.2000 could not furnish any answer as to why the change was necessary and in the latest communication, it was communicated that the local Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police had no objection but this was no answer. 

 23. The High Court Division on consider action of the provisions of rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 and 27A(2) of the Rules, 1954 held that in the instant case, neither new village nor any separate settlement unit was required to he constituted or formed, so none of the rides was at all applicable in the circumstances the High Court Division further held that the whole proceeding was initiated at the  instance of a villager and concluded without any concurrence of "the Board of Land Revenue." The High Court Division further observed that neither the report of the Zonal Settlement Officer nor the Director General of the Land Records and Surveys Directorate relates to any land of a "previously settled village found is he unsuitable and required, change." The High Court Division concluded that "In the circumstances, them is no scope from the conclusion that the administrative approval issued vide annexure-'H' on behalf of the Government for severing of 35 acres of land of village Patleechak and Moijpur and then, adding them with village Darikhanjanpur was issued without following any law and/or rules and not in public interest." 

 26. Let us examine the second submission on which leave was granted. To examine this submission, we consider, it necessary to see the law on the subject as it stood on 15.01.1996, when as per the own case of the respondent, applications were filed by him before the Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate, Tejgaon for correction of the mouza map/change of mouza map of the 3(three) mouzas in question and till the date when the impugned administrative approval was given on 27.08.2000 vide annexure-'11' to the writ petition. 

 27. Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique is his written submission has given in detail the historical background right from the formation of Revenue Council and passing of Regulation, 1790 on 10th February, 1790 for the Decennial Settlement, Regulations No.  XLVIII of 1793 up to the enactment of the B.T. Act and the Rules framed thereunder and domination of village and mouza, but we do not consider it necessary to travel in those laws except looking at the provisions of the Act, 1950 and the Rule framed thereunder being the State Acquisition Rules, 1951 and the Rules, 1954. We also do not consider it necessary to dwell on the question of mouza and village, both being synonym. However, let it be on record that in the Act, 1950, in section 2(29), village has been defined as follows: 

 "village" means the area defined, maxi eyed and recorded as a district and separate village in any survey made by, or under the authority of, the Government, and, where no such survey has been made, such area as the Collector may, with the sanction of the Board of Revenue, by general or special order, declare to constitute a village; 

 28. There is no dispute that after whole-sale acquisition of the rent receiving interests with effect from the 14th April, 1956 including the Sylhet District (till 1984 Sunamganj was part of the Sylhet District), preparation of fresh rent roll, compensation assessment roll and fresh record-of-rights was required. Chapter-IV, Part-IV of the Act, 1950 has provided for preparation of record-of-rights and section 17 has authorized the Government to make an order for preparation of such record-of-rights. Section 18 of the Act, 1950 has provided for prescribing the particulars to be included in such record-of-rights and section 19 has provided for draft publication, objection, appeal and final publication of such record-of-rights. Rules were framed under Part- IV called the State Acquisition Rule, 1951. Chapter-IV of the said Rules consisting rules 17-38 has provided for preparation and publication of record-of-rights. Sections 32 to 46 in Chapter-V of the Act, 1950 have provided fine preparation of compensation assessment roll and acquisition of rent receiving interests. Section 46 of the Act, 1950 has provided for modification of the record-of-rights prepared under Chapter-IV by eliminating the entire chain of interest of rent receivers and then for reprint and distribution of the record-of-rights. Part II Chapter II, Part III Chapter III, Part IV, Chapters VA, VI to X1 of the Act, 1950 are with regard to acquisition of rent receiving interests and for payment, of compensation for such acquisition. Sections 81 to 143 of the Act have dealt with class, status, right and liabilities of tenants, enhancement and reduction of rents, collection and realisation of rent, subdivision and amalgamation holdings and maintenance of Record of rights. Section 144 of the Act and subsequently added section 144A (inserted by amendment, 1967) are in Part- V. Chapter-XVII in Part-V of the Act has provided for maintenance and revision of the record-of-rights and a presumption of correctness has been attached to the revised record-o rights. Section 152 has empowered the: Government to make rules for Part-V and in exercise of the said power the Rules, 1954 was framed. It is also pertinent to mention that Chapters l-IV of the Rules, 1954 were published in the Dacca Gazette on 7th April, 1955 and Chapters V-IX of the Rules were published in the Dacca Gazette on 14th August, 1955. 

 29. Rules 26-35 of the Rules, 1954 have provided detailed procedure for revision of record-of-rights. Rules 27 and 27A thereof have laid down almost the same procedure as was made by rule 49 of the Rules, made under the B. T. Act. Rule 28 of the Rules, 1954 has directed that the work up to the stage of attestation, as mentioned in rule 27 thereof, shall be completed in accordance with the Technical Rules and Instructions of the Settlement Department, as modified, from time to time, by the Director of Land Records and Surveys and under such other instructions as may be issued in this behalf by the Director of Land Records and Surveys or by the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer in any district or part of a district or local area. It is also a fact that record-of-rights prepared under Part-IV of the Act, 1950 for the entire present Bangladesh was finally published by 1962/1963, (In Sylhet District, it was published in 1963). It is also a fact that in 1967, by way of amendment, section 143A was inserted in the Act, 1950 giving scope for correction of the record-of-rights, if prepared wrongly through the intervention of the Court, but that section did not vest the Court with the power to correct/alter the exterior boundary of a mouza map; the section was repealed in 1975. Thus, it is obvious that once a record-of-rights is finally published, it goes out of the administrative executive domain of the Government to alter it and only a pronouncement by a civil Court can say whether it was correct or wrong. From section 80 in Part-V of the Act, 1950, it is also clear that from the date of coming into force of Part-V, the enactment specified in the schedule shall be repealed and the schedule clearly shows that both B. T. Act and Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 along with several other statutes have been repealed. It is also a fact that the Sylhet Tenancy Act was enacted in 1936 where provisions were made for survey and preparation of record-of-rights, but no survey was made and no record-of-rights was prepared therein before the Act, 1950 came into operation, mouza map was prepared in the greater Sylhet district in course of preparation of record rights under section 17 of the Act, 1950 and became final with the final publication of the record-of-rights (S.A. Khatian) in 1963. So the executive branch of the Government in Sylhet lost all its administrative power to alter/correct and modify the map and record-of-rights finally published in 1963. Part-V of the Art, 1950 having already come into effect, the Government, in exercise of its power under section 144 thereof, may, in any case f it thinks fit, make an order directing that a record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or a local area be prepared or revised and if such an order is made, then and then, only Settlement Officer can start a proceeding under rule 27A of the Rules, 1954 for alteration /correaction of the exterior boundary of a mouza strictly following the requirements of that rule and a successful completion on the process would permit preparation of new mouza map including or excluding any land which was not therein in the S.A. map of that mouza. 

 30. Rules 1 and 2 of the Manual, 1935 have clearly stated that it is a compilation of the principal rules of procedure relating to surveys and settlements. Survey and settlement operations or survey operations alone are/week conducted under different Regulations and Acts. But the rules of procedure and the technical rules relate primarily to surveys and settlements under the Settlement Laws, the B.T. Act and the Bengal Survey Act. Thus, it is clear that the rules of the Manual, 1935 cannot over-ride   or supersede the laws, namely: the Act, 1950 and the Rules, 1954(55). Consequently, rules 321 and 322 or any other rule(s) of the said Manual does not authorize the Government to alter the exterior boundaries of any mouza shown in the S.A. map after final publication of the S.A. khatian in 1962-63. And if an order is made under section 144 of the Act, 1950, to prepare or revise the record-of-rights for any area, then and then, only Settlement Officer can start a proceeding under rule 27A of the Rules, 1954(55) for alteration of the exterior boundary of a mouza strictly following the requirements of that Rules and a successful completion of the process would permit preparation of a new mouza map including or excluding only land which was not there in S.A. map of that mouza. Any other action to change the exterior boundary limits of any mouza shall be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect as rightly submitted by Mr. Siddique.

 47. The Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate wrote to the Secretary, Ministry of Land, respondent No. 1 vide his Memo No.  ৩০/৯০/২য় খন্ড dated 18.01.2000 for giving the administrative approval of the inclusion of the 9(nine) acres of lands of 48 plots of Patlecchak mouza and 26 acres of lands of 106 plots of Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur mouza under rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 and rule 27(2) of the Rules, 1954(55). In reply to this, the Ministry of Land wrote a letter to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate on 17.04.2 (100 vide Memo No.  ভূঃমঃ/শা-(মৌঃনাঃপঃ)৫/৯৯/১৫১ under the signature of respondent No. 2 to the following effect: 

 48. In reply to this, instead of the Director General, Director (Survey) of the Land Records and Surveys gave a reply on 08.08.2000 vide his Memo No. ৬৬/৯০/২য় খন্ড/১০১৩-জরিপঃ which is as follows: 

 50. The proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1999 was not produced before the High Court Division and no date is also available from the record as to its initiation, but obviously the case was not initiated before 1999. It is also apparent from the order of the Assistant Settlement Officer dated 25.04.1999 that after the miscellaneous case was started, no attempt was made to lake the opinions of the people of the 3(three) mouzas who would be the most affected persons in case the mouza map is changed/corrected. From the said order, it is also apparent that there was heavy tadbir from the respondent to get the job done any how and this further shows that the concerned functionaries did not give their opinions on the application of the respondent independently in accordance with rule 321 of the Manual, 1935 and rule 27A (2) of the Rules, 1954(55). It is also pertinent to state at the risk of repetition that in the meantime, the respondent's application filed to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj on 27.08.1997 for addition of 9.00 acres and 26.00 acres of lands of Patleechak and Moizpur mouza respectively with Darikhanjanpur mouza was rejected on 14.06.1998; application filed by the respondent for reviewing the said order was also rejected on (12.12.1998 against which he filed Revenue Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 1998 before the Divisional Commissioner, Sylhet who without disposing of the said revenue miscellaneous appeal on merit sent the records to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys for final decision relying on the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent that the issue had been pending for final decision by the Survey and Settlement Department, but from the correspondences of the Assistant Settlement Officer, the Zonal Settlement Officer and the Director General, Land Records and Surveys, it does not appear that the fact of rejection of the prayer of the respondent adding 9.00 acres of lands of Patleechak mouza and 26.00 acres of lands of Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur mouza by the Deputy Commissioner was, at all, noticed. The High Court Division, in deciding the merit of the Rule, took notice of this fact of rejection of respondent's prayer twice by the highest local authority. The High Court Division further noticed that only the Chairman of Patleechak Union Parishad informed the Thana Nirbahi Officer that the people had no objection if the said lands were added with Darikhanjanpur mouza and on such report the Zonal Settlement Officer, the Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Additional Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police acted. From the various reports and the inter sc correspondences amongst the concerned functionaries as discussed above, we also find substances in the finding of the High Court Division that “There is no dispute that in the process the opinion of the people of village ‘Moizpur’ or ‘Darkhanjanpur’ (sic) was never sought for.” 

 51. On receipt of the proposal from the Director General, Land Records and Surveys to give administrative approval to include 9.00 acres and 26.00 acres of lands of Patleechak mouza and Moizpur mouza respectively with Darikhanjanpur mouza the Ministry of Land, by its letter dated 17.04.2000 asked him to state clearly as to the necessity of such inclusion of the lands of the said two mouzas as in his letter there was nothing in that respect, but instead of the Director General, the Director (Survey) replied to the said letter saying that on behalf of Darikhanjanpur mouza, the respondent, Jamshed Mia filed an application for inclusion of the lands of the said two mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza and that the local people, the Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police, had no objection if the lands of the said two mouzas were included in Darikhanjanpur mouza. But merely no objection from the local people and the local administration to change the mouza map could not be a ground to substitute the statutory requirements under rule 27A (2) of the Rules, 1954(55) that proposal for determination of the area to be adopted as a unit of survey and record has to be submitted by the Assistant Settlement Officer, after ascertaining, as far as possible, the opinions of the local people through the Officer to whom he is subordinate, i.e. the Zonal Settlement Officer to the Government and that too only when the area contained within the boundaries of a village map of a previous survey is unsuitable as a unit of survey and record (here map of the concerned mouzas was prepared during the S.A. khatian). But in the instant case as is revealed from the order of the Settlement Officer dated 25.04.1999 that the opinions of the people of mouzas in question were not ascertained; in none of the reports and inter se correspondences of the local administration as sought to be relied upon by the respondent in his affidavit-in-opposition, there is anything to show that the area contained within the boundaries of the map of the 3(three) mouzas in question was found to be unsuitable and required to be changed. Not only that all the authorities acted at the instance of an individual the respondent. We like to further observe that in the applications filed by the respondent as quoted in the body of the affidavit in-opposition, he failed to make out an case nor in the reports submitted by the Chairman of Patleechak Union Parishad and the other Government functionaries any case to correct the mouza map/change of mouza map of the three mouzas as contemplated in section 144 of the Act, 1955 and in rule 27A (2) of the Rules, 1954(55) could be made out. It appears to us that the Director General, Land Records and Surveys, the Settlement officers and the other functionaries were either totally ignorant of the provisions of law as discussed above or were bent upon to act at the behest of an individual by flouting the law. In the context, the High Court Division rightly found that 

 52. Of course the High Court Division was not correct in holding that no concurrence of the "Board of Land Revenue" was taken before the conclusion of the proceeding as in view of the change of law in 1972 there was no necessity to submit the proposal and the record to the Board of Revenue as correctly stated in the concise statement filed by the writ-respondent-appellant. 

 53. In this case, in fact, the cart was put before the horse inasmuch as after acting on the application filed by the sole respondent for correction of the mouza map/change of mouza map of 3(three) mouzas, namely; Patlecehak, Moizpur and Darikhanjanpur which were finally published in the S.A. Khatian as evidenced from the application filed by the Chairman of Patleechak Union Parishad to the Thana Nirbahi Officer, Jagannathpur, the reports of the Assistant Settlement Officer, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and the concurrence by the other local administration, the Director General, Land Records and Surveys gave tagged to the Zonal Settlement Officer to send his opinion by starting a miscellaneous case who in turn by a letter dated 15.06.1999 under Memo No. 33/29/P:/834 requested the Deputy Commissioner to give his opinion on the subject. And from the letter written by the Zonal Settlement Officer to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys Directorate on 05.08.1999 it appears that a miscellaneous case being No. 1 was started in the office of the Assistant Settlement Officer, Jagannathpur only in 1999. Although as per own admission of the respondent long before of the said letter reports were given by the local administration including the Thana Kanangu and the Assistant Settlement Officer in favour of correction of the mouza map/change of the mouza map of the mouzas in question as discussed hereinbefore. In this regard, it is also relevant to state that the Assistant Settlement Officer himself did not start any case as per provisions of rule, 27(2) of the Rules, 1954 and rule 321 of the Manual, 1935, rather he started the case being directed by the Zonal Settlement Officer at the instance of the Director General, Land Records and Surveys. 

 55. From the discussions made above, it is abundantly clear that the conditions for correction of mouza map/change of mouza map of the 3(three) mouzas, namely Patleechak, Moizpur and Darikhanjanpur as articulated by the legislature in section 144 of the Act and rule 27A(2) of the Rules, 1954 being absent, the whole exercise made in that behalf by the Assistant Settlement Officer, the Zonal Settlement Officer, the Director General of Land Records and Surveys, the opinion given by the local administration including the Deputy Commissioner and the approval given by respondent No. 1 vide annexure-'H' to the writ petition on such exercise could by no term be said to be with jurisdiction but without jurisdiction. Therefore, the High Court Division acted within its jurisdiction of exercising its power of judicial review in declaring the impugned administrative approval given by the Government to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

Mr Md. Jahangir Alam, Deputy Attorney General, instructed by Mr Haridas Paul, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the appellants

Government of Bangladesh, Represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Natore and others -------- Appellants
-Vs-
Most Majeda Beowa and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiffs instituted Other Class SuitNo.247 of 1996 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Natore stating, inter alia, that on 15.11.1996, the defendant No.4 claimed the suit property as Government khas land on the basis of acquiring the property by way of L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67, the plaintiffs title became clouded and thus filed the suit for declaration of title contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Jahir Uddin Mondal. State Acquisition (in short S.A.) and Revisional Survey (in short R.S.) Khatians have correctly been recorded in his name and a portion of the suit land was transferred by him to Sarjan Beowa and accordingly R.S. Khatian No.70/71 has been recorded in her name. Thereafter, Sarjan Beowa died childless leaving behind her brother Jahir Uddin and thereby said Jahir Uddin became full owner of the suit land, and then died leaving behind the plaintiff Nos.1-14 as his legal heirs, who are in possession of the suit land. 

 9. Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that in view of the fact that for the construction and extension of road, the Government having intended to acquire the suit land and accordingly L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67 having being started and notice under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act having been served on 10.04.1968 upon the owners concerned and no objection having been raised, from any quarter, the suit land having been finally acquired and possession having been taken on payment of full compensation money, but, the High Court Division erred in law in rejecting the revisional application summarily and maintaining the judgment and decree by the Courts below occasioning failure of justice in the case. He further submits that the suit of the plaintiffs being false and having been filed with the design to grab the suit property, and the High Court Division erred in law in rejecting the revisional application summarily and maintaining the judgment and decree passed by the Courts below on an erroneous view. The learned Deputy Attorney General brought the original lower court's records of L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67 and produced before the Court for perusal of the Court. Accordingly, we have perused the L.C. records of the L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67 from which it transpires that land was acquired and compensation was paid and received by the Awardee. 

 11. But on perusal of the L.C. records of L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67 concedes that Awardee accepted the compensation and case land was rightly acquired by the authority. 

 12. We have heard the learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellants and the learned Advocate for the respondents. Perused the impugned judgment and connected other materials on record. 

 13. On perusal of the judgments and orders of the learned Assistant Judge and District Judge as appellate court it is to be noted that both of the court decreed and affirmed the suit on grounds that the appellant-defendant i.e. the Government did adduce no oral or documentary evidence concerning the pivotal acquisition of the suit land through L.A. case of 48 of 66-67 and the same was recorded in the S.A. and R.S. Khatians in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiffs. 

 14. In the case of Executive Engineer, Roads and Highways and Ors vs Abirun Begum and Ors cited in LEX/BDAD/ 0111/2017 this Division accepting L.A. case records as public documents observed concerning the evidentiary value and status of the L.A. case records as follows: 

 "In fact the defendants did not produce Ext. 2 or Ext. 2 series. They produced Ext. Ka, which is a copy of the L.A. case records. It being a public document, the appellate Court accepted this exhibit as genuine and proof of title because it was attested copy of the records relating to the L.A. case. Our view is that the appellate Court was correct in accepting that Ext. Ka was admissible and it is proof of the existence of the land acquisition case by which the defendants acquired title to the suit land." 

 "Presumption as to correctness of record of rights 144A. Every entry in a record-of rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect." 

 16. Referring the explanation of the Judicial Committee of Privy Council on the nature of an entry in a record of right in the ensuing words- 

 "A record of rights has been described by Sir Henry Maine as a detailed statement of all rights in land drawn up periodically by the functionaries employed in setting the claims of the Government to its shares of the rental Though it does not create a title, it gives rise to a presumption in its support, which prevails until its correctness is successfully impugned. 

 18. The aforementioned view was maintained by this Division in the case of Ahab Ali and others vs. Zahiruddin Kari and others reported in 30 DLR (AD) (1978) 81 and reiterated in the case of The Chief Engineer, Roads and Highway Directorate vs. Asaduzzaman Siddique and Ors. reported in 69 DLR(AD) (2017) 440 that mere record of rights does not create a title. As such, merely entries of the predecessors of the plaintiffs in the S.A and R.S. Khatians without any documents of title or ownership did not create of the respondents-plaintiffs title over the suit land. And the mere presumption arisen in its support, by the said S.A. and R.S. record of rights fails as its correctness is successfully impugned by the presence of the L.A. case records. 

 19. As the L.A. case records are public documents, mere the facts that they were not submitted and exhibited in the courts below that cannot be a ground for defeating public interest and justice. 

 20. Moreso, said S.A. and R.S. records of right were published in the name of the previous owners from whom through L.A. Case No.48 of 1966-67, the land in question was acquired. We are, therefore, of the considered view that such record of rights neither established the right title of the previous owners or their heirs upon the suit properties, because of acquisition of the said property.

lawyer:
M Qnamrul Hoque Siddique Advocate, instructed by Mvi, Md. Wahidullah Advocate-on-Record ......  For the Appellants. 
Md. Ali Reza Advocate, instructed by Ni. Bhuiyan Advocate-on-Record and Abdul Hye Bhuiyan Advocate-on-Record ......... For Respondent Nos. 1 (a) (i)- 1 (a) (vii) and 1 (b) - 1 (e) 
Respondent No. 2-4 ....... None represented
parties:
Nazimuddin Mondal and another ------ Appellants
-Vs-
Kushal Mondal being Dead his heirs: 1 (a) Son Md. Nasaruddin @ Nazor Ali deing dead his heirs:1 (a) (i) . Md. Kurman Ali and others --------  Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in short, are that Kushal Mondal, predecessor of the respondents herein as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 275 of 1975 in the Court of the then Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Rajshahi for declaration of title to the suit land. The plaintiff stated, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Askar Mondal, who possessed the same and died leaving behind his brother's son Saber Mondal. Saber Mondal during his lifetime used to possess the suit land and after his death his heir, the original plaintiff Kushal Mondal as his son inherited the property. During S.A. operation, the land in dispute was correctly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and, accordingly, he paid rent to the Government and the Government after accepting him as tenant granted rent receipts in his favour. During R.S. operation, the suit land was erroneously recorded in the name of the defendants. Accordingly, the plaintiffs title to the suit property was doused. Hence, the plaintiff filed the suit. 

 3. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint. Their case, in short, is that the disputed property originally belonged to Askar Mondal. But during his lifetime, he surrendered the same in favour of ex-landlord, who settled the same to one Chhoto Babu Mondal, who died leaving behind defendant Nos.1 and 4 as daughters and one Saira Bewa as wife. Saira Bewa gifted her share in favour of her grandsons, defendant Nos.2 and 3 and one Rahim Uddin Mondal, Rahim Uddin Mondal died leaving behind defendant No.5 as father and defendant No4 as mother. Accordingly, defendant Nos.1-5 had been possessing the suit land after acquiring the same and paid rent to the Government. The R.S. record of the sit property has correctly been published in the names of defendant and possession in the suit land and as such, the suit was liable to be dismissed. 

 III. That the defendants' claim was that their names were recorded in S.A. khatian and in support of their claim they called for the record from the local settlement office and it was evidently proved that the volume stood in the names of defendant Nos. 1-4 but the High Court Division without looking into this aspect made the Rule absolute and as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. 

 6. Mr. Md. Ali Reza, learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.1(a)(i)- 1(a)(vii) and 1(b)-1(e) made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that Askar Mondal died leaving Saber Mondal as brother's son who inherited the property left behind by Askar Mondal and subsequently Saber Mondal died leaving son Kushal Mondal and the High Court Division rightly found that Saber Mondal possessed the suit land for more than 12(twelve) years and the S.A. record was duly prepared in the name of the son of Suber Mondal and he paid rents to the Government and, accordingly, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute. He further submitted that all the P.Ws. categorically proved that the plaintiff is owning and possessing the suit land and the S.A. khatian was rightly prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants miserably failed to prove the basis of the recording of the R.S. khatian in respect of the suit land in their names and accordingly the High Court Division disbelieved the case of the defendants and rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that the defendants have miserably failed to prove that the original owner of the suit land namely Askar Mondal surrendered the suit land in favour of the ex-landlord and the defendants failed to adduce any documentary evidence and also failed to examine any pertinent witness to prove this issue and as such, the High Court Division has rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that the defendants have failed to prove by adducing any documentary evidence that after surrender of the suit land by Askar Mondal, when the ex-landlord took the same in his khas possession and also when he settled the same to Chhoto Babu Mondal (the predecessor-in-interest of defendant No.1-5), and the trial Court and the High Court Division rightly found that that the defendants miserably failed to prove their case and, therefore, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that P.V1s.4 and 5 are independent witnesses who clearly stated in the deposition that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land and they have land near the suit land and that the High Court Division rightly believed the evidentiary value of the deposition of these two independent witnesses and observed that the witnesses of the defendants contradicted themselves in their depositions in respect of possession of the suit land their testimony is not cogent and credible and, therefore the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He also submitted that the Court of appeal below, as the final Court of fact, did not discuss and consider a single witness examined by the contesting parties while reversing the judgment of the trial Court as is required by Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He lastly submitted that the High Court Division as well as the trial Court rightly came to a finding that the plaintiff proved his title and possession in the suit land and the defendants have miserably failed to prove their title and possession in the suit land and hence the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Division. 

 7. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 8. At the outset we are constrained to hold that the finding of the High Court Division to the effect that, "It is the established principle of civil law that the R.S. records of rights have got no presumptive value of its correctness "such observation is clearly contrary to section 114 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, of which the relevant provisions are reproduced here:- 

 144. Revision of record-of-rights -(1) The Government may in any case if it thinks fit make an order directing that a record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or local area be prepared or revised by a Revenue-officer, in accordance with such rule as may be made by the Government in this behalf. 

 (4) When an order is made under sub-section (1), the Revenue-officer shall record in the record-of-rights to be pre-pared or revised in pursuance of such order such particulars as may be pre-scribed. 

 (5)When a record-of-rights has been prepared or revised so as to contain or include therein the particulars referred to in sub-section (4), and rents assessed or re-assessed under sub-section (4a), the Revenue-officer shall publish a draft of the record-of-rights so pre-pared or revised in the prescribed manner and for the prescribed period and shall receive and consider any objections which may be made to any entry therein or to any omissions therefrom during the period of such publication. 

 (7) When all such objections and appeals have been considered and dis-posed of according to such rules as the Government may make in this behalf, the Revenue-officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause such record to be finally published in the pre-scribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this section. 

 (8) When a record-of-rights has been finally published under sub-section(7), the Revenue-officer shall, within such time as the Director of Land Records and Surveys may fix in this behalf, make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof and shall date and subscribe the same with his name and official title. 144A. Presumption as to correctness of record of rights-Every entry in a record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect." 

 11. Hence, there can be no doubt that the record of rights in the names of the defendants creates a rebuttable presumption in their favour. 

 12. The plaintiff claims title in the suit land by way of inheritance from Saber Mondal who was the nephew of the original owner, namely Askar Mondal. The S.A. record was in the name of the plaintiff, but the R.S. record for the suit land was wrongly in the name of the defendants. On the other hand the defendants claim that the original owner Askar Mondal surrendered the suit land in favour of the superior landlord who settled the land in favour of Chhoto Babu Mondal more than 50 years previously and the land is now in the possession of the successors of said Chhoto Babu Mondal. They also claimed that the documents produced by the plaintiff were forged. 

 14. The moot question in the instant case is whether the plaintiff was able to prove that title in the suit land passed to him through his father Saber Mondal who was the brother of the original owner Askar Mondal. The trial Court decreed the suit upon observing that, "It has not been challenged by the defendants that the plaintiff is not the brother's son of Askar Mondal." The trial Court also relied on the fact that the S.A. record was in the name of the plaintiff, which was also supported by rent receipts showing that the government realised rent for the suit land from the plaintiff up to 1967 (1374 B.S.) admitting the plaintiff as tenant. The trial Court also observed that the defendants, did not adduce any evidence to prove that the ex-landlord got the suit land in his khas possession after surrender by Askar Mondal or that Chhoto Babu Mondal got settlement. 

 17. Although the plaintiff claimed title to the land with support from Ext-1 the S.A. Khatian, he did not challenge the genuineness of the original volume of the S.A. record, which was, produced before the appellate Court at the instance of the defendants. The appellate Court found on penisal of the volume in question that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 1-4 in the name of one Saira Bewa, wife of Chhoto Babu Mondal. In allowing the appeal by the defendants, the appellate Court took into consideration the rent receipts produced by the defendants showing payment of rent to the government. 

 18. In view of the above facts and circumstances, it is abundantly clear that the judgment and decree of the trial court was patently erroneous and based upon misreading of evidence. The appellate Court properly reversed the judgment of the trial Court. Evidently the claim of the plaintiff was falsified by the production of the S.A. record of rights, which falsified the claim of the plaintiff and, on the other hand, proved that the S.A. records were in the names of the defendants.

lawyer:
Md Nurul Amin, Senior Advocate instructed by Mohammad Ali Azam, Advocate-on-record—For the Appellants. 
Md Firoz Shah, Advocate-on-record—For Respondent Nos. 3, 4, 5(n), 5(b)(i)-5(b)(iii), 5(c) and 5(d).

parties:
Abdul Hanif (Md) @ Abu Hanif and others……………. Appellants
vs
Bhupen Nath and others...........Respondents
full_judgment:
4. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the land in CS Khatian No. 300 belonged to Bhim Sarder, who died leaving son Padda Sarder. Due to arrear of rents the landlord Binode Bihari Saha and others filed rent suit in the Court of the then Munsif, Pabna against Padda Sarder for realization of rent for the years 1360-62 BS and subsequently he paid rent to the Landlord and got "Dakhila". At the time of preparation of SA record Padda Sarder became blind and his 3 sons i.e. the plaintiffs were minor. As a result the suit land was recorded in the name of Shorot Shundori. That record was wrong. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land and the defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit land. The plaintiff No. 1 went to Ataikula Tahsil Office in the 1st part of Poush 1383 BS for payment of rent and came to learn that the suit land was not recorded in their name, and the defendants claimed the suit land. Hence the suit was filed. 

 12. On the other hand, Mr Md Firoz Shah, the learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the respondents made his submissions supporting the decision of the High Court Division. He contends that the continuous possession by the plaintiffs as the heirs of Padda Sarder was not proved. He further submits that the plaintiffs produced rent receipts of the year of 1385 and 1387 BS but they failed to produce rent receipts ranging from the year of 1362-1385 BS. Moreover, the plaintiffs did not produce the nephew of Padda, Rupendranath whose testimony was very much important as he was in possession of the suit land on behalf of Padda Sarder well before the advent of the plaintiffs in the scenario as the heirs of Padda Sarder. 

 14. He also submits that SA khatian was rightly recorded in the name of Shorot Shundori as Padda Lal Sarder waived the claim of the suit land through clause 3 of the solenama submitted in the Mortgage Suit No. 36/41 filed in first Munsif Court of Pabna acknowledging the possession of had Ali. (Exhibit C1). After the compromise decree dated 24-4-42 the claim of Padda Lal Sarder does not exist on the suit land as the same was waived and duly recorded in the name of Shorot Shundori, the mother of the defendants. 

 15. We have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and gone through the judgments of the Courts below. We have also perused the evidence on record. 

 17. The defendants' endeavor to put forward Exhibit C1 on record was erroneous since the same was not in their pleadings as opposed to Order VI, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 22. The presumption of correctness as to CS record-of-rights is not certainly available with regards to the state acquisition Khatians in pursuance of the provisions under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act but subsequently by an amendment in the year 1967, section 144A was incorporated in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is reproduced below: 

 "Every entry in a record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect." 

 25. In the instant case admittedly, RS Khatian was prepared in the name of plaintiffs. The trial Court as well as the Appellate Court below clearly mentioned and admitted regarding the same. We don't find any positive steps that have been taken to dislodge the said presumption of correctness from the record, only a feeble attempt was made by the Court to that effect in its observations which is as under: " উক্ত আর, এস, খতিয়ানে বিরুদ্ধে বিবাদী পক্ষ কর্তৃক আনীত ১৩ নং .... কেস ও ১৬৮৮/৭৯ নং আপীলের যথাক্রমে ১৪-৬-৭৮ ও ১৪-৯-৮১ ইং তারিখের আদেশে জাবেদা নকল দাখিল করিয়াছেন। যাহা হইতে দেখা যায় যে, উক্ত আপীল কেস ও আপীল বিবাদীপক্ষ কর্তৃক আনীত হইলেও পরবর্তী পর্যায়ে তাহা পরিচালিত হয় নাই।" 

 "It is true that record-of-right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record-of-right. The presumption of correctness as to CS record-of-right is not certainly available with regard to the State Acquisition Khatians. There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians as it is to be found in case of CS khatians in pursuance of the provision under section 103-B of the Bengal Tenancy Act." 

 29. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Tenu Miah Tofadar 14 LM (AD) 30 it was observed: "If we glean the said provision, it transpires that a finally published record-of-rights revised under section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has a presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by reliable evidence. This proposition of law is well settled. The oldest record-of-rights being the cadastral survey prepared under section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act (Act No. VIII of 1885) also got a high presumptive value as to correctness of entries therein as it has also been enjoined under section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Of course this is a rebuttable piece of presumption, if it has been so rebutted by evidence. Since the entry of the land in question as per the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act recorded in the name of the government as land, in the absence of any positive evidence oral and documentary onus was upon the plaintiff to discharge the presumption proving the same to be wrongly recorded in the record-of-rights bereft of which title and interest cannot vest upon the plaintiff. The case of Government of Bangladesh vs AKM Abdul Hye 56 DLR (AD) 53 is an authority on this issue. The decision of High Court Division is totally devoid of consideration of all these settled principles of law adversely reversing the lower appellate Court's judgment committing a palpable wrong which required to be intervened by this Division." 

 32. The decision also highlighted: "Referring the explanation of the Judicial Committee of Privy Council on the nature of an entry in a record-of-right in the ensuing words—"A record-of-rights has been described by Sir Henry Maine as a detailed statement of all rights in land drawn up periodically by the functionaries employed in setting the claims of the Government to its shares of the rental  Though it does not create a title, it gives rise to a presumption in its support, which prevails until its correctness is successfully impugned." 

 33. To sum up, we have found that the Court of Appeal below put special emphasize as to how the defendants proved their case ignoring the plaintiffs' steps of proving the same on evidence. The law enjoins it is the bounden duty of the Court to discuss first how the plaintiff proved its case to the hilt. In a judicial proceeding, where all souls solicit justice equally and are entitled to the same, the plaintiff usually has to prove its case. In this situation, the plaintiffs' ownership of the land is backed by official records more specifically the RS record-of-rights. But when the case went to the lower appellate Court in the appeal, it didn't give enough importance to these records. Even though the lower appellate Court acknowledged the plaintiffs' rights supported by the unchallenged RS record-of-rights, it didn't impartially and objectively handle the proceedings to rectify the true ownership of the suit land. We acknowledge that in the realm of judicial proceedings related to land rights, where the plaintiff bears the weight of proof, the sanctity of RS records serves as an unwavering beacon of truth as cemented by the section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We also record, since the matter has been decided to the hilt as aforesaid, question of registration of solenama (Exhibit Cl) has become redundant.
